questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — overview; Environmental Social Governance framework; project management integration
questions.text: What does ESG stand for and why is it increasingly relevant to project management?

answers.text: ESG stands for Environmental, Social, and Governance — a framework that evaluates organizations (and projects) across three dimensions: environmental impact (carbon footprint, resource use), social impact (labor practices, diversity, community), and governance (ethics, transparency, compliance); projects increasingly must consider ESG factors because stakeholders, regulators, and investors expect organizations to operate responsibly beyond just financial returns
ESG stands for Enterprise Software Guidelines — technical standards for software development
ESG stands for Executive Steering Group — the committee that approves project charters
ESG is only relevant to publicly traded companies — private organizations and their projects are exempt

explanations.a: ESG FRAMEWORK IN PROJECT MANAGEMENT: ENVIRONMENTAL (E): how a project affects the natural environment; includes: carbon emissions from project activities; energy consumption; waste generated; resource depletion; ecological impact; GREEN IT considerations (data center energy, e-waste); SOCIAL (S): how a project affects people — employees, communities, and society; includes: diversity and inclusion in the project team; labor practices (fair wages, safe working conditions); community impact of the project deliverable; supply chain labor practices (ethical sourcing); employee well-being and work-life balance; GOVERNANCE (G): how a project is directed and controlled ethically; includes: transparency and honest reporting; regulatory compliance; anti-corruption and anti-bribery; data privacy and security; ethical decision-making; board-level oversight; WHY RELEVANT TO PMs: organizations now face ESG reporting requirements (EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, SEC climate disclosure rules); investors use ESG scores to make investment decisions; customers prefer organizations with strong ESG performance; regulatory penalties for ESG violations are increasing; project managers must account for ESG factors in project planning, risk assessment, and execution.
explanations.b: ESG is not a technical software standard. It is a sustainability and organizational responsibility framework originating in investment and corporate governance.
explanations.c: Executive Steering Group describes a governance committee — not the ESG acronym.
explanations.d: ESG increasingly applies to organizations of all types — public, private, government, and non-profit — as regulations expand and stakeholder expectations grow.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Environmental factors; carbon footprint; green IT; sustainability in projects
questions.text: A project manager is planning a large-scale data center upgrade. What ENVIRONMENTAL considerations should be part of the project planning?

answers.text: Environmental project considerations include: energy efficiency of new server hardware (Power Usage Effectiveness — PUE); renewable energy sourcing for the data center; heat waste and cooling system efficiency; e-waste disposal plan for decommissioned hardware; carbon offset options for unavoidable emissions; compliance with environmental regulations; embodied carbon in new hardware procurement
Environmental considerations are not a project manager's responsibility — only the facilities team handles environmental issues
Environmental factors only apply to construction projects — IT projects have no environmental footprint
Environmental considerations only affect the final product, not the project activities themselves

explanations.a: ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS for data center upgrade: ENERGY EFFICIENCY: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) = total data center energy / IT equipment energy; industry average PUE ≈ 1.57; hyperscaler efficiency ≈ 1.1-1.2; specify PUE targets for new hardware in the requirements; servers: choose Energy Star certified hardware; RENEWABLE ENERGY: can the data center be powered by renewable energy (solar, wind)? are Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) available? HEAT AND COOLING: hot aisle/cold aisle containment reduces cooling waste; free cooling (using outside air or water when temperature allows) reduces energy; waste heat recovery (using server heat for building heating). E-WASTE: where do decommissioned servers go?; responsible e-waste recycling certification (R2, e-Stewards); avoid sending e-waste to developing countries; CARBON FOOTPRINT: calculate the project's Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (electricity), and Scope 3 (supply chain) emissions; identify carbon offset opportunities; HARDWARE PROCUREMENT: ask vendors about their manufacturing emissions; consider refurbished or remanufactured equipment to reduce embodied carbon; REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: applicable environmental regulations for IT disposal and energy use.
explanations.b: Environmental considerations are part of comprehensive project planning in modern project management. The project manager is responsible for integrating all relevant considerations into the project plan, including ESG factors.
explanations.c: IT projects have significant environmental footprints: data centers account for approximately 1-2% of global electricity consumption; e-waste is the fastest-growing waste stream globally; manufacturing of servers and devices produces significant carbon emissions.
explanations.d: Environmental factors affect BOTH the project process (team travel, materials consumed, energy used during the project) AND the delivered product (the data center's ongoing energy consumption).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social factors; diversity and inclusion; labor practices; community impact
questions.text: What SOCIAL factors within the ESG framework are relevant to project management practice?

answers.text: Social factors in project management include: diversity and inclusion in team composition and hiring practices; fair labor practices for all team members and vendor staff; employee well-being (work-life balance, psychological safety, burnout prevention); community impact of the project deliverable; ethical sourcing in procurement; accessibility of the project deliverable for all users
Social factors only concern the marketing team — project managers focus on delivery metrics
Social factors only apply to human resources decisions, not project execution
Social factors are optional considerations that have no impact on project outcomes

explanations.a: SOCIAL FACTORS in project management: DIVERSITY AND INCLUSION (D&I): TEAM COMPOSITION: does the project team reflect diverse backgrounds, genders, ethnicities, and perspectives?; COGNITIVE DIVERSITY: teams with diverse thinking approaches solve problems more effectively; INCLUSIVE PRACTICES: are all team members heard in meetings?; is language and communication inclusive?; are accommodations provided for disabilities?; FAIR LABOR PRACTICES: internal team: fair compensation; reasonable working hours; no discriminatory practices; overtime managed appropriately; VENDOR LABOR: are vendors in the project's supply chain using fair labor practices?; no child labor, forced labor, or unsafe working conditions; EMPLOYEE WELLBEING: preventing burnout through sustainable workloads; psychological safety (team members can raise concerns without fear); mental health support awareness; COMMUNITY IMPACT: does the project deliverable positively or negatively affect the community?; example: a ride-sharing app project should consider gig worker rights; ACCESSIBILITY: project deliverables should be designed for accessibility (WCAG compliance for digital products); meeting ADA requirements; ETHICAL SOURCING: hardware procurement should consider whether suppliers use conflict minerals; RELEVANCE TO OUTCOMES: diverse teams make better decisions (McKinsey research consistently shows D&I correlates with financial performance); psychologically safe teams innovate more; unsustainable workloads produce quality problems and turnover.
explanations.b: Social factors are directly relevant to project management — the PM manages a team and makes procurement decisions that have social implications.
explanations.c: Social factors affect BOTH HR decisions AND project execution: how team members collaborate, how vendors are selected, how community members are affected.
explanations.d: Social factors have demonstrated impact on project outcomes: diverse teams have higher performance; sustainable workloads reduce defect rates; ethical sourcing reduces supply chain risk.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance factors; corporate governance; transparency; regulatory compliance; ethics
questions.text: What GOVERNANCE factors within the ESG framework should a project manager incorporate into project practices?

answers.text: Governance factors in project management include: transparent and accurate reporting (honest status reports without misleading spin); regulatory compliance (ensuring the project and its deliverables meet all applicable laws and regulations); data privacy and security (protecting personal data per GDPR, CCPA); anti-corruption and ethics (no bribery, no fraudulent billing, honest vendor evaluation); accountability (clear ownership and audit trails for decisions)
Governance only applies to board-level decisions — project managers are not involved in governance
Governance factors are only relevant for regulated industries — commercial software projects are exempt
Governance means ensuring every decision is approved by the board — daily project decisions don't involve governance

explanations.a: GOVERNANCE FACTORS in project management: TRANSPARENT REPORTING: accurate, honest status reporting even when news is bad (discussed throughout this course); no 'spin' or misleading framing of project performance; budget reporting accuracy; REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: ensuring project deliverables comply with applicable laws; examples: GDPR compliance for any project involving EU personal data; ADA/accessibility compliance for digital products; industry-specific regulations (HIPAA for healthcare, SOX for financial systems, FDA for pharmaceutical IT); failure to comply creates legal liability for the organization; DATA PRIVACY AND SECURITY: proper handling of personal data throughout the project; privacy-by-design principles incorporated into project requirements; security requirements built into architecture (not added at the end); ANTI-CORRUPTION AND ETHICS: no bribery in vendor selection (decisions based on merit, not gifts or kickbacks); honest disclosure of conflicts of interest; accurate expense reporting; whistleblower protection; ACCOUNTABILITY: audit trails for all significant decisions; clear chain of authority documented in project governance; ETHICS IN DECISION-MAKING: when facing ethical dilemmas, the PM uses established ethical frameworks (PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct: responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty).
explanations.b: Project managers implement governance within their project context. Board-level governance sets organizational standards; PMs implement those standards in daily project management.
explanations.c: Governance principles (transparency, compliance, ethics) apply to all projects. While regulated industries have specific requirements (HIPAA, SOX), basic governance principles of honest reporting and ethical conduct apply universally.
explanations.d: Governance operates at ALL levels — from board oversight down to daily project decisions. A PM who makes an honest status report is implementing governance. A PM who hides problems is violating governance principles.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Environmental; carbon footprint reduction; green IT practices; project environmental management
questions.text: A project manager is leading a 12-month cloud migration project for a financial services company. The company has committed to net-zero carbon by 2030. How should the PM integrate carbon footprint considerations into the project?

answers.text: Integrate carbon considerations throughout: specify cloud regions powered by renewable energy in the procurement requirements; select cloud instance types with the lowest carbon intensity for the workload; build carbon emissions tracking into the project success metrics alongside budget and schedule; evaluate whether cloud migration reduces or increases carbon vs. on-premises (typically reduces carbon due to hyperscaler efficiency); document carbon impact in the project closeout report
Carbon considerations are a post-project operational concern — the project team focuses only on delivery
Carbon footprint is only reduced by planting trees — technical project decisions don't affect carbon
The company's net-zero commitment is a corporate strategy issue irrelevant to individual project execution

explanations.a: CARBON INTEGRATION in cloud migration project: PROCUREMENT REQUIREMENTS (Planning Phase): specify in the SOW/RFP that the selected cloud provider must: use renewable energy for the target data center region; have publicly available carbon reporting; GCP, AWS, and Azure all offer regions with 100% renewable energy; this is a vendor evaluation criterion; TECHNICAL DESIGN (Architecture Phase): SELECT EFFICIENT INSTANCES: right-sizing instances (not over-provisioning) reduces energy waste; serverless and containerized architectures typically use resources more efficiently than always-on VMs; REGIONAL SELECTION: 'carbon-aware scheduling' — deploy workloads to regions with cleaner electricity grids; AWS's carbon footprint tool, GCP's Carbon Sense, Azure's Sustainability Calculator can identify lower-carbon options; ON-PREMISES vs. CLOUD COMPARISON: typically cloud migration REDUCES carbon (hyperscalers run at 1.1-1.2 PUE vs. typical enterprise data center 1.5-2.0 PUE); include this calculation in the business case as a co-benefit; SUCCESS METRICS: add 'projected annual carbon reduction (tonnes CO₂e)' as a project metric alongside budget and schedule; CLOSEOUT REPORT: document actual carbon reduction achieved; compare to baseline (on-premises) and estimate; contribute to the company's corporate carbon accounting.
explanations.b: Cloud migration decisions — which cloud provider, which regions, which instance types — have significant carbon implications. These are project-level decisions, not post-project operational ones.
explanations.c: Cloud provider selection, instance sizing, and regional deployment are all technical project decisions with direct, measurable carbon implications. These decisions collectively can reduce or increase carbon footprint by 30-60% for a cloud migration.
explanations.d: Corporate commitments (net-zero by 2030) are achieved through individual project decisions. Each project either contributes to or detracts from the corporate target. Treating the commitment as 'irrelevant to this project' creates a gap between corporate strategy and project execution.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; diversity and inclusion; team formation; inclusive project practices
questions.text: A project manager is assembling a team for a 9-month healthcare app development project. She wants to apply diversity and inclusion (D&I) principles to team formation and project execution. What specific practices should she implement?

answers.text: D&I practices in project team formation and execution: consider diverse candidate pools when requesting team members from functional managers; set inclusive meeting norms (language, time zones, and accessibility); ensure psychological safety (all team members' ideas are heard and valued); provide equitable opportunities (all team members get meaningful assignments, not just senior ones); be aware of unconscious bias in task assignment (ensure junior or underrepresented team members aren't always assigned support roles)
D&I only applies to corporate HR policies — individual project teams are assembled based purely on technical skills
D&I means ensuring all team members have identical assignments regardless of skill — equal work distribution
D&I only applies to gender diversity — other dimensions of diversity are not relevant to project teams

explanations.a: D&I PRACTICES in project team formation and execution: TEAM FORMATION: request team members from diverse talent pools when working with functional managers; if all available candidates are from the same demographic, flag this as a concern; avoid defaulting to 'people I know' (which perpetuates existing homogeneity); consider cognitive diversity — different thinking styles and backgrounds approach problem-solving differently (researchers consistently find that diverse teams produce better solutions for complex problems like healthcare app design); INCLUSIVE MEETING PRACTICES: time zone equity — don't always schedule meetings at times that are inconvenient for one office location; language accessibility — avoid jargon that creates barriers for non-native speakers; active inclusion — solicit input from quieter team members, not just the most vocal; PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY: team members should feel safe raising quality concerns, dissenting opinions, or admitting mistakes without fear of retaliation; the PM models this by acknowledging their own mistakes and encouraging candid feedback; EQUITABLE OPPORTUNITY: meaningful project roles and leadership opportunities should be distributed across team members, not concentrated among the most senior; ACCESSIBLE DELIVERABLES: the healthcare app should be designed with accessibility in mind from the start (WCAG compliance for users with visual, motor, or cognitive disabilities); UNCONSCIOUS BIAS AWARENESS: be conscious of patterns in task assignment; if all the visible/presentable work goes to some team members and all the hidden/support work goes to others, that's a bias pattern worth examining.
explanations.b: D&I principles apply at every level of organizational activity — including individual project teams. While formal D&I policies are set at the HR level, the PM implements them in daily team management.
explanations.c: D&I is not about identical assignments — it's about equitable opportunity, inclusive culture, and representation. Different people have different skills and appropriate different roles; D&I ensures those role distinctions are based on merit and skill, not demographic factors.
explanations.d: D&I encompasses many dimensions: gender, ethnicity/race, age, disability, sexual orientation, socioeconomic background, cognitive style, cultural background, religion, and more. All dimensions are relevant to project teams.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; regulatory compliance; compliance as a project requirement
questions.text: A project manager is implementing a new HR system for a company with employees in the EU and US. During planning, she identifies multiple regulatory frameworks that affect the project. What GOVERNANCE approach should she take to ensure regulatory compliance is built into the project?

answers.text: Integrate compliance requirements as project requirements from the start: identify all applicable regulations (GDPR for EU employees, CCPA for California employees, HIPAA if health data is involved, SOX if financial data is included); engage the legal and compliance team as project stakeholders; add compliance requirements to the requirements document; include compliance testing in the QA plan; build privacy-by-design into the architecture; schedule regulatory review as a project milestone
Compliance is the legal team's responsibility — the PM delivers the system and legal handles compliance after
Compliance requirements are added at go-live during the final testing phase — earlier is too speculative
Only the regulations the PM personally knows about need to be addressed — it's not the PM's job to research regulations

explanations.a: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE INTEGRATION in project planning: IDENTIFY ALL APPLICABLE REGULATIONS: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): applies to processing personal data of EU residents; requires: consent management; right to erasure; data minimization; privacy notices; data breach notification; DPA (Data Processing Agreement) with any third-party vendors; CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act): similar to GDPR for California residents; HIPAA: if the HR system captures health-related data (disability accommodations, medical leave); SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley): if HR data feeds financial controls (payroll, equity compensation); ENGAGE COMPLIANCE AS STAKEHOLDERS: add Data Protection Officer (DPO) or legal counsel to the stakeholder register; compliance requirements must come from people who understand the regulations; REQUIREMENTS INTEGRATION: GDPR-specific requirements: 'Users can request deletion of their personal data within 30 days'; 'Personal data is not retained beyond 7 years'; 'Data is encrypted in transit and at rest'; these go into the requirements document, not in a separate compliance document; PRIVACY-BY-DESIGN in architecture: data minimization (collect only what's needed); purpose limitation (use data only for its stated purpose); storage limitation (automated deletion after retention period); COMPLIANCE TESTING: specific test cases for each regulatory requirement; REGULATORY REVIEW MILESTONE: a phase gate where the legal/compliance team formally reviews and approves the design before development begins.
explanations.b: A PM who delivers a system without built-in compliance features leaves the organization with a non-compliant system that is expensive to retrofit. Compliance is NOT 'legal's problem after delivery' — it must be built into the project from the start.
explanations.c: Compliance requirements addressed at go-live testing produce: expensive architectural rework (encryption added late, data model redesigned); missed compliance requirements that testing reveals; potential go-live delays. Compliance built in during requirements costs dramatically less.
explanations.d: Not researching applicable regulations is negligence — the PM must identify and engage experts to determine what regulations apply. 'I didn't know' is not a defense against regulatory penalties.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; ethical sourcing; supply chain responsibility; vendor evaluation criteria
questions.text: A project manager is procuring hardware for a manufacturing IoT project. The procurement specifications include price and technical specifications. An ESG officer suggests adding ethical sourcing criteria to the vendor evaluation. What ethical sourcing criteria should be added and why are they relevant?

answers.text: Ethical sourcing only applies to food and clothing industries — electronics procurement is unaffected
Price is the only relevant criterion — ethical considerations drive up costs unnecessarily

Ethical sourcing criteria for electronics procurement: conflict mineral due diligence (Section 1502 of Dodd-Frank requires disclosure of conflict minerals — tin, tantalum, tungsten, gold — from conflict regions); vendor labor practices (no child labor, forced labor, or unsafe working conditions throughout the supply chain); environmental manufacturing practices (RoHS compliance — restriction of hazardous substances; recycling programs); corporate social responsibility certifications; these are relevant because electronics supply chains often involve regions with known labor and conflict issues
Ethical sourcing is enforced by governments — companies have no independent responsibility

explanations.a: Electronics supply chains are among the industries with the most significant ethical sourcing concerns: conflict minerals from the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighboring regions; labor conditions in manufacturing (Foxconn controversies); rare earth mining environmental impacts.
explanations.b: Ethical sourcing does create some cost premium — but the risk mitigation value (regulatory penalties, reputational damage) and the organizational values alignment justify it. Short-term cost savings from the cheapest unscrutinized supplier can create long-term liability.
explanations.c: ETHICAL SOURCING CRITERIA for electronics/IoT hardware: CONFLICT MINERALS (3TG — Tin, Tantalum, Tungsten, Gold): Dodd-Frank Section 1502 (US) and EU Conflict Minerals Regulation require disclosure and due diligence; these minerals are found in many electronic components (capacitors, circuit boards); some mining operations in conflict regions fund armed groups; VENDOR CRITERION: ask vendors to provide Conflict Minerals Reporting Template (CMRT); prefer vendors with Responsible Minerals Initiative (RMI) certification; LABOR PRACTICES IN SUPPLY CHAIN: ask vendors about their factory auditing programs; look for Social Accountability International (SA8000) certification or equivalents; no child labor (ILO Conventions); reasonable working hours (not forced excessive overtime); safe working conditions; ENVIRONMENTAL MANUFACTURING: RoHS Compliance: Restriction of Hazardous Substances (restricts lead, mercury, cadmium in electronics); WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) compliance for disposal; manufacturer take-back programs for end-of-life hardware; SUSTAINABILITY CERTIFICATIONS: EPEAT (Electronic Product Environmental Assessment Tool); Energy Star; ISO 14001 (environmental management system). WHY RELEVANT: organizations face reputational risk if their supply chain is linked to labor abuses or conflict funding; regulatory reporting requirements are expanding; investors score organizations on supply chain ESG performance; doing the right thing is an organizational value.
explanations.d: Voluntary corporate due diligence is both ethically required and increasingly legally required (EU Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, US Forced Labor Prevention Act for specific regions). Organizations cannot outsource ethical responsibility to governments.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; psychological safety; employee wellbeing; sustainable workloads
questions.text: A project is in a critical 3-month delivery phase. The PM notices the team is working consistently 60-hour weeks. A key developer says they're exhausted. The PM is tempted to continue the pace to 'push through' to delivery. What SOCIAL ESG considerations should inform the PM's decision?

answers.text: The PM should maintain the 60-hour weeks — delivery commitments override employee wellbeing
The developer's complaint should be ignored — professional project team members accept whatever hours are required

Social ESG considerations support reducing the unsustainable pace: employee wellbeing is a social responsibility dimension; sustained overwork produces diminishing quality returns, increases defect rates, and increases burnout/attrition risk; alternative approaches (scope reduction, timeline extension, additional resources) should be explored before accepting team burnout as the solution
Wellbeing concerns are HR's responsibility — the project manager should not get involved

explanations.a: Research consistently shows that sustained 60-hour weeks produce diminishing productivity and increasing defect rates within 3-4 weeks. 'Pushing through' to delivery on an unsustainable schedule typically produces: lower quality deliverables (tired workers make more mistakes); burnout and potential resignations mid-project (worst possible timing); health impacts for team members; these create project risks, not solutions.
explanations.b: 'Professional team members accept whatever hours are required' is a toxic mindset that creates the burnout culture that harms individuals and organizations. Professionalism includes raising unsustainable workload concerns through appropriate channels.
explanations.c: SOCIAL ESG AND EMPLOYEE WELLBEING: DIRECT SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY: employee wellbeing is explicitly a Social ESG factor; organizations that systematically overwork employees are failing on the social dimension of ESG; the PM who enables or mandates unsustainable hours is contributing to this failure; PRODUCTIVITY RESEARCH: 'crunch culture' data shows: productivity peaks at approximately 50 hours per week; beyond 55 hours, productivity per hour DECREASES; after 3-4 weeks of 60+ hours, cumulative output of 60 hours = roughly same as 50 hours (diminishing returns); defect rates increase 15-20% in the fourth week of crunch; ALTERNATIVE APPROACHES (the PM should evaluate): SCOPE REDUCTION: can low-priority features be deferred to Phase 2?; TIMELINE EXTENSION: can the delivery date be extended by 2-4 weeks? (often less costly than burnout-induced quality failures); ADDITIONAL RESOURCES: can a contractor be temporarily added to relieve the critical path bottleneck?; SCOPE NEGOTIATION: can the stakeholder accept a reduced MVP at the original date?; PM RESPONSIBILITY: the PM is not just a deliverer of features — they are responsible for the team's sustainable operation; raising this concern with the sponsor ('we can hit the date but the current pace is unsustainable — here are the options') is professional project management.
explanations.d: The project manager is DIRECTLY responsible for the team's workload — it is precisely their responsibility to manage the team in a sustainable manner and escalate when the workload becomes unsustainable.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; transparency; honest reporting; anti-corruption in project management
questions.text: A project manager discovers that a vendor selection decision was influenced by a personal relationship between the evaluation committee chair and the winning vendor's sales director (the chair received free sports tickets). This is a conflict of interest that was not disclosed. What GOVERNANCE ESG obligations arise and what should the PM do?

answers.text: Ignore it — the winning vendor technically met all the evaluation criteria
Confront the committee chair privately — personal resolution is more appropriate than formal reporting

This is a conflict of interest and potential corruption issue requiring escalation: the PM should document the concern; report it through the organization's ethics reporting channel (or to the legal/compliance department); the concern must be investigated to determine whether the vendor selection was fair; if the selection was compromised, the procurement may need to be reconsidered — the governance ESG principle of fair, transparent decision-making was violated
Mention it casually at the next team meeting — informal awareness is sufficient for governance issues

explanations.a: Ignoring a conflict of interest because 'the vendor met the criteria' enables the misconduct. Even if the vendor was genuinely the best choice, an undisclosed conflict of interest compromises the integrity of the decision-making process and must be investigated.
explanations.b: Private confrontation is inappropriate because: it places the PM in direct conflict with a more senior person without organizational backing; it may be perceived as a threat; it doesn't create a documented record; formal channels protect both the reporter and ensure proper investigation.
explanations.c: GOVERNANCE ESG — CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND ANTI-CORRUPTION: WHAT HAPPENED: vendor selection committee chair received gifts (sports tickets) from a vendor bidder; the chair did not disclose this relationship; this is a CONFLICT OF INTEREST — the chair had a personal interest that may have influenced their evaluation; depending on jurisdiction and organization policy, this may also constitute BRIBERY (vendor provided value to influence a public official or corporate decision-maker). GOVERNANCE ESG OBLIGATIONS: ANTI-CORRUPTION: ESG governance requires honest, unbiased decision-making; personal gifts influencing procurement decisions corrupt this principle; TRANSPARENCY: the decision-making process should be transparent — undisclosed relationships undermine this; FAIRNESS: all vendors must compete on a level playing field — personal relationships create unfair advantages. PM OBLIGATIONS: PMI Code of Ethics requires PMs to report unethical behavior through appropriate channels; DOCUMENT: record what was observed and when; REPORT: use the organization's ethics hotline, compliance department, or ombudsperson; do NOT report to the committee chair directly (they are the subject); ESCALATION: if internal reporting channels are compromised, external reporting (board audit committee, regulatory authority) may be appropriate; INVESTIGATION: the organization should investigate whether the selection was influenced; potentially re-run the procurement with the chair recused; PROTECTION: whistleblower protection laws protect employees who report in good faith.
explanations.d: 'Mentioning it casually' doesn't trigger a formal investigation, doesn't protect the organization from liability, and doesn't fulfill the PM's ethical reporting obligation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG integration in business cases; project selection; ESG as decision criterion
questions.text: An organization is reviewing two competing project proposals for the same budget: Project Alpha (new marketing automation platform, expected ROI 180%); Project Beta (employee well-being digital health platform, expected ROI 95% but significantly improves employee mental health and engagement scores). Using an ESG lens, how should the organization evaluate these projects?

answers.text: Select Project Alpha — ROI is always the primary selection criterion and higher ROI wins
Select Beta — ESG always overrides financial considerations in project selection

An ESG-informed evaluation considers multiple dimensions: Alpha has higher financial ROI but only serves business efficiency; Beta has lower financial ROI but contributes to Social ESG (employee wellbeing, mental health, engagement) which may reduce turnover costs (replacing an employee costs 50-200% of annual salary), reduce absenteeism, and increase productivity — when these are quantified, Beta's total value may exceed Alpha's
ESG considerations only apply after a project is selected — they should not influence project selection decisions

explanations.a: ROI-only project selection ignores significant organizational value dimensions. The 'true' ROI of Beta may be higher than it appears when all social value is quantified.
explanations.b: ESG considerations INFORM project selection but don't automatically override financial considerations. Projects must still demonstrate sufficient financial return — ESG is an additional value dimension, not a replacement for financial analysis.
explanations.c: ESG-INFORMED PROJECT EVALUATION: ALPHA (Marketing Automation, ROI 180%): FINANCIAL VALUE: strong (180% ROI on direct marketing efficiency gains); ESG DIMENSION: limited — primarily a business efficiency tool; governance benefit from better marketing data quality; TOTAL VALUE: primarily financial; BETA (Employee Well-Being Platform, ROI 95%): FINANCIAL VALUE: 95% direct ROI; SOCIAL ESG VALUE (quantifiable): TURNOVER REDUCTION: if Beta reduces voluntary turnover by 5% (typical effect of well-being programs), and average replacement cost is $50K/employee: 500 employees × 5% turnover reduction × $50K = $1.25M in saved hiring costs annually; ABSENTEEISM REDUCTION: well-being programs typically reduce sick days by 1-2 days per employee annually; PRODUCTIVITY: engagement improvement has measurable productivity correlation; RECRUITMENT: organizations with strong ESG social programs attract talent more easily (important in tight labor markets); ADJUSTED TOTAL VALUE: when these social benefits are monetized, Beta's 'true' ROI may be 150-200%; GOVERNANCE BENEFIT: demonstrates organizational values alignment; SELECTION FRAMEWORK: both financial ROI and ESG value should be evaluated; QUANTIFY ESG VALUE where possible (the approach above); CONSIDER STRATEGIC ALIGNMENT: does the project advance the organization's stated ESG commitments?; CONSIDER ORGANIZATIONAL RISK: ignoring employee wellbeing in a burnout-prone industry is a talent retention risk.
explanations.d: ESG considerations are increasingly part of organizational strategic planning and project selection criteria. Investors, employees, and customers evaluate organizations on their ESG performance, making it relevant to project portfolio decisions.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; data privacy; privacy by design; GDPR compliance in projects
questions.text: A project team is building a customer data analytics platform that will process EU customer data. The GDPR applies. What PRIVACY BY DESIGN principles should the project manager ensure are incorporated into the project requirements and architecture?

answers.text: GDPR compliance is achieved by adding a privacy policy page at launch — no architectural changes are needed
GDPR only applies to European companies — companies outside the EU can process EU data without restrictions

Privacy by design principles for the analytics platform: proactive privacy protection (not reactive); privacy as the default setting (minimum data collection); privacy embedded into the architecture (not bolted on later); full lifecycle protection (data minimized, retained only as long as needed, securely deleted when no longer required); user control over their own data (access, rectification, deletion); transparency (clear disclosure of data use)
Privacy is the security team's responsibility — the project team only implements business features

explanations.a: A privacy policy page is a notification requirement — but GDPR compliance requires much more: data minimization in the database design; purpose limitation in how data is used; technical controls for data subject rights (access, deletion); consent management systems; breach notification procedures. These are architectural requirements, not afterthoughts.
explanations.b: GDPR applies to processing of EU residents' personal data REGARDLESS of where the processing organization is located. A US company processing EU customer data is fully subject to GDPR.
explanations.c: PRIVACY BY DESIGN PRINCIPLES (Ann Cavoukian's 7 Foundational Principles, adopted by GDPR): (1) PROACTIVE, NOT REACTIVE: anticipate and prevent privacy risks BEFORE they occur; in project context: involve the Data Protection Officer from the start; conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before architecture is finalized; (2) PRIVACY AS DEFAULT: default settings should protect maximum privacy; users should not need to take action to protect their privacy; in project context: analytics platform default: no data collected unless user explicitly opts in; data retention default: minimum retention period; (3) PRIVACY EMBEDDED INTO DESIGN: privacy is a core architectural element, not an add-on; in project context: data minimization in the database schema (only collect fields actually needed for the analysis purpose); separate databases for personally identifiable information (PII) vs. anonymized analytics data; (4) FULL FUNCTIONALITY (NOT ZERO-SUM): privacy AND functionality can coexist; security is not achieved by removing features — design for both; (5) END-TO-END SECURITY: protect all personal data throughout its lifecycle — collection, storage, processing, and deletion; in project context: encryption at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3); secure deletion procedures; (6) VISIBILITY AND TRANSPARENCY: processing activities documented; users informed of data use; in project context: privacy notices; data processing records; (7) RESPECT FOR USER PRIVACY: user-centric design; data subject rights: access to their data; right to rectification; right to erasure ('right to be forgotten').
explanations.d: Privacy is a project-wide responsibility: the project manager ensures privacy requirements are in the requirements document; architects design privacy-preserving solutions; developers implement them; the security team validates. The entire project team implements privacy, not just security.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG reporting; project contribution to ESG metrics; closeout ESG documentation
questions.text: An organization reports ESG metrics annually to investors and regulators. The project manager's project (a manufacturing process automation project) is expected to contribute to the organization's ESG metrics. How should the PM capture and report the project's ESG contribution?

answers.text: ESG reporting is the sustainability team's responsibility — the PM delivers the project and others report ESG
ESG metrics are captured only at project closure — baseline data is unnecessary

The PM should plan for ESG metric capture from the start: identify in the planning phase which ESG metrics the project will affect (energy reduction, waste reduction, employee safety improvement, efficiency gains); establish baselines before the project begins; track project-specific ESG contributions throughout execution; document ESG outcomes in the closeout report; provide data to the sustainability team for inclusion in the annual ESG report
The project's financial ROI subsumes all ESG contributions — no separate ESG metric tracking is needed

explanations.a: The sustainability team needs data to compile the ESG report — that data comes from projects. Without PM cooperation in tracking and reporting ESG contributions, the organization cannot substantiate its ESG claims.
explanations.b: Without baselines, there is nothing to compare post-project performance to. A 'we reduced energy by 30%' claim requires knowing what the baseline was. Baseline measurement must happen before the project changes the process.
explanations.c: ESG METRIC CAPTURE in manufacturing process automation project: PLANNING PHASE — IDENTIFY RELEVANT ESG METRICS: ENVIRONMENTAL: energy consumption of the automated process vs. manual process (kWh/unit); waste generated per production run (material waste reduction); CO₂e emissions from manufacturing (if energy mix is known); SOCIAL: employee safety incidents (automation typically reduces human exposure to hazardous conditions); worker redeployment (are workers retrained for higher-skill roles vs. displaced?); ergonomic improvements (reduced repetitive strain injuries); GOVERNANCE: quality control transparency (automated systems produce auditable quality records); ESTABLISH BASELINES: before the project begins, measure CURRENT state of each metric; without a baseline, post-project improvement cannot be calculated; example: current energy consumption = 450 kWh/unit; current safety incidents = 12/year; PRE-LAUNCH MEASUREMENT: after project implementation but before operational period, validate systems are ready to capture metrics; POST-IMPLEMENTATION TRACKING: the first 6-12 months of operation provide the actual ESG performance data; the PM should establish what data will be captured and by whom; CLOSEOUT REPORT ESG SECTION: 'Project ESG Outcomes': Energy reduction: 450 → 310 kWh/unit (−31%); Safety incidents: 12 → 3/year (−75%); Annual CO₂e reduction: 240 tonnes; PROVIDE TO SUSTAINABILITY TEAM: the project closeout report's ESG section feeds the annual ESG disclosure.
explanations.d: Financial ROI measures economic value — ESG metrics measure a broader set of impacts that financial metrics don't capture. An investor reading a sustainability report needs specific ESG data, not a financial ROI number.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; vendor ESG assessment; supply chain ESG risk
questions.text: A project manager is evaluating two software development vendors for a 2-year engagement. Both vendors meet all technical and commercial criteria. Vendor A has a strong ESG program (diverse workforce at 45% women in tech, carbon-neutral operations, transparent pay equity reports). Vendor B has no ESG disclosures and recent news reports allege unfair labor practices. How should ESG factors inform the vendor selection?

answers.text: Select Vendor B — price and technical capability are the only relevant selection criteria
Vendor B's labor practices are their business — the client company has no responsibility for vendor HR policies

Vendor B's lack of ESG disclosure AND alleged unfair labor practices represent significant governance and social risks: supply chain labor practices are an ESG concern for the client organization; organizations can face reputational risk if their vendors are linked to labor abuses; Vendor A's ESG strengths (diverse team, carbon neutrality) align with modern organizational values and regulatory trends; ESG-conscious vendor selection is good governance; recommend Vendor A unless Vendor B can demonstrate credible remediation
Ask both vendors to submit ESG reports and then ignore them — compliance theater satisfies governance requirements

explanations.a: Technical capability and price are necessary but not sufficient for responsible vendor selection in modern project management. Supply chain ESG risks can become the client organization's risks.
explanations.b: Supply chain due diligence is an increasingly recognized legal and ethical obligation. The UK Modern Slavery Act, US Forced Labor Prevention Act, and EU Supply Chain Due Diligence Act all create obligations for organizations regarding their vendors' labor practices.
explanations.c: ESG-INFORMED VENDOR SELECTION: VENDOR B RISKS — SOCIAL ESG: LABOR PRACTICES ALLEGATIONS: if true, Vendor B is violating social ESG standards; the client organization could be seen as enabling these practices by engaging the vendor; REPUTATIONAL RISK: if press stories about Vendor B's labor practices escalate, the client may be associated with the controversy; NO ESG DISCLOSURE: a vendor with no ESG disclosures is either: not measuring their ESG performance (poor governance); or measuring it and not disclosing it (suggesting poor results); EU Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (effective 2024+) requires larger companies to conduct ESG due diligence on their suppliers — this regulatory trend is expanding. VENDOR A ADVANTAGES — ESG: DIVERSE WORKFORCE: 45% women in tech is above industry average (~28%); research shows diverse software teams produce better code and have lower defect rates; CARBON NEUTRAL: aligns with client's own carbon commitments (if any); TRANSPARENT PAY EQUITY: indicator of good governance and ethical culture. VENDOR SELECTION RECOMMENDATION: add ESG evaluation criteria to the vendor scoring matrix; if both vendors are technically and commercially equivalent, Vendor A's ESG advantage is a clear differentiator; if Vendor B offers significantly lower price, present the ESG risk to the sponsor and make an informed decision with full information. VENDOR B DUE DILIGENCE: before ruling out Vendor B, the PM could request a formal response to the labor practice allegations — a credible remediation plan with documented changes might address the concern.
explanations.d: Collecting ESG reports while having no intention of acting on them is greenwashing — it creates false appearances of ESG compliance without actual ESG consideration. Responsible governance means using the information collected.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; accessibility; inclusive design; universal design principles
questions.text: A project team is developing a citizen-facing government digital services portal. The project manager wants to ensure the portal is accessible to all citizens, including those with disabilities. How should accessibility be built into the project?

answers.text: Accessibility is added after launch based on user complaints — it's too speculative to address upfront
Accessibility is the UI team's sole responsibility — other project roles are not involved
Accessibility only matters for users with severe disabilities — average users are not affected by inaccessibility

Accessibility should be built in from the requirements phase: include WCAG 2.1 AA compliance as a requirements standard; add accessibility testing to the QA plan; engage users with disabilities in user testing; ensure accessibility is a gate criterion for go-live; train developers on accessible coding practices; this is both a social ESG obligation (ensuring equal access) and often a legal requirement (ADA, UK Equality Act, Section 508)

explanations.a: Retrofitting accessibility after launch is 10-20× more expensive than designing for it from the start. Accessibility complaints after launch also mean citizens who needed access were denied it during the interim period — an equity failure.
explanations.b: Accessibility requires involvement from: PMs (include in requirements and QA plan); architects (semantic HTML structure, ARIA patterns); developers (implementation); designers (color contrast, visual hierarchy); testers (automated + manual testing); it is a cross-functional responsibility.
explanations.c: Approximately 15% of the world's population has some form of disability. Beyond disability, accessibility benefits: people using mobile devices in bright sunlight (high contrast); non-native language speakers (clear language); elderly users (larger text, simple navigation); everyone benefits from good accessibility design.
explanations.d: ACCESSIBILITY INTEGRATION in government portal: REQUIREMENTS PHASE: include in the requirements document: 'All pages must comply with WCAG 2.1 Level AA'; 'Assistive technology compatibility: JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver'; 'Color contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 for normal text'; 'All form fields have descriptive labels'; 'All images have meaningful alt text'; 'All functionality available via keyboard (no mouse-only interactions)'; WCAG 2.1 PRINCIPLES (POUR): Perceivable (content can be perceived by all users); Operable (interface can be operated by all users); Understandable (content is understandable); Robust (compatible with assistive technologies); DEVELOPMENT: provide accessibility training to developers before coding begins (how to write semantic HTML, ARIA attributes); use accessibility-aware component libraries; TESTING: automated accessibility testing tools (axe, WAVE) as part of CI/CD; manual testing with screen readers; INCLUSIVE USER TESTING: recruit test participants who use assistive technologies; their feedback reveals real-world barriers that automated tools miss; QA PLAN: accessibility test cases for all user journeys; specific test for keyboard navigation; color contrast verification; screen reader compatibility; GO-LIVE GATE CRITERION: 0 WCAG AA violations for critical user journeys; LEGAL CONTEXT: US Section 508 (federal government); ADA Title III (public accommodation); EU Web Accessibility Directive (public sector websites); UK Equality Act.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG risks in risk register; regulatory ESG risk; reputational ESG risk
questions.text: A project manager is developing the risk register for a large infrastructure project. An ESG consultant suggests adding ESG-specific risks. What categories of ESG risk should the PM consider adding to the risk register?

answers.text: ESG risks are not project risks — they belong in a separate sustainability document
ESG risks are always low probability — they don't need formal risk register entries
Only financial ESG risks should be in the risk register — social and environmental risks are intangible

ESG risk categories for the risk register: Environmental risks (regulatory environmental compliance failure, environmental incident during construction, carbon pricing policy changes affecting project economics); Social risks (labor dispute, community opposition, reputational damage from labor practices, diversity-related legal action); Governance risks (regulatory compliance failure, data breach, conflict of interest, anti-corruption violation, board scrutiny of ESG performance)

explanations.a: ESG risks are PROJECT risks — they can affect the project's schedule, budget, scope, and reputation. A risk that results in a regulatory shutdown is a project risk of the highest severity.
explanations.b: Some ESG risks have significant probability: data breaches affect 1 in 5 organizations annually (not low probability); regulatory compliance failures for organizations new to GDPR have common occurrence; community opposition to infrastructure projects is a frequent project risk.
explanations.c: Social and environmental ESG risks have measurable, tangible financial impacts: a regulatory shutdown costs lost revenue per day; a labor dispute costs schedule delay × daily project cost; a data breach costs an average $4.45M (IBM 2023 Cost of Data Breach Report). These are concrete financial risks, not intangible concerns.
explanations.d: ESG RISK CATEGORIES in project risk register: ENVIRONMENTAL RISKS: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: probability that project activities violate environmental regulations (e.g., unauthorized construction near wetlands); impact: regulatory shutdown, fines, remediation costs; mitigation: environmental impact assessment before construction begins; ENVIRONMENTAL INCIDENT: accidental spill, contamination, or habitat disturbance; impact: regulatory action, remediation cost, reputational damage; mitigation: environmental management plan, incident response plan; CARBON PRICING: if a carbon tax is enacted or increases during the project, energy-intensive project activities become more expensive; mitigation: hedge with renewable energy contracts. SOCIAL RISKS: LABOR DISPUTE: contractors' workers go on strike due to unfair labor practices; impact: schedule delays, cost overruns; mitigation: ensure contractor labor practices compliance; include labor dispute contingency in schedule; COMMUNITY OPPOSITION: community groups oppose the project (noise, disruption, perceived inequitable impacts); impact: delays, regulatory scrutiny, reputational damage; mitigation: proactive community engagement, transparent communication; REPUTATIONAL RISK: press coverage of a labor incident at a project vendor; impact: client dissatisfaction, business loss; mitigation: vendor labor practice due diligence. GOVERNANCE RISKS: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE FAILURE: project deliverable found non-compliant post-launch (GDPR violation, ADA non-compliance); impact: fines, remediation, reputational damage; DATA BREACH: personal data handled during the project is breached; impact: regulatory penalty, litigation; CONFLICT OF INTEREST: undisclosed vendor relationship influences procurement; impact: procurement re-do, legal liability.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG as project success dimension; beyond triple constraint; sustainable project outcomes
questions.text: Traditional project management defines success through the triple constraint (scope, schedule, cost). An ESG officer suggests expanding the definition of project success to include ESG outcomes. What would expanded ESG success criteria look like for a new manufacturing facility project?

answers.text: ESG success criteria dilute the real measures of project success — stick to scope, schedule, cost
ESG success is binary — the project either passes or fails ESG, with no middle ground or measurement
ESG criteria can only be measured after the project is 5 years into operations — they're not project success metrics

ESG-expanded success criteria for a manufacturing facility: Environmental — facility achieves LEED Gold certification; energy use intensity 25% below industry average; zero on-site hazardous waste to landfill. Social — zero workplace safety incidents during construction; 30% of construction jobs filled from local community; facility designed to WCAG standards for employee management systems. Governance — all permits obtained with full regulatory compliance; no instances of bribery in contractor selection; conflict of interest disclosures made and reviewed for all key procurement decisions

explanations.a: ESG success criteria don't dilute traditional success — they expand the definition to capture dimensions that matter to stakeholders, communities, investors, and regulators. A facility built on time, on budget, and to scope that causes environmental damage or was built with bribery is not truly 'successful.'
explanations.b: ESG success is measured on a continuum — LEED certification has specific point thresholds (Silver: 50-59 points, Gold: 60-79 points, Platinum: 80+); safety incidents are counted; local hiring percentages are calculated. ESG success is measurable and specific, not binary.
explanations.c: Some ESG criteria ARE measurable at project close: LEED certification is awarded before or at occupancy; construction safety incidents are tracked throughout the project; regulatory permits are obtained before the project proceeds. Operational ESG metrics (ongoing energy performance) are post-project, but design ESG metrics are project-phase outcomes.
explanations.d: ESG-EXPANDED SUCCESS CRITERIA for manufacturing facility: TRADITIONAL TRIPLE CONSTRAINT (retained): scope: all facility capabilities delivered per specifications; schedule: facility operational by the committed date; cost: total project cost within authorized budget. ENVIRONMENTAL SUCCESS CRITERIA: LEED CERTIFICATION: building energy and environmental performance standard; Gold or Platinum certification signals environmental quality; ENERGY PERFORMANCE: energy use intensity (kWh/m²/year) vs. industry benchmarks; renewable energy percentage; WASTE: construction waste diverted from landfill; ongoing operational waste management plan; WATER: water efficiency measures; stormwater management; SOCIAL SUCCESS CRITERIA: SAFETY: zero lost-time incidents during construction (measured throughout the project, not just at end); COMMUNITY BENEFIT: local hiring percentage; community investment (local suppliers, training programs); WORKER WELFARE: wages paid to construction workers; working hours compliance; GOVERNANCE SUCCESS CRITERIA: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: all environmental permits obtained; no regulatory violations during construction; PROCUREMENT INTEGRITY: documented clean procurement process; no conflicts of interest; MEASUREMENT FRAMEWORK: each criterion is measured at project close AND through an agreed post-occupancy period (typically 12 months); the project closeout report documents both traditional and ESG performance.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — all three dimensions integrated; ESG in project lifecycle; systemic ESG approach
questions.text: A PMO director wants to integrate ESG considerations into the organization's standard project management methodology. She asks the PM to design an ESG integration framework covering all three dimensions across the project lifecycle. Describe the key ESG integration points for each phase.

answers.text: ESG integration is a post-project activity — it doesn't fit within project lifecycle phases
ESG integration means creating separate parallel documentation — it should not change core project documents
ESG only needs to be addressed in one phase — doing it everywhere creates bureaucratic overhead

ESG integration by phase: Discovery (ESG in business case — quantify environmental/social/governance benefits alongside financial ROI); Initiation (ESG stakeholder identification, ESG constraints in charter); Planning (ESG requirements, ESG in risk register, ESG in vendor evaluation criteria, ESG in success metrics); Execution (ESG monitoring in status reports, ethical decision-making, sustainable workloads); Closing (ESG outcomes in closeout report, ESG lessons learned, ESG data for corporate reporting)

explanations.a: ESG considerations are most effective when integrated throughout the project lifecycle — reactive ESG management (addressing ESG issues after they occur) is far more expensive than proactive ESG integration.
explanations.b: ESG integration should ENRICH existing project documents: the business case gets ESG value quantification; the risk register gets ESG risks; the requirements document gets ESG requirements; the closeout report gets ESG outcomes. Creating parallel shadow documentation creates administrative overhead without governance value.
explanations.c: ESG risks and impacts occur at every phase: environmental impacts start in planning (vendor selection) and continue through construction and operation; social impacts manifest from team formation through execution; governance risks arise from the first stakeholder interaction. Phase-specific ESG integration is necessary.
explanations.d: ESG LIFECYCLE INTEGRATION FRAMEWORK: DISCOVERY / CONCEPT PHASE: BUSINESS CASE: include ESG value in the ROI calculation (carbon reduction monetized; turnover reduction from employee wellbeing; regulatory risk reduction from compliance investment); add ESG opportunity statement: 'This project reduces carbon emissions by 240 tonnes annually (monetized at $50/tonne = $12K/year co-benefit)'; ESG RISK IDENTIFICATION: initial scan for environmental, social, and governance risks early in the project concept. INITIATION PHASE: ESG STAKEHOLDER IDENTIFICATION: identify ESG-relevant stakeholders (ESG officer, DPO, community representatives, sustainability team); CHARTER CONSTRAINTS: document ESG constraints: 'Project must comply with GDPR'; 'Project must meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards'; 'Vendor selection must include ESG evaluation criteria'. PLANNING PHASE: ESG REQUIREMENTS: integrate ESG requirements into the requirements document alongside functional requirements; ESG IN RISK REGISTER: add environmental, social, and governance risks with probability, impact, and mitigation; ESG VENDOR CRITERIA: add ESG criteria to vendor evaluation scorecards (labor practices, environmental certifications, diversity); ESG SUCCESS METRICS: establish ESG KPIs alongside schedule and budget KPIs. EXECUTION PHASE: ESG STATUS MONITORING: ESG KPIs tracked in status reports (energy metrics, safety incidents, compliance milestone status); ETHICAL DECISION-MAKING: apply governance ESG principles to all vendor and procurement decisions; SUSTAINABLE WORKLOADS: monitor team workload sustainability (social ESG); ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT: implement environmental management plan (waste, energy during project activities). CLOSING PHASE: ESG CLOSEOUT REPORT SECTION: document actual ESG outcomes vs. targets; LESSONS LEARNED: ESG-specific lessons; CORPORATE ESG REPORTING: provide data to sustainability team for annual ESG disclosure; KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT: file ESG approach for future project reference.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Environmental; green IT; sustainable technology choices; right-sizing
questions.text: A project manager is making infrastructure decisions for a new analytics platform. She wants to apply Green IT principles to minimize the environmental footprint. What specific Green IT decisions can she influence?

answers.text: Green IT is only about recycling old computers — new infrastructure projects are not affected
The cheapest infrastructure option is always the most sustainable — cost and sustainability always align
Green IT only matters for the operating company — project teams have no responsibility for environmental impact

Green IT decisions include: right-sizing cloud instances (avoid over-provisioning); choosing cloud regions powered by renewable energy; implementing auto-scaling to prevent idle resource waste; selecting energy-efficient database and compute options; optimizing queries and code to reduce compute time; considering lifecycle carbon of hardware in procurement; implementing efficient data tiering (hot/warm/cold storage) to reduce unnecessary active storage

explanations.a: Green IT encompasses the full lifecycle of technology: manufacturing, deployment, operations, and disposal. New infrastructure decisions are among the highest-impact environmental choices a PM can make.
explanations.b: Cost and sustainability sometimes align (right-sizing reduces both cost and energy) but sometimes conflict (renewable energy regions may cost slightly more; quality hardware may cost more upfront but lasts longer). The PM must evaluate both dimensions, not assume they always align.
explanations.c: The project team makes the infrastructure choices that determine operating energy consumption for years. Project decisions (which region, which instance type, auto-scaling policy) determine whether the system consumes 100 kWh/month or 400 kWh/month.
explanations.d: GREEN IT DECISIONS for analytics platform: RIGHT-SIZING: over-provisioned servers waste energy (idle CPU still consumes 40-70% of peak power); right-size based on actual workload analysis (not 'we might need it'); use performance monitoring to down-size over-provisioned instances; RENEWABLE ENERGY REGIONS: AWS us-east-1 (Virginia): powered significantly by renewable energy; AWS eu-west-1 (Ireland): 100% renewable energy committed; Google Cloud: carbon-neutral since 2007; all regions carbon-free by 2030; Azure: 100% renewable energy committed; SELECT THE CLOUD REGION WITH THE CLEANEST ENERGY GRID for the target workload; AUTO-SCALING: shut down or scale down resources when workloads are low (nights, weekends for internal analytics); prevents 24/7 compute for 8-hour/day actual use; ENERGY-EFFICIENT COMPUTE: ARM-based instances (AWS Graviton, Google Tau) provide 20-40% better energy efficiency than x86 for many workloads; serverless computing (Lambda, Cloud Functions) scales to zero when not in use; QUERY AND CODE OPTIMIZATION: inefficient database queries consume more compute time → more energy; investing in query optimization has both performance AND environmental benefits; DATA TIERING: hot data (frequently accessed) in fast, expensive storage; warm data in lower-power storage; cold data (rarely accessed, e.g., backups) in tape or archive storage (significantly lower energy than SSD/HDD); HARDWARE LIFECYCLE: specify minimum 5-year hardware lifecycles in procurement (manufacturing is the biggest carbon source for many devices); consider refurbished/remanufactured equipment.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; ethics; PMI Code of Ethics; whistleblower; ethical reporting
questions.text: A junior project team member tells the PM privately: 'I've noticed our software is collecting more user data than the privacy policy discloses. I'm worried this is a GDPR violation, but I'm scared to report it because the CTO approved the current design.' What should the PM do and what PMI ethical obligations are relevant?

answers.text: Tell the junior team member to stay quiet — challenging the CTO's decision is career-damaging
Escalate directly to the press — public disclosure is the appropriate first step for governance violations
Dismiss the concern — the CTO's approval makes the design acceptable regardless of regulatory compliance

Thank the team member for raising the concern; validate that this could be a serious governance issue (GDPR violation); investigate whether the data collection is truly undisclosed; if confirmed, escalate through appropriate channels (legal/compliance/DPO) regardless of who approved the design; protect the team member from retaliation by following formal ethics channels — the PMI Code of Ethics requires reporting ethical violations

explanations.a: Telling a team member to suppress a potential regulatory violation is itself an ethical violation. The PM's duty extends to supporting ethical reporting through proper channels.
explanations.b: Press disclosure before exhausting internal channels is generally inappropriate (and may be legally problematic in some jurisdictions). Internal reporting (ethics hotline, compliance, board) is the appropriate first step; regulatory body reporting is the next step if internal channels fail.
explanations.c: CTO approval is an internal governance decision — it does not override GDPR requirements. A design that violates GDPR is non-compliant regardless of who internally approved it. The organization faces regulatory liability regardless of the internal approval chain.
explanations.d: PMI CODE OF ETHICS AND ESG GOVERNANCE INTEGRATION: PMI CODE OF ETHICS — RELEVANT PRINCIPLES: RESPONSIBILITY: 'We take ownership of our decisions and their consequences, including maintaining ethical conduct even when it is difficult.'; HONESTY: 'We do not engage in or condone behaviors that are designed to deceive others.'; FAIRNESS: 'We make decisions and act impartially and objectively, without favoritism or prejudice.'; PMI explicitly states PMs must report unethical behavior through appropriate channels. PM ACTIONS: ACKNOWLEDGE AND VALIDATE: tell the team member: 'Thank you for bringing this to me. This is exactly the kind of concern that should be raised. I'll investigate and make sure it goes through the right channels.'; INVESTIGATE: review the actual data collection code vs. the privacy policy disclosure; is the collection genuinely undisclosed?; CONFIRM WITH LEGAL/COMPLIANCE: involve the Data Protection Officer or legal counsel immediately; ESCALATE THROUGH APPROPRIATE CHANNELS: compliance department; DPO; legal counsel; internal ethics hotline; the board audit committee if internal channels are blocked; PROTECT THE REPORTER: ensure the team member faces no retaliation; document the concern and the PM's response; whistleblower protection laws (EU Whistleblower Directive, SEC whistleblower program in the US) protect good-faith reporters; CTO APPROVAL DOESN'T OVERRIDE LAW: the CTO's approval of a GDPR-violating design doesn't make the violation acceptable; executives can also be wrong; regulatory compliance is an objective standard, not a matter of seniority.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; community impact; stakeholder communities; social license to operate
questions.text: A project is building a large data center in a rural community. Local residents are concerned about: water usage (data centers use significant water for cooling), noise from cooling equipment, the aesthetic impact on the rural landscape, and whether local workers will be employed. How should the project manager address these SOCIAL ESG community concerns?

answers.text: Community concerns are a legal/PR matter — the project manager focuses only on technical delivery
Community support is not required for the project to proceed — regulatory approval is sufficient
Community concerns should be addressed after the data center is operational — engaging them during construction creates unrealistic expectations

Address community concerns as legitimate social ESG stakeholder issues: engage the community early and transparently through town halls; commit to specific water efficiency targets and share the water usage plan publicly; specify noise limits in the construction and operating specifications; evaluate aesthetic mitigation (landscaping, architectural design); commit to local hiring targets; create a community liaison role to maintain ongoing communication throughout the project

explanations.a: Community relations are a core social ESG concern and an operational risk for large infrastructure projects. Unaddressed community concerns can lead to: permit challenges; regulatory delays; media coverage; operational restrictions; community opposition that damages organizational reputation.
explanations.b: Regulatory approval provides the legal right to operate — social acceptance (social license to operate) is different and increasingly important. Organizations that have legal rights but not community support face: public pressure campaigns; regulatory scrutiny; employee recruitment challenges in the local area.
explanations.c: Early engagement is far more effective than post-construction communication: design changes are cheapest before construction; early community input can produce better designs; trust built early prevents adversarial relationships that emerge when communities feel ignored.
explanations.d: SOCIAL ESG — COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT for data center: EARLY ENGAGEMENT (planning phase): hold town halls BEFORE design is finalized; community input can influence decisions when it's still cheap to change; 'We're planning a data center here — here are our initial plans. What questions and concerns do you have?'; WATER USAGE PLAN: quantify actual water usage and compare to local water availability; commit to water efficiency targets (e.g., Water Usage Effectiveness — WUE); consider air-cooled or liquid-cooled direct contact systems that use less water; publish the water management plan publicly; NOISE MITIGATION: specify noise limits in dB at the property boundary in the construction requirements; acoustic engineering to muffle cooling equipment; commit to continuous monitoring; AESTHETIC MITIGATION: architectural guidelines for the exterior appearance; landscaping plan (trees and vegetation to screen the facility); community input on preferred design elements; LOCAL EMPLOYMENT: establish a local hiring target (e.g., 60% of construction jobs and 40% of permanent operational roles filled from within 30 miles); partner with local technical colleges for training programs; supplier diversity (prioritize local suppliers and contractors); COMMUNITY LIAISON: appoint a community liaison who attends community meetings throughout construction; provides updates; receives and escalates community concerns; SOCIAL LICENSE TO OPERATE: organizations that engage communities proactively earn 'social license to operate' — community acceptance that reduces conflict and enables smoother operations.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Governance; anti-corruption; anti-bribery; fair procurement practices
questions.text: A project manager is overseeing a $5M procurement. A vendor that is NOT the winner sends the PM a $1,000 gift card 'as a thank you for the fair process.' The vendor's representative says: 'We appreciate the opportunity to bid and hope to work with you in the future.' What should the PM do and what governance ESG principles apply?

answers.text: Accept the gift card — it's a thank-you for past service, not a bribe (the vendor didn't win)

Decline the gift card and report the attempted gift through the ethics/compliance channel: even unsolicited gifts from vendors who didn't win can create future conflicts of interest (they may bid on future work) and violate organizational gift policies and anti-corruption laws; the PM's decision-making integrity must be protected from even the appearance of conflict; accept no gifts from ANY vendor in a supplier relationship, regardless of the bidding outcome
Accept the gift card and donate it to charity — this eliminates the conflict of interest
Keep the gift but don't use it — possession without use eliminates the ethical issue

explanations.a: Accepting a gift from a vendor — even one that didn't win and even as a 'thank you' — creates: a CONFLICT OF INTEREST in future procurements (you now have a favorable impression of this vendor before they compete again); violation of most organizational gift policies; potential violation of anti-corruption laws (FCPA, UK Bribery Act); the appearance of impropriety even if no actual influence occurred.
explanations.b: ANTI-CORRUPTION AND GIFT POLICY GOVERNANCE: ORGANIZATIONAL GIFT POLICIES: most organizations have explicit policies limiting gifts from vendors to: $0 (strict no-gift policy); or $25-50 maximum with disclosure requirements; a $1,000 gift card vastly exceeds typical limits; even $50 gifts must typically be disclosed; CONFLICT OF INTEREST CREATION: the vendor may bid on future work; having accepted a gift creates a favorable disposition that could bias future evaluation; even if the PM believes they'd evaluate fairly, the appearance of conflict damages procurement integrity; ANTI-CORRUPTION LAWS: UK Bribery Act: prohibits giving/receiving advantages to influence business decisions; no requirement for quid pro quo — the gift itself is the violation; FCPA (US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act): applies to payments to foreign officials (slightly different scope); REPORTING: decline the gift card politely and professionally: 'Thank you for the gesture. I appreciate the kind words. Our policy doesn't allow us to accept gifts from vendors. I'll need to return this.'; report the attempted gift to compliance: this isn't about punishing the vendor (they may genuinely not know your policy) but creating a record of the interaction; PROTECTING FUTURE PROCUREMENTS: by reporting and declining, the PM creates a documented record that protects them if any allegation of favoritism arises in a future procurement involving this vendor. CHARITY DONATION (option C): donating to charity removes the PM's personal benefit — but it doesn't eliminate the conflict of interest (future procurement decisions could still be influenced) or the policy violation.
explanations.c: Accepting and donating is a common misconception — the conflict of interest exists REGARDLESS of what the PM does with the gift. The appearance of impropriety is created by the acceptance, not the personal use.
explanations.d: Possession alone creates the conflict of interest and policy violation — not use. 'I took the gift but didn't spend it' is not a defense against a conflict of interest allegation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG communication; stakeholder ESG expectations; transparency
questions.text: An organization's institutional investors now include ESG performance in their investment criteria. They want quarterly ESG project updates in addition to financial updates. A project manager is asked to contribute ESG data from their project. What ESG data should the PM track and provide and how does this change project reporting?

answers.text: ESG investor reporting is the CFO's responsibility — project managers don't interact with investors

The PM should track and provide: Environmental data (carbon emissions from project activities; energy consumption; waste generated); Social data (team diversity metrics; overtime hours per week; training hours; incident rates; local employment percentage); Governance data (compliance milestone status; open ethics violations; conflict of interest disclosures; vendor ESG certification status); these add ESG dimensions to the project closeout report and contribute to the corporate ESG disclosure
Project managers cannot provide ESG data because it's too difficult to measure at the project level
ESG data is identical to financial data — the standard financial reports cover all ESG requirements

explanations.a: While PMs don't directly report to investors, the corporate ESG reports that investors receive are built from data contributed by all projects. The PM's role is to collect and provide accurate project-level ESG data to the sustainability team.
