explanations.b: PROJECT-LEVEL ESG DATA for corporate ESG reporting: ENVIRONMENTAL METRICS: CARBON: 'Project team air travel: 45 flights × average 1.2 tonnes CO₂e = 54 tonnes'; 'Cloud infrastructure carbon: 12 tonnes CO₂e (as reported by AWS/GCP/Azure carbon calculator)'; 'Paper and consumables: 0.5 tonnes'; total project carbon: 66.5 tonnes CO₂e; ENERGY: data center energy consumption (kWh/month) during project; WASTE: construction waste diverted from landfill (for physical projects); e-waste properly disposed; SOCIAL METRICS: TEAM DIVERSITY: % women; % underrepresented groups; % junior vs. senior roles; WORKING CONDITIONS: average weekly hours (flag if consistently >45); overtime hours; unplanned absences (indicator of burnout); TRAINING: hours per team member per quarter; SAFETY: incidents (zero target for physical projects); COMMUNITY: local hiring %; GOVERNANCE METRICS: COMPLIANCE STATUS: all required regulatory filings on time (Green/Red); open compliance findings; ETHICS VIOLATIONS: number of reported ethics concerns; time to resolution; VENDOR COMPLIANCE: % of vendors with completed ESG certification; CONFLICTS DISCLOSED: number of conflict of interest disclosures; REPORTING ENHANCEMENT: the quarterly project status report adds an ESG section: 1 page with the above metrics; RAG status for each metric vs. target; narrative on significant variances; the PM doesn't analyze this for investors — they provide accurate data to the sustainability team who compiles the corporate ESG report.
explanations.c: ESG metrics are measurable at the project level — many tools exist: cloud providers provide carbon calculators; HR systems track workforce diversity; travel expense systems can calculate trip carbon; incident tracking systems record safety data.
explanations.d: ESG data and financial data are completely different dimensions: financial data measures monetary value flows; ESG data measures environmental, social, and governance impacts. Standard financial reports (P&L, balance sheet) contain no ESG content.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — Social; organizational culture; culture of ethics; psychological safety and ESG
questions.text: An organizational culture assessment reveals that employees regularly feel pressure to cut corners on quality and reporting accuracy to meet aggressive deadlines. Team members are afraid to raise quality concerns. How does organizational culture relate to ESG Governance, and what cultural changes would improve ESG performance?

answers.text: Culture is a soft topic unrelated to ESG governance — governance is about formal rules and procedures

A culture where corner-cutting is normalized and dissent is suppressed directly undermines Governance ESG: honest reporting and quality compliance are governance requirements; a fear culture prevents early warning of compliance issues; psychological safety (people feeling safe to raise concerns) is a prerequisite for effective governance. Cultural improvements include: leadership modeling ethical behavior; celebrating people who raise concerns; removing penalties for honest bad news; implementing anonymous ethics reporting channels
Organizational culture can only be changed through new policy documents — cultural change is not a project management responsibility
Aggressive deadlines are a business necessity that employees must accept — cultural concerns are secondary to delivery

explanations.a: Governance ESG encompasses HOW organizations are actually controlled, not just what policies say. Culture IS governance — a culture that tolerates corner-cutting and suppresses dissent means formal governance procedures are not actually followed.
explanations.b: CULTURE-GOVERNANCE ESG RELATIONSHIP: HOW THE DESCRIBED CULTURE UNDERMINES GOVERNANCE ESG: HONEST REPORTING FAILURE: when employees fear negative consequences for reporting problems, status reports become inaccurate; the PM's misleading status reporting discussed earlier in the course is a symptom of this culture; QUALITY COMPLIANCE: corner-cutting on quality = cutting corners on acceptance criteria, testing standards, and specification compliance; this is a governance failure; EARLY WARNING SUPPRESSION: governance requires early escalation of problems; a fear culture means problems are hidden until they become crises; REGULATORY COMPLIANCE RISK: employees afraid to raise compliance concerns means violations go unreported and uncorrected. PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY AS GOVERNANCE PREREQUISITE: Amy Edmondson's research (Harvard Business School) defines psychological safety as: 'the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes'; teams with high psychological safety have BETTER quality outcomes (more defects reported and fixed) and BETTER governance compliance (issues escalated before they become crises). CULTURAL IMPROVEMENTS: LEADERSHIP MODELING: executives and PMs openly acknowledge their own mistakes; reward the messenger (not shoot them); don't shoot messengers; CELEBRATE CONCERN RAISING: publicly acknowledge when team members raise quality concerns that prevent problems; 'This week, [team member] identified a compliance issue that could have become a $500K regulatory fine — this is exactly the behavior we want'; REMOVE DEADLINE PRESSURE WORKAROUNDS: if deadlines are creating quality corner-cutting, the problem is the deadline or scope — not the people; ANONYMOUS REPORTING CHANNELS: ethics hotlines allow concerns to be raised without identity exposure; this is important until psychological safety is fully established.
explanations.c: Cultural change requires policy changes, leadership behavior changes, reward system changes, and consistent enforcement — it is multi-dimensional. PMs can influence culture within their own teams through their daily behavior, regardless of organizational culture.
explanations.d: 'Aggressive deadlines are a business necessity' is true — but accepting corner-cutting and suppressed dissent as the inevitable consequence is not. Project managers should escalate when delivery commitments create unsustainable quality pressure.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — comprehensive ESG assessment; ESG balanced scorecard; project ESG performance
questions.text: A PMO is evaluating the ESG performance of a recently completed $3M IT infrastructure modernization project. The project delivered on time and on budget. ESG assessment reveals: carbon footprint was 40% higher than baseline (used non-renewable energy data centers); team worked 60+ hours per week for 4 months; 85% of vendor contracts went to 3 vendors with no diversity; governance: all compliance requirements met but one near-miss data breach was handled informally without incident reporting. How should the PMO assess this project's overall ESG performance?

answers.text: The project was successful — on time and on budget is all that matters for project success

The project was a mixed success: strong traditional metrics (time, cost, scope) but significant ESG deficiencies; environmental failure (40% carbon increase); social failure (sustained overwork creating burnout risk; lack of vendor diversity); partial governance failure (compliance met but near-miss incident not formally reported — undermines transparency and organizational learning); overall ESG rating: Red — despite strong traditional performance
The ESG deficiencies are acceptable because the traditional metrics were met — ESG is secondary
The project failed entirely — any ESG shortcoming makes the entire project a failure

explanations.a: On time and on budget measures only financial efficiency — it does not assess sustainability of the means used. A project that delivers on time but burns out half the team is not sustainably successful.
explanations.b: BALANCED ESG ASSESSMENT: TRADITIONAL METRICS (STRONG): schedule: delivered on time ✅; cost: delivered on budget ✅; scope: all requirements delivered ✅; ENVIRONMENTAL (RED — SIGNIFICANT FAILURE): 40% HIGHER carbon vs. baseline; this is the opposite of ESG improvement — the project made environmental performance worse; likely cause: data center selection without renewable energy requirement; correction needed for next project: specify renewable energy regions in procurement requirements; ESG LESSON: environmental considerations were not included in vendor selection criteria. SOCIAL (RED — SIGNIFICANT CONCERNS): 60+ HOURS/WEEK FOR 4 MONTHS: this is unsustainable burnout territory; team members are likely leaving or damaged (health impacts, disengagement); replacement costs for burnout-induced turnover may significantly exceed any savings from 'pushing through'; ESG LESSON: schedule compression was accepted over workload sustainability; no escalation of workload concern; VENDOR DIVERSITY: 85% of contracts to 3 vendors; lack of vendor diversity may indicate non-competitive or relationship-based procurement; ESG LESSON: vendor diversity criteria should be in the evaluation scorecard. GOVERNANCE (AMBER — PARTIAL SUCCESS): compliance requirements met ✅ — this is positive; NEAR-MISS NOT FORMALLY REPORTED ❌ — informal handling of a data security near-miss: prevents organizational learning (others can't learn from the close call); may violate incident reporting obligations (GDPR requires reporting of security incidents within 72 hours even if no breach occurred); demonstrates a culture of informal problem resolution that undermines governance transparency; OVERALL PROJECT ASSESSMENT: strong delivery against traditional metrics (Green); significant ESG deficiencies (Red); overall: Amber/Red — successful delivery by narrow metrics but with unsustainable and potentially harmful means.
explanations.c: The 'ESG is secondary' viewpoint is increasingly untenable: investors score organizations on ESG performance; regulations require ESG compliance; employee wellbeing affects long-term organizational capability; environmental impacts are becoming regulated; this project's ESG failures create future risks and costs.
explanations.d: ESG deficiencies should be assessed by their severity and impact — a project with minor ESG issues is not a total failure. This project has meaningful ESG concerns that need to be learned from and corrected, but the traditional delivery success is still real value.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — ESG in Agile and Waterfall; methodology-specific ESG considerations
questions.text: A project team debates whether Agile or Waterfall methodology is more compatible with ESG principles. What ESG advantages does each methodology offer and what ESG risks does each create?

answers.text: Agile is always more ESG-friendly than Waterfall — iterative methods are inherently sustainable

Each methodology has ESG trade-offs: Agile advantages include early feedback reducing wasted work (environmental efficiency), team collaboration improving social outcomes; Agile risks include sustainable pace violations when sprint commitments are overloaded. Waterfall advantages include comprehensive upfront planning allowing thorough ESG requirement integration; Waterfall risks include late discovery of ESG issues making them expensive to fix. Neither is inherently superior — ESG must be intentionally integrated into whichever methodology is used
Waterfall is always more ESG-friendly than Agile — formal documentation supports governance better
Methodology choice has no impact on ESG outcomes — ESG depends entirely on team culture

explanations.a: Both methodologies have ESG advantages and risks. Agile's iterative nature reduces some waste but creates specific social risks around sprint sustainability. Neither is inherently 'more sustainable.'
explanations.b: METHODOLOGY ESG COMPARISON: AGILE ESG ADVANTAGES: ENVIRONMENTAL: iterative delivery reduces waste — if a feature turns out to be unnecessary, an Agile team discovers this earlier (after 1-2 sprints) and stops; Waterfall might build it over 6 months before discovering it's not needed; SOCIAL: collaboration-first culture can build stronger team cohesion; frequent retrospectives provide regular opportunities to surface workload concerns; GOVERNANCE: regular sprint reviews create frequent stakeholder visibility and accountability; AGILE ESG RISKS: SUSTAINABLE PACE: Agile's Manifesto principle 8 states 'sustainable pace' but in practice, sprint commitments are frequently overloaded; '60-hour weeks are common in many Agile shops that get the Sprint cadence but not the sustainable pace principle'; TECHNICAL DEBT: moving fast can accumulate technical debt that creates security (governance) risks later; WATERFALL ESG ADVANTAGES: ENVIRONMENTAL: comprehensive upfront requirements mean less mid-project scope change waste (if requirements are stable); GOVERNANCE: detailed documentation required by Waterfall provides clear audit trails (good for regulatory compliance); comprehensive risk registers planned upfront allow more thorough ESG risk identification; SOCIAL: clearer role definitions may create more equitable work distribution; WATERFALL ESG RISKS: LATE DISCOVERY OF ESG ISSUES: if ESG requirements weren't identified in planning, they're discovered expensively late (the 'adding encryption at the end' problem); SOCIAL: long phases without feedback can delay recognition of overwork or team culture issues; ESG INTEGRATION APPROACH: regardless of methodology, explicitly include ESG checkpoints: Agile: ESG items in backlog and retrospectives; Waterfall: ESG in requirements, risk register, and phase gate reviews.
explanations.c: Waterfall documentation supports governance — but documentation without enforcement is theater. An Agile team with strong governance practices can have better actual governance outcomes than a Waterfall team with comprehensive documentation that isn't followed.
explanations.d: Culture is the most important factor, but methodology does create different structural incentives and risks for ESG outcomes. Ignoring methodology's impact on ESG would miss important systemic influences.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — applying ESG to project decisions; ethical dilemmas; values-based decision-making
questions.text: A project manager faces a dilemma: a cheaper vendor can deliver the required software at 30% below the next competitor's price. However, research reveals this vendor has a poor track record on labor practices (employees work 70+ hours/week without overtime pay). The sponsor is focused on cost savings. How should the PM approach this decision?

answers.text: Select the cheaper vendor — cost savings are the PM's primary responsibility

Present the full picture to the sponsor: quantify the cost savings ($X); identify the social ESG risks (labor practices violation, potential reputational risk, supply chain due diligence obligations under emerging regulations); recommend the alternative vendor with a risk-adjusted total cost comparison; the sponsor makes the informed decision — the PM's role is to ensure the ESG risks are visible, not to override the sponsor's authority
Select the more expensive vendor without telling the sponsor about the cheaper option — unilateral ethical decisions are appropriate
Accept the cheaper vendor but add a contractual clause requiring them to improve labor practices — the PM can fix the vendor's culture through contract terms

explanations.a: Cost savings is one dimension of the PM's responsibility — not the only one. Recommending a vendor with known ESG violations without disclosure would be a governance failure.
explanations.b: TRANSPARENT ESG-INFORMED DECISION SUPPORT: THE PM'S ROLE: present all relevant information to the decision-maker (sponsor); not to make the values-based decision unilaterally, but to ensure the decision is fully informed. INFORMATION TO PRESENT TO SPONSOR: FINANCIAL DIMENSION: 'Vendor B is $X less than Vendor A (30% savings = $Y in absolute terms)'; SOCIAL ESG RISK: 'Vendor B has documented labor practices concerns: employees work 70+ hours/week without overtime pay. This represents a violation of [country] labor law and ILO Convention 1'; REPUTATIONAL RISK: 'If press coverage of Vendor B's labor practices emerges during our project, we could be associated with the controversy'; REGULATORY RISK: 'The EU Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (applicable to organizations of our size) requires due diligence on contractor labor practices. Using Vendor B without remediation could create regulatory exposure'; RISK-ADJUSTED TOTAL COST: 'The $Y savings must be weighed against: probability × impact of reputational damage; regulatory compliance costs; potential vendor lock-in with a contractor that may face labor regulatory action'; RECOMMENDATION: 'I recommend Vendor A for this engagement based on the risk-adjusted total cost analysis. The labor practice risks with Vendor B represent organizational liability that exceeds the $Y savings. However, this is your decision as project sponsor — I want to ensure you have the full picture.' THE SPONSOR DECIDES: the sponsor may accept the ESG risk for the cost savings — that is their organizational authority; the PM's duty is TRANSPARENCY, not unilateral ethical override.
explanations.c: Hiding the cheaper option from the sponsor is dishonest — even with ethical intent. The PM must disclose all material information to the sponsor. Making unilateral values-based decisions that bypass the sponsor's authority also violates governance principles.
explanations.d: Contract clauses requiring cultural change in a vendor organization are rarely effective — organizations don't change their culture because a client contract says so. This approach gives false assurance without actually addressing the risk.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: ESG — all three dimensions; comprehensive ESG scenario; ESG decision-making
questions.text: A new PM takes over a troubled project. She discovers: (1) The project's cloud migration plan routes all data through servers in a coal-powered region when renewable options exist at the same cost; (2) The previous PM normalized 70-hour weeks and one senior developer is exhibiting burnout symptoms; (3) A pending regulatory audit has been hidden from the sponsor because 'the team wanted to handle it internally'; (4) The requirements don't include accessibility features despite a government mandate requiring them. Prioritize these ESG issues by urgency and describe the PM's immediate actions for each.

answers.text: All four issues have equal priority — address them sequentially in the order discovered

Priority order: (1) Hidden regulatory audit (Governance — immediate risk of regulatory action and legal liability, requires sponsor notification TODAY); (2) Accessibility requirements gap (Governance + Social — legal mandate creates compliance risk and user equity failure; add to requirements and QA plan immediately); (3) Developer burnout (Social — human health risk; address this week through workload reduction); (4) Coal-powered cloud region (Environmental — important but no immediate crisis; fix in the architecture planning phase)
Only address the regulatory audit — the other three are too minor to prioritize
Address the burnout first because human wellbeing is always the highest priority regardless of other factors

explanations.a: ESG issues, like other project risks, have different urgency levels. Equal priority treatment would misallocate immediate attention to issues that can wait while urgent governance crises go unaddressed.
explanations.b: URGENCY-PRIORITIZED ESG RESPONSE: ISSUE 1 — HIDDEN REGULATORY AUDIT (GOVERNANCE — HIGHEST URGENCY): WHY FIRST: a hidden regulatory audit is an active governance crisis; if the audit proceeds without sponsor awareness, the sponsor cannot help manage the regulatory relationship; the previous PM's decision to hide this from the sponsor is a transparency/governance violation; IMMEDIATE ACTION (TODAY): the new PM informs the sponsor immediately: 'I've just learned about a pending regulatory audit that was not disclosed. You need to know about this immediately. Here's what I know: [details]. I recommend we engage legal counsel and prepare a response strategy this week.'; REGULATORY PREPARATION: engage legal counsel; gather required documentation; submit a response to the regulatory body (if one is pending); hiding a regulatory audit is not the same as not having one — regulators generally view proactive transparency favorably and concealment unfavorably. ISSUE 2 — ACCESSIBILITY GAP (GOVERNANCE + SOCIAL — HIGH URGENCY): WHY SECOND: a government mandate for accessibility is legal compliance — non-delivery creates regulatory violation and potential legal liability; failure to provide accessible government services is also an equity issue (social ESG); IMMEDIATE ACTION (THIS WEEK): add accessibility requirements to the requirements document; add accessibility testing to the QA plan; assess timeline impact of the addition; consult with legal on the compliance timeline; add 'accessibility compliance' as a go-live gate criterion. ISSUE 3 — DEVELOPER BURNOUT (SOCIAL — HIGH URGENCY, IMMEDIATE): WHY THIRD: a team member showing burnout symptoms is a human health concern; sustained 70-hour weeks create burnout, quality decline, and potential departure risk; IMMEDIATE ACTION (THIS WEEK): one-on-one with the affected developer; immediate workload assessment; work with the sponsor to identify relief options (contractor support, scope reduction, schedule extension); normalize sustainable working hours as a team expectation. ISSUE 4 — COAL-POWERED CLOUD REGION (ENVIRONMENTAL — MEDIUM URGENCY): WHY FOURTH: no immediate legal or health crisis; the renewable option costs the same — switching is simple; IMMEDIATE ACTION (WITHIN 2-3 WEEKS): update the cloud architecture to specify a renewable energy region; validate with the cloud team that switching regions is technically feasible; update the procurement specification.
explanations.c: All four issues require action. The regulatory audit is most urgent — but the accessibility gap (legal compliance) and developer burnout (health risk) are also time-sensitive concerns that cannot be deferred.
explanations.d: While developer burnout is a human health concern deserving immediate attention, the hidden regulatory audit creates a time-critical legal exposure that must be surfaced to the sponsor first. Health concerns and governance crises can be addressed in parallel.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — CIA triad; Confidentiality Integrity Availability
questions.text: The CIA triad is the foundational information security model. What do the three components mean and how do all three apply equally to project management?

answers.text: CONFIDENTIALITY (data accessible only to authorized parties); INTEGRITY (data is accurate and unaltered without authorization); AVAILABILITY (data and systems are accessible when needed). All three must be balanced — excessive security controls can impair availability; excessive openness compromises confidentiality; project managers must optimize all three for the specific risk context
CIA stands for Central Intelligence Agency security classification levels
CIA triad refers to Cipher, Identification, Authentication — three encryption types
CIA triad only applies to government/defense projects — commercial projects use different models

explanations.a: CIA TRIAD in PROJECT MANAGEMENT: CONFIDENTIALITY: only authorized individuals access information; PROJECT USE: project financial models and IP classified appropriately; NDA enforcement for vendors; data classification determines who can see what; INTEGRITY: information is complete, accurate, and unmodified by unauthorized parties; PROJECT USE: audit trails for requirement changes; version control for documents; database integrity constraints; ensuring vendor deliverables are untampered; AVAILABILITY: systems accessible when needed by authorized users; PROJECT USE: SLA requirements in the system design (99.9% uptime); disaster recovery planning; downtime windows for maintenance; TRADE-OFFS: maximizing one dimension can compromise another; a healthcare portal must achieve HIGH CONFIDENTIALITY (patient data is sensitive), HIGH INTEGRITY (medical records cannot be altered without audit trail), AND HIGH AVAILABILITY (emergency departments need 24/7 access — lives depend on it); achieving all three simultaneously requires careful security architecture.
explanations.b: In information security, CIA refers to Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability — not the government agency.
explanations.c: Cipher, Identification, Authentication are security mechanisms — not the three properties of the CIA triad.
explanations.d: The CIA triad is a universal security framework applicable to all projects involving information systems or sensitive data, regardless of sector.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — physical security controls; server room security; access controls
questions.text: A project team is implementing a new server room. What PHYSICAL SECURITY controls should be specified in the project requirements?

answers.text: Physical security is irrelevant — only network/logical security matters for server rooms
Badge/card access control limiting entry to authorized personnel only

Physical security controls include: badge access control; security cameras (CCTV); biometric authentication for highest-security areas; man-trap/airlock (anti-tailgating); environmental monitoring (temperature, humidity, smoke/fire); equipment locking; visitor log with escort policy; hardware asset tracking; clean desk policy
A strong server OS password is sufficient — logical controls replace physical ones

explanations.a: Physical security is critical — an attacker with physical access to a server can bypass almost all logical (software) security controls.
explanations.b: Badge access alone is valuable but insufficient. A comprehensive physical security program requires multiple overlapping controls.
explanations.c: PHYSICAL SECURITY CONTROLS for server room: PERIMETER CONTROL: BADGE ACCESS: electronic access control; only authorized personnel; access logs maintained; regular access review (remove departed staff); BIOMETRICS: fingerprint/retina for highest-security zones (adds 'something you are' factor); MAN-TRAP/AIRLOCK: two-door system — second door won't open until first is closed; prevents tailgating; SURVEILLANCE: CCTV at entry/exit and inside the room; retained footage (30-90 days for financial services compliance); ENVIRONMENTAL: temperature sensors; humidity sensors; smoke detection; clean-agent fire suppression; water/flood detection; UPS and generator for power continuity; EQUIPMENT SECURITY: server rack locking; hardware asset tags; OPERATIONAL: visitor escort required; visitor log (name, time in/out, escort); no unaccompanied visitors; INCIDENT RESPONSE: alarmed doors; connection to security operations center.
explanations.d: Physical access allows: direct console access; boot from USB to bypass OS authentication; disk removal for data extraction. 'Just a strong password' is entirely insufficient.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — data classification; sensitivity levels; handling requirements
questions.text: A project is building a document management system storing documents at different sensitivity levels. What are the four standard data classification levels and key handling requirements for each?

answers.text: PUBLIC (no access restrictions, freely shareable); INTERNAL (employees only, no special encryption); CONFIDENTIAL (need-to-know basis, encryption in transit, password-protected); RESTRICTED/SECRET (strictest controls, encryption at rest and in transit, strict authorized user list, audit logging for all access)
All documents get maximum security — differentiated classification creates unnecessary complexity
Data classification only applies to government projects — commercial organizations don't classify data
There are only two levels: Secure and Not Secure

explanations.a: DATA CLASSIFICATION LEVELS: PUBLIC: freely distributable; examples: press releases, public website content; no access controls required; INTERNAL: employees only; examples: employee handbook, meeting minutes, internal policies; reasonable access controls; no encryption typically required; CONFIDENTIAL: limited sharing on need-to-know basis; examples: financial projections, contracts, client lists, personnel records; encryption in transit; secure disposal (shredding); password protection; limited distribution lists; RESTRICTED/SECRET: most sensitive; unauthorized disclosure = severe harm; examples: M&A plans, source code for proprietary algorithms, medical records; strong encryption at rest AND in transit; strict access control with audit log; no removable media; limited authorized personnel list; PROJECT IMPLICATION: the document management system must enforce classification labels; access controls must match classification level.
explanations.b: Treating all documents with maximum security wastes resources and creates access friction. Classification allocates security effort proportionally to actual sensitivity.
explanations.c: Every organization with sensitive information uses data classification. Regulatory frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) essentially mandate classification of specific data types.
explanations.d: Most mature organizations use 3-5 classification levels to enable proportional security allocation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — MFA; authentication factors; something you know have are
questions.text: A security architect recommends Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for a new financial application. What are the three authentication factor types and why does MFA significantly improve security over passwords alone?

answers.text: Three factors: SOMETHING YOU KNOW (password, PIN); SOMETHING YOU HAVE (hardware token, authenticator app OTP, smart card); SOMETHING YOU ARE (biometrics: fingerprint, facial recognition). MFA requires at least two DIFFERENT factor types — even if one factor is compromised (password stolen in a breach), the attacker cannot authenticate without the second factor
MFA uses three different passwords — using multiple passwords is multi-factor authentication
MFA only applies to administrator accounts — regular users use single-factor authentication
Two passwords from different systems together constitute MFA because they come from different sources

explanations.a: THREE AUTHENTICATION FACTORS: SOMETHING YOU KNOW (knowledge factor): password/passphrase; PIN; security question answers; LIMITATION: can be stolen via phishing, data breach, shoulder surfing; SOMETHING YOU HAVE (possession factor): hardware security key (YubiKey); OTP from authenticator app (Google Authenticator); SMS code; smart card; LIMITATION: can be stolen or lost; SMS vulnerable to SIM swap; SOMETHING YOU ARE (inherence/biometric factor): fingerprint; facial recognition; retinal/iris scan; behavioral biometrics; LIMITATION: cannot be changed if compromised; WHY MFA WORKS: even with a stolen password, an attacker cannot authenticate without the SECOND factor; Microsoft research: MFA blocks 99.9% of account compromise attacks; VERIZON DBIR: 80%+ of hacking-related breaches involve compromised credentials — MFA eliminates this attack vector.
explanations.b: Multiple passwords are multiple instances of the SAME factor (something you know) — this is NOT MFA. MFA requires factors from DIFFERENT categories.
explanations.c: MFA should apply to all user accounts in sensitive applications. Regular user accounts are actually the highest-volume targets for credential stuffing attacks.
explanations.d: Two passwords are two instances of 'something you know' — single factor type, not MFA.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — encryption at rest and in transit; AES; TLS
questions.text: A project manager must ensure sensitive data is properly encrypted. What are the two primary encryption contexts and the common standards for each?

answers.text: ENCRYPTION AT REST protects stored data (databases, backups, disk); standards: AES-256 for database/disk encryption, BitLocker/FileVault for full-disk encryption. ENCRYPTION IN TRANSIT protects data moving across networks; standards: TLS 1.3 for HTTPS web traffic, SSH for remote administration, VPN for network tunneling. Both are required — defense in depth against different attack scenarios
Encryption is only needed during network transmission — stored data doesn't need encryption
Encryption is only required for classified government data
Only in-transit encryption matters if the network is secure — database encryption is redundant

explanations.a: ENCRYPTION AT REST: protects data stored in databases, files, backups, disk; protects against physical theft and unauthorized database access; STANDARDS: AES-256 (government standard for data at rest); BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (macOS), dm-crypt/LUKS (Linux) for full-disk encryption; transparent database encryption (TDE) for database engines; ENCRYPTION IN TRANSIT: protects data moving across networks; protects against man-in-the-middle attacks and packet sniffing; STANDARDS: TLS 1.3 for HTTPS (current standard; TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated); SSH for remote server administration; SFTP for secure file transfer; VPN (IPSec or OpenVPN) for site-to-site and remote access tunneling; WHY BOTH REQUIRED: a breach may involve physical disk theft (at rest protection needed) or network interception (in transit protection needed); defense in depth requires both; REGULATORY REQUIREMENT: GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS all explicitly require appropriate encryption for sensitive data.
explanations.b: Stored data absolutely needs encryption — hard drives can be stolen; databases can be accessed by unauthorized users; backups can be lost. Without encryption at rest, physical access to storage media = access to data.
explanations.c: GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS all require encryption for regulated data categories. Encryption is standard practice across all industries for sensitive data.
explanations.d: Database encryption and network encryption address different attack vectors. An attacker who compromises the database server directly (not through the network) would access unencrypted data without database encryption.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — zero trust; never trust always verify; least privilege; micro-segmentation
questions.text: A security architect recommends ZERO TRUST architecture for a new cloud application. What is zero trust and how should it shape the project's security requirements?

answers.text: Zero trust — 'never trust, always verify' — means no user, device, or network location is trusted by default even inside the corporate perimeter. Requirements include: verify identity explicitly for every access request (strong MFA); enforce least privilege access; implement micro-segmentation to limit lateral movement; assume breach and design accordingly; continuously validate session security
Zero trust means all users are denied access — the system is inaccessible to everyone
Zero trust only applies to large enterprises with dedicated security teams
Zero trust eliminates authentication — network location establishes trust automatically

explanations.a: ZERO TRUST PRINCIPLES: TRADITIONAL PERIMETER MODEL FAILURE: once inside the network (firewall), users are broadly trusted; fails when employees work remotely (no clear perimeter), attackers breach the perimeter, or insiders abuse trust; ZERO TRUST CORE PRINCIPLES: VERIFY EXPLICITLY: authenticate and authorize every access request based on identity, device health, location, and service requested; never grant broad network-location-based trust; USE LEAST PRIVILEGE: minimum permissions for specific tasks; just-in-time and just-enough access; time-limited permissions; MICRO-SEGMENTATION: divide the network so an attacker who breaches one segment cannot reach all systems; the HR server should only be able to talk to the HR database, not all servers; ASSUME BREACH: design as if attackers are already inside; monitor all traffic including internal; minimize blast radius; PROJECT REQUIREMENTS: IDENTITY: MFA for all users; conditional access (block from unusual locations, unmanaged devices); DEVICE: device health checks before granting access (patched? antivirus running?); NETWORK: micro-segmentation; mutual TLS between services; MONITORING: all access logged; anomaly detection; WHY IMPORTANT FOR PROJECTS: remote team members and external vendors accessing systems from outside the perimeter require zero trust principles for adequate protection.
explanations.b: Zero trust grants access to authorized users after explicit verification — it does not deny all access. It is about CONTINUOUS VERIFICATION, not blanket denial.
explanations.c: Zero trust principles scale to all sizes. Cloud-native applications especially benefit from zero trust because there is no traditional perimeter.
explanations.d: Zero trust is the OPPOSITE of location-based trust. Traditional models trust network location; zero trust explicitly rejects this and requires identity verification regardless of where the connection comes from.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — defense in depth; layered security; multiple security controls
questions.text: A developer says: 'We have a firewall — that's enough security.' A security reviewer responds that the application has no defense in depth. Who is correct and what does defense in depth mean?

answers.text: The security reviewer is correct: a firewall is one layer at the network perimeter but doesn't protect against application-layer attacks, stolen credentials, insider threats, or unpatched vulnerabilities. Defense in depth means multiple overlapping security controls across layers: perimeter (firewall), network segmentation, application-level authentication, database access controls, data encryption, endpoint security, and monitoring
The developer is correct — a properly configured firewall provides comprehensive security protection
Defense in depth only applies to physical security — digital systems use single-layer protection
Adding more security layers always improves security regardless of the specific controls chosen

explanations.a: DEFENSE IN DEPTH — LAYERED SECURITY: CONCEPT: multiple overlapping security controls so failure of any single control doesn't compromise the entire system; LAYERS FOR A WEB APPLICATION: LAYER 1 — PERIMETER/NETWORK: firewall (network-layer filtering), DDoS protection; LAYER 2 — NETWORK SEGMENTATION: web servers in DMZ; database servers in restricted internal segment; database not directly accessible from internet; LAYER 3 — APPLICATION: Web Application Firewall (WAF) filters application-layer attacks; secure coding (input validation, parameterized queries); LAYER 4 — AUTHENTICATION AND AUTHORIZATION: MFA; RBAC (role-based access control); LAYER 5 — DATA: encryption at rest; encryption in transit; data masking for non-production; LAYER 6 — ENDPOINT: OS and application patching; endpoint detection and response (EDR); antivirus; LAYER 7 — MONITORING: SIEM; intrusion detection; audit logging; security operations center; EACH LAYER addresses different attack vectors — no single layer is sufficient; if Layer 1 (firewall) is bypassed, Layer 3 (WAF) may catch the attack; if Layer 3 fails, Layer 4 (authentication) creates another barrier.
explanations.b: A firewall blocks unauthorized NETWORK connections — it doesn't protect against: SQL injection through allowed ports (HTTP/443); compromised user credentials; insider threats; unpatched application vulnerabilities; social engineering.
explanations.c: Defense in depth is a fundamental digital security principle. Physical security also uses layered controls (fence, guards, badge readers, cameras, locked cabinets).
explanations.d: More layers are only better if each layer provides genuine security value for the specific threat model. Security theater adds cost without protection. Quality and relevance of each layer matters.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — RBAC; ABAC; least privilege; need-to-know access control
questions.text: A new EHR system needs access controls for physicians, nurses, billing staff, and researchers. Each needs different access to patient data. Which access control model is most appropriate?

answers.text: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) combined with ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): physician role = clinical records for assigned patients only (ABAC: treatment relationship attribute); nurse role = medication administration records; billing role = billing codes and insurance data; researcher role = de-identified aggregate data only. Implements least privilege — each role accesses only what's needed for their job function
Give all clinical staff full access — restricting access in healthcare creates dangerous delays
Let users request their own access level — self-service access is most efficient
Single access level for all staff — simplified administration outweighs security risks

explanations.a: ACCESS CONTROL DESIGN for EHR: ROLE-BASED ACCESS CONTROL (RBAC): permissions organized by role rather than individual; PHYSICIAN ROLE: clinical notes, lab results, imaging, medication orders for assigned patients; NURSE ROLE: medication administration records, vital signs, nursing notes; BILLING ROLE: demographics, insurance information, billing codes, claim status; RESEARCHER ROLE: de-identified aggregate statistical data only; ATTRIBUTE-BASED ACCESS CONTROL (ABAC) ENHANCEMENT: physicians: RBAC grants 'clinical record access' + ABAC attribute 'assigned patients only'; a physician cannot access records for patients they are not treating; LEAST PRIVILEGE PRINCIPLE: each user receives exactly the access needed — no more; HIPAA MINIMUM NECESSARY: access limited to 'minimum necessary for the employee's job function'; IMPLEMENTATION: define roles clearly in requirements; map permissions to roles in access matrix; automated provisioning through HR system; periodic access reviews (quarterly re-certification); EMERGENCY ACCESS: some systems allow 'break-glass' emergency access override with mandatory audit notification.
explanations.b: 'All clinical staff access everything' violates HIPAA's minimum necessary standard. A billing clerk with access to psychiatric notes and a nurse with access to financial records creates unnecessary exposure — healthcare insider threats are the most common breach type.
explanations.c: User self-service access management enables uncontrolled privilege escalation. Access decisions must be made by administrators based on job requirements, not user preference.
explanations.d: A single access level (physicians + billing clerks + researchers) violates both HIPAA and basic least privilege — billing clerks would see complete patient medical histories with no clinical justification.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — phishing; social engineering; security awareness; incident reporting
questions.text: A team member receives an email from 'IT Department' demanding credential verification within 24 hours or their account will be suspended. They click a link and enter their password. What attack occurred and what should happen next?

answers.text: This is a legitimate IT request — IT departments routinely send credential verification emails
Delete the email and change the password privately — no need to involve IT security

This is a PHISHING attack (social engineering). The team member's credentials are now compromised. Immediate actions: notify the IT security team immediately; the security team should invalidate the compromised credentials; investigate whether the attacker has already used the stolen credentials; conduct a forensic review of the account; train the team member on phishing recognition; alert the entire project team about the phishing campaign
Ignore it — if nothing bad happened within an hour, the click was harmless

explanations.a: Legitimate IT departments NEVER ask for passwords via email. Secure authentication systems mean IT cannot and should not need your password. This is a universal red flag.
explanations.b: Self-managed password change without IT security involvement: may not invalidate existing sessions (attacker still logged in); prevents forensic investigation of the breach scope; misses the team alert that could prevent other members from falling for the same attack.
explanations.c: PHISHING ATTACK — CREDENTIAL COMPROMISE RESPONSE: WHAT HAPPENED: PHISHING EMAIL: used urgency (24-hour deadline) and authority (IT Department) to override careful thinking; CREDENTIAL HARVEST: the link led to a fake login page that captured the credentials; the attacker now has the team member's username and password; IMMEDIATE RESPONSE (security team actions): INVALIDATE COMPROMISED CREDENTIALS: immediately reset the compromised account password and revoke active sessions; the attacker may have already logged in — session invalidation prevents ongoing access; INVESTIGATE: check access logs — did the attacker log in? what did they access? was data exfiltrated?; FORENSIC REVIEW: examine email headers to trace the phishing infrastructure; check whether other team members received the same email; SCOPE ASSESSMENT: did the attacker access project data? was any data exported?; NOTIFICATION: if sensitive project data was accessed, sponsor notification; if personal data was exposed, potentially regulatory notification; TEAM ALERT: notify all project team members about the phishing campaign with examples of how to recognize similar attacks; PREVENTION GOING FORWARD: phishing simulation exercises; security awareness training; suspicious email reporting channel.
explanations.d: Credential theft is a serious security incident even if nothing obvious happened immediately. Attackers often wait weeks or months before acting on stolen credentials. 'Nothing happened yet' ≠ 'safe.'

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — DMZ; WAF; network segmentation; firewall architecture
questions.text: A project is deploying a public-facing web application. The security architect specifies a DMZ with a WAF. What does this architecture provide and why are both a DMZ and WAF needed?

answers.text: A DMZ is a geographic war zone — the term doesn't apply to IT security
A WAF is identical to a traditional firewall — both filter by IP address and port

DMZ (Demilitarized Zone): a network segment between the internet and the internal network; the web server sits in the DMZ — accessible from the internet but isolated from internal databases by a second firewall. WAF (Web Application Firewall): filters HTTP/HTTPS application-layer traffic for attacks like SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and OWASP Top 10. Together: the DMZ limits the blast radius if the web server is compromised (attacker cannot directly reach internal systems); the WAF catches attacks that network firewalls miss (operating at the application layer)
A DMZ reduces security requirements — it allows more open access in a designated zone

explanations.a: DMZ in IT is a well-established networking concept — not related to the geographic term. The analogy: a neutral zone between two territories (internet and internal network).
explanations.b: Traditional firewall: filters at network layer (IP/port). WAF: filters at application layer (HTTP content). Different OSI layers, complementary controls.
explanations.c: DMZ ARCHITECTURE: NETWORK ZONES: INTERNET (untrusted); DMZ (semi-trusted — contains web/email servers, load balancers); INTERNAL NETWORK (trusted — contains databases, internal applications, finance systems); FIREWALL 1 (internet-facing): allows only HTTP/HTTPS into the DMZ; blocks all other traffic; FIREWALL 2 (internal-facing): allows only specific DMZ-to-database traffic (e.g., web server to PostgreSQL on port 5432); if the web server is compromised, the attacker is trapped in the DMZ — they must also breach Firewall 2 to reach the database; SECURITY VALUE: breach of the web server gives access to the DMZ only, not the entire internal network; WAF PURPOSE: network firewalls filter at Layer 3-4 (IP address, port, protocol); WAF filters at Layer 7 (HTTP content, application patterns); WAF detects and blocks: SQL injection (attacker sends SQL commands in web inputs); cross-site scripting (malicious scripts injected into web responses); OWASP Top 10 application vulnerabilities; WHY BOTH NEEDED: firewall blocks unauthorized network connections; WAF blocks application-layer attacks that come through authorized connections (HTTP on port 443).
explanations.d: A DMZ has MORE security structure, not less — it adds a second firewall layer that isolates internal systems from the internet-accessible web tier.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security by design; SDLC security integration; security in project planning
questions.text: A PM is building a new e-commerce platform. A security consultant recommends 'security by design.' What does this mean for project planning and why is it better than addressing security at the end?

answers.text: Security review should be the final gate before go-live — all other testing should come first
Security review delays launch — defer to post-launch monitoring and fix issues as they appear
Cloud platforms provide security automatically — developers don't need to build in security

Security by design means: including security requirements alongside functional requirements from day 1; conducting threat modeling during architecture design; requiring secure coding practices throughout development; including security testing (SAST/DAST/penetration testing) in the QA plan; defining security acceptance criteria that must pass before go-live. Cost of fixing security vulnerabilities: design phase ~$100; development ~$1,000; testing ~$5,000; production ~$50,000+

explanations.a: Security addressed only at go-live produces: architecturally insecure systems requiring expensive redesign; delayed launches when security testing fails at the last moment; unpatched vulnerabilities remaining in production.
explanations.b: Security monitoring after launch detects breaches AFTER harm has occurred (data stolen, fraudulent charges, regulatory violation). Security by design prevents vulnerabilities from reaching production.
explanations.c: Cloud shared responsibility model: cloud provider secures the infrastructure; the PROJECT secures the application code, data, and access management. Application vulnerabilities are entirely the project's responsibility.
explanations.d: SECURITY BY DESIGN in project planning: REQUIREMENTS PHASE: explicit security requirements alongside functional requirements; AUTHENTICATION: 'All user sessions require MFA'; AUTHORIZATION: 'Users access only resources permitted by their RBAC role'; ENCRYPTION: 'Payment card data encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)'; INPUT VALIDATION: 'All user inputs validated and sanitized before processing'; AUDIT LOGGING: 'All authentication events and financial data access logged'; THREAT MODELING (architecture phase): identify threats for the e-commerce design; STRIDE methodology: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege; design security controls addressing identified threats; SECURE DEVELOPMENT: OWASP Top 10 developer training; code review security standards; dependency scanning; SECURITY TESTING IN QA PLAN: SAST: scan source code during development (every CI/CD commit); DAST: test the running staging application; penetration test: pre-launch external firm test; SECURITY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: no Critical/High vulnerabilities unresolved at go-live; THE COST ARGUMENT: design fix: ~$100; production fix: ~$50,000+ (remediation + regulatory fine exposure); security by design is dramatically more cost-effective.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — patch management; vulnerability management; SBOM; CVE response SLAs
questions.text: The security team asks for a patch management plan as a project deliverable during transition. The PM wasn't planning this. Why is patch management a project deliverable and what should the plan cover?

answers.text: Patch management is entirely the operations team's responsibility — the project team has no role
Only the operating system needs patching — application code doesn't require patch management
Modern cloud applications are automatically patched — patch management plans are outdated

Patch management is a project deliverable because the project creates the system and knows all its components. The plan must cover: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) listing all components requiring patches; patch testing procedures (staging before production); patch deployment windows; SLAs by severity (Critical CVEs within 7 days, High within 30 days); automated vulnerability scanning schedule; documented in the operations runbook

explanations.a: The project must define patch procedures because: the project team knows all components; handover without patch procedures leaves operations with an unmanaged attack surface; ongoing patch management is impossible without knowing what needs patching.
explanations.b: Application frameworks, libraries, and runtimes all require patching: Log4Shell affected thousands of applications using the Log4j library; Spring4Shell affected Spring Framework applications; dependency vulnerabilities are the most common source of post-launch security incidents.
explanations.c: Cloud providers patch THEIR infrastructure (physical servers, hypervisors). Customer applications — custom code, application libraries, container images, OS of self-managed VMs — are the CUSTOMER's responsibility to patch. This is the cloud shared responsibility model.
explanations.d: PATCH MANAGEMENT PLAN as PROJECT DELIVERABLE: SBOM (SOFTWARE BILL OF MATERIALS): complete inventory of: OS (Windows Server, RHEL, Ubuntu); web server (Nginx, Apache); application runtime (Node.js, Java, Python); database (PostgreSQL, MySQL); application frameworks; all third-party libraries with version numbers; SBOM enables rapid identification of which systems are affected when a new CVE is published; PATCH TESTING PROCEDURE: test patches in staging environment first; acceptance criteria (system functions normally); rollback procedure if a patch breaks functionality; PATCH DEPLOYMENT WINDOWS: scheduled maintenance windows (e.g., Sunday 2-4 AM); change advisory board (CAB) approval; user notification; SEVERITY-BASED SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9.0-10.0): within 7 days; High (CVSS 7.0-8.9): within 30 days; Medium (CVSS 4.0-6.9): within 90 days; Low: next scheduled maintenance window; VULNERABILITY SCANNING: automated weekly scans using Nessus, Qualys, or Tenable; alerts for new critical CVEs.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — incident response; security incident handling; breach notification timeline
questions.text: During execution, a developer discovers that the project's collaboration tool was accessed by unauthorized accounts and 6 months of project communications may be exposed. What is the correct incident response sequence?

answers.text: Fix the vulnerability quietly and hope no one notices — public disclosure damages the project
Only report if financial data was exposed — other data types don't require breach notification
Investigate alone for a week before involving security — gather all facts first

Follow the incident response process: IDENTIFY (confirm breach scope); CONTAIN (revoke unauthorized access, isolate affected systems); ASSESS (determine what data was exposed); REPORT (notify security team and sponsor immediately; regulatory notification if personal data is involved within 72 hours under GDPR); REMEDIATE (fix the underlying vulnerability); RECOVER (restore normal secure operations); REVIEW (post-incident analysis to prevent recurrence)

explanations.a: Hiding a security breach is both ethically wrong and illegal in most jurisdictions. GDPR requires notification within 72 hours. Concealment is penalized far more harshly than proactive disclosure.
explanations.b: Project communications frequently contain personal data (team members' names, contact details, HR discussions) and confidential business information. Many types of non-financial data trigger breach notification obligations.
explanations.c: The security team must be involved immediately — not after a week of solo investigation. Time is critical: 72-hour GDPR notification window starts from discovery; attackers may be actively using access; evidence preservation requires forensic expertise.
explanations.d: INCIDENT RESPONSE SEQUENCE: IDENTIFY: confirm the unauthorized access occurred (log analysis, forensic review); determine scope: which accounts compromised? what data was in the tool? was data exported?; CONTAIN: immediately revoke unauthorized account access; rotate credentials for the collaboration tool; notify legitimate users to change passwords; if needed, take the system offline to stop ongoing breach; ASSESS: inventory what data was exposed: project communications may contain sensitive client information, proprietary technical design, personnel discussions; determine if personal data is included (GDPR/CCPA implications); REPORT: INTERNAL (immediately): security team; project sponsor; legal/compliance if personal data involved; REGULATORY: if EU personal data was involved → GDPR notification to supervisory authority within 72 hours of discovery; if personal data breach affects individuals → notify affected individuals without undue delay; REMEDIATE: address the root cause (compromised credentials? misconfigured permissions? phishing attack?); implement security improvements; RECOVER: restore normal operations; verify no remaining unauthorized access; REVIEW: post-incident review — what failed? what early warning signs were missed? what prevents recurrence?

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security risk register; threat modeling; vulnerability prioritization
questions.text: During security review, the team identifies: (1) the application stores full credit card numbers; (2) an API accepts file uploads; (3) an authentication library has a known unpatched CVE. How should each be classified and addressed?

answers.text: All three have equal severity — address them in discovery order
Wait for the security audit to identify risks — the project team shouldn't self-assess security risks
Only the file upload is a risk — credit card storage and authentication library issues are normal

(1) Storing full card numbers: CRITICAL — PCI-DSS violation; response: AVOID by switching to a payment tokenization service (Stripe/Braintree) — removes the risk entirely; (2) File upload endpoint: HIGH — common attack vector for malware and server-side exploits; response: MITIGATE with strict file type allowlist, antivirus scanning, isolated storage; (3) Unpatched authentication CVE: CRITICAL — authentication vulnerabilities are the highest-severity class; response: emergency patch within 24-48 hours or switch libraries

explanations.a: The three risks have different severity levels and require fundamentally different responses. Equal treatment would misallocate remediation effort.
explanations.b: Proactive security risk identification during development is the cheapest possible time to find vulnerabilities. The project team has the best knowledge of the system to identify security risks.
explanations.c: All three are significant. Credit card storage creates massive regulatory liability; authentication vulnerabilities enable complete system compromise.
explanations.d: SECURITY RISK CLASSIFICATION: RISK 1 — STORING FULL CREDIT CARD NUMBERS (CRITICAL/AVOID): PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) prohibits storing full Primary Account Numbers (PANs) without extensive security controls; non-compliance: fines $5,000-$100,000/month; AVOID STRATEGY: use payment tokenization — the payment processor (Stripe, Braintree, Authorize.net) stores the card number and provides a token; the project database stores only the token; this eliminates PCI scope for stored data and is cheaper than achieving PCI compliance for direct card storage. RISK 2 — FILE UPLOAD ENDPOINT (HIGH/MITIGATE): file uploads can contain: malware/ransomware; PHP shells that execute server-side commands; oversized files causing disk exhaustion; MITIGATION: strict file TYPE allowlist (e.g., PDF, JPG, PNG only — not executable extensions); antivirus/malware scanning of every upload; isolated storage outside the web server root; auto-generated server-side filenames; file size limits. RISK 3 — UNPATCHED AUTHENTICATION CVE (CRITICAL/MITIGATE IMMEDIATELY): authentication vulnerabilities enable: authentication bypass; session hijacking; TREATMENT: P1 emergency — patch or replace within 24-48 hours; cannot wait for the next sprint.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — remote work security; VPN; endpoint security; distributed team
questions.text: A project team has 8 remote members working from home across three countries handling sensitive client data. What security controls should the PM ensure are in place?

answers.text: Remote workers can use personal devices and home networks — trust the team to self-manage security
Remote security is entirely the IT department's responsibility — the PM has no role
A strong team password policy is sufficient for remote work security

VPN required for all remote access to project systems; company-managed devices (not personal) for sensitive work; full disk encryption on work devices; MFA for all system access; no access from public WiFi without VPN; prohibition on storing project data in personal cloud storage; endpoint detection and response (EDR) software; remote access session logging

explanations.a: Personal devices and home networks create significant risks: unpatched personal devices; family members sharing the device; home routers with default passwords; no endpoint monitoring; these are vectors for data exfiltration and malware infection.
explanations.b: The PM ensures the project team follows security requirements and that those requirements are included in the project scope. The PM and IT share responsibility — the PM enforces compliance within the project.
explanations.c: Password policy addresses only credential strength — it doesn't protect against network interception (VPN), unpatched devices, or stolen sessions.
explanations.d: REMOTE TEAM SECURITY CONTROLS: VPN: all remote access to company systems routes through VPN; creates encrypted tunnel from device to corporate network; prevents eavesdropping on home/public networks; prevents direct internet exposure of internal systems; COMPANY-MANAGED DEVICES: IT configures and controls the device; enforces OS patches; full disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault — critical if laptop is lost/stolen); endpoint detection and response (EDR); mobile device management (MDM) for remote lock/wipe capability; PERSONAL DEVICE RISKS: unpatched; shared with family; no endpoint monitoring; ENDPOINT SECURITY: current OS and application patches; antivirus/anti-malware; EDR software; disk encryption; MFA FOR ALL SYSTEMS: even with VPN access, stolen VPN credentials protected by MFA; POLICY CONTROLS: no project data on personal cloud storage (personal Dropbox, Google Drive); sensitive documents not visible during video calls; secure document disposal; PUBLIC WIFI PROHIBITION (without VPN): coffee shop WiFi is unencrypted; attackers at the same location can intercept traffic; always VPN before any corporate access on public WiFi.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — supply chain security; SBOM; open-source dependency risk; CVE monitoring
questions.text: The security team warns that the project's 47 open-source libraries create 'supply chain security risk.' What is this risk and how should the project address it?

answers.text: Open-source libraries are always secure — community review ensures safety
Eliminate all external dependencies — zero libraries eliminates supply chain risk
Library vulnerabilities are the library authors' responsibility — the project team has no obligation

Supply chain security risk: vulnerabilities in third-party libraries that the project ships as part of its application. Addressed through: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM — complete inventory of all dependencies with versions); automated dependency scanning (Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check); selecting actively maintained libraries; version pinning; CVE monitoring with defined response SLAs (Critical CVE: patch within 7 days)

explanations.a: 'Community review' does not guarantee security. Major vulnerabilities in widely-used open-source libraries: Log4Shell (Log4j): one of the most critical vulnerabilities ever, affecting millions of applications; Heartbleed (OpenSSL): critical flaw in the world's most used encryption library; Event-Stream: malicious code deliberately injected into a popular npm package. Open source ≠ secure.
explanations.b: Modern software development requires libraries — rebuilding TLS, authentication, and data parsing from scratch would be less secure and less efficient. Manage supply chain risk; don't try to eliminate dependencies.
explanations.c: When you distribute a vulnerable library in your application, you are responsible for the security of what you deliver. Courts and regulators hold organizations responsible for the security of the software they release.
explanations.d: SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY: DEFINITION: vulnerabilities in third-party code incorporated into your application make YOUR application vulnerable; your application inherits all vulnerabilities of all its dependencies; SOFTWARE BILL OF MATERIALS (SBOM): machine-readable inventory of all software components: direct dependencies; transitive dependencies (what your libraries depend on); version numbers; license information; US Executive Order 14028 mandates SBOM for software sold to US federal government; SBOM enables: automated vulnerability scanning; rapid identification of 'which of our systems uses Log4j?'; DEPENDENCY SCANNING: automated CVE database checking (Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, GitHub Dependabot); integrate into CI/CD for continuous scanning; alert when vulnerabilities found; LIBRARY SELECTION CRITERIA: active maintenance (last commit < 6 months); dedicated security response team; history of prompt CVE remediation; wide adoption (more security research); VERSION PINNING: pin specific versions; prevent automatic updates to vulnerable new versions; intentional upgrades after review; CVE RESPONSE SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9+): remediate within 7 days; High (CVSS 7-8.9): within 30 days.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security awareness training; phishing simulation; human element
questions.text: 40% of security incidents at the organization are caused by human error. A PM decides to implement security awareness training for the project team. What should effective training cover and how often should it be delivered?

answers.text: Security training is only for the IT and security departments — project team members don't need it
A single comprehensive annual training session covers all security awareness needs permanently
Detailed technical security training produces the best results — more technical depth equals better security behaviors

Effective security awareness training covers: phishing recognition and reporting; password hygiene (strong passwords, password managers, no reuse); data handling per classification level; social engineering recognition (pretexting, vishing, tailgating); device security (lock screen, secure disposal); incident reporting procedures. Delivered as: annual comprehensive session plus monthly micro-learning (10-20 min) plus phishing simulation exercises — ongoing, not one-time

explanations.a: Project team members handle sensitive data (client information, financial models, proprietary designs) — they are prime phishing targets. Security awareness is everyone's responsibility, not just IT.
explanations.b: Security threats evolve continuously — a one-time training from 3 years ago doesn't address current phishing techniques, ransomware tactics, or social engineering methods. Ongoing training is required.
explanations.c: Highly technical security training for non-technical project team members reduces retention and engagement. Effective security awareness is role-appropriate, practical (what do you DO?), and delivered in short regular sessions.
explanations.d: EFFECTIVE SECURITY AWARENESS TRAINING: CONTENT: PHISHING RECOGNITION: identify urgency + authority + suspicious link = phishing; never click suspicious links; report immediately to security team; PHISHING SIMULATION: fake phishing emails sent to employees; those who click get immediate training — most effective method; PASSWORD HYGIENE: length > complexity for memorability; passphrase (20+ chars) is stronger than complex 8-char password; password manager (LastPass, 1Password) for unique passwords per account; MFA everywhere possible; DATA HANDLING: what data can I share, with whom, through which channels?; no sensitive data to personal email/cloud; secure disposal (shredding); SOCIAL ENGINEERING: pretexting (caller impersonating IT asking for credentials); vishing (voice phishing phone calls); tailgating/piggybacking (following through secure door); DEVICE SECURITY: lock screen when leaving device; report lost/stolen devices immediately; INCIDENT REPORTING: how to report (specific contact); report quickly = minimize damage; no punishment for good-faith reporting; DELIVERY: annual comprehensive training (60-90 min); monthly micro-learning (10-20 min focused topics); quarterly phishing simulations; current threat intelligence sharing.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — access deprovisioning; identity lifecycle; offboarding
questions.text: A security audit finds that 5 former project team members still have active access to production systems 6 months after leaving the project. What governance failure occurred and what process should have prevented it?

answers.text: Maintaining access for former team members is acceptable — they may need it for future questions
Only external contractors need access removed — internal employees can retain access indefinitely

This is an access deprovisioning failure — a security governance breakdown where the principle of least privilege is violated. Prevention requires: a formal project closing checklist with mandatory access deprovisioning step; ideally, automated identity lifecycle management that revokes access when the project role ends; periodic access reviews (quarterly) that would catch orphaned accounts; access should only persist as long as there is a legitimate business need
Access removal is the departing team member's responsibility — they should deactivate their own accounts

explanations.a: Former employees with unnecessary access create: insider threat scenarios — disgruntled former employees can abuse retained access; accidental access — former employees might inadvertently access data they no longer have authorization to see; stolen credentials — if a former employee's account is compromised, the attacker gains access to production systems via those credentials.
explanations.b: Both internal employees AND contractors must have access revoked when their role ends. Internal employees with unnecessary access are an insider threat risk. Many high-profile breaches involved current or former internal employees.
explanations.c: ACCESS DEPROVISIONING GOVERNANCE FAILURE: PRINCIPLE VIOLATED: least privilege requires access ONLY while there is a legitimate business need; when the project ends and team members are released, the need ends → access must be revoked; PREVENTION MECHANISMS: PROJECT CLOSING CHECKLIST: mandatory step: for each released team member, list all systems they have access to; submit deprovisioning requests for all accounts; confirm deprovisioning is complete before signing off on resource release; AUTOMATED IDENTITY LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT: connect HR system to access management system; when employee marked as 'project released' in HR → automatic trigger to revoke associated system access; PERIODIC ACCESS REVIEWS (quarterly certification): access owners actively confirm each user's continued need; orphaned accounts surface during reviews; the question 'does this person still need this access?' is asked regularly; ZERO-STANDING PRIVILEGE (ideal): access granted just-in-time for specific tasks; automatically revoked after task completion; DEPROVISIONING TIMELINE: upon project role ending: revoke access within 24 hours; account suspension can be automated; documented in the offboarding checklist.
explanations.d: Access removal should NEVER be the departing person's responsibility: creates inconsistency (not all departing staff comply); disgruntled individuals might intentionally retain access; departing staff don't know all systems they have access to; access deprovisioning is an IT and project governance responsibility.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — SAST; DAST; penetration testing; vulnerability assessment; security testing types
questions.text: A QA plan specifies SAST, DAST, vulnerability assessment, and penetration testing. A team member asks why all four are needed. How does each serve a distinct purpose?

answers.text: They are redundant — pick the cheapest and skip the rest
Penetration testing alone is sufficient — it finds every type of security vulnerability

SAST (Static Application Security Testing) finds vulnerabilities in source code without running the application — catches hardcoded credentials, insecure patterns, SQL injection vulnerabilities in code; DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests the running application from the outside — catches runtime configuration issues, authentication flaws, session management vulnerabilities; VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT scans infrastructure for known CVEs in OS and application components; PENETRATION TESTING simulates a real attacker against the full system to find complex multi-step attack chains. Each finds different vulnerabilities — all four provide comprehensive coverage
Security testing is the vendor's responsibility — the project team doesn't conduct security testing

explanations.a: Each type finds different vulnerabilities that the others miss. Eliminating any one leaves an uncovered attack surface. SAST without DAST misses runtime issues; pen testing without automated scanning is too expensive to be comprehensive.
explanations.b: Penetration testing is targeted and expensive — it cannot comprehensively cover all code paths or all infrastructure components. Automated scanning (SAST, DAST, vulnerability assessment) provides breadth; pen testing provides depth.
explanations.c: FOUR SECURITY TESTING TYPES: SAST (STATIC APPLICATION SECURITY TESTING): analyzes SOURCE CODE without executing the application; WHEN: during development (every code commit in CI/CD pipeline); WHAT FOUND: hardcoded credentials; insecure coding patterns (SQL injection vulnerabilities, XSS patterns); use of deprecated cryptographic algorithms; TOOLS: SonarQube, Checkmarx, Semgrep, GitHub CodeQL; MISSES: runtime behavior, configuration issues. DAST (DYNAMIC APPLICATION SECURITY TESTING): tests the RUNNING APPLICATION from outside; WHEN: against staging/test environment; WHAT FOUND: authentication and authorization vulnerabilities; server configuration issues; runtime injection vulnerabilities; session management flaws; TOOLS: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite (automated mode); MISSES: source code logic flaws not visible in HTTP responses. VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT: scans infrastructure (servers, databases, network devices) for known CVEs; WHEN: automated weekly scanning; WHAT FOUND: unpatched OS vulnerabilities; default configurations; TOOLS: Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS. PENETRATION TESTING: skilled security professional actively attempts to compromise the system like a real attacker; WHEN: before major launches or annually; WHAT FOUND: complex multi-step attack chains automated tools miss; business logic vulnerabilities; security control bypasses; MISSES: comprehensive code-level scanning (too expensive for full coverage).
explanations.d: The project team is responsible for ensuring the system they deliver is secure — including conducting or commissioning all required security testing before handover.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — cloud shared responsibility; IaaS PaaS SaaS security division
questions.text: A project team member says: 'We use AWS — AWS is responsible for security so we don't need to worry about it.' A security architect disagrees. Who is correct and what is the cloud shared responsibility model?

answers.text: The team member is correct — cloud providers are fully responsible for all security in cloud deployments
The shared responsibility model splits security exactly 50/50 between provider and customer

AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, hardware, hypervisors, managed service infrastructure). The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud (application code, data protection, access management, OS patching for IaaS VMs, network configuration). The most common cloud breaches are caused by customer misconfiguration — not cloud provider failures
Shared responsibility only applies to government cloud — commercial projects are fully covered by the provider

explanations.a: 'AWS handles security' is one of the most dangerous cloud security misconceptions. The vast majority of cloud security incidents are caused by customer misconfiguration (S3 buckets publicly readable, IAM with excessive permissions, unpatched EC2 instances) — not AWS failures.
explanations.b: The division is not 50/50 — it varies significantly by service model. IaaS customers have far more security responsibility than SaaS customers.
