explanations.c: AWS SHARED RESPONSIBILITY MODEL: AWS RESPONSIBILITY ('Security OF the Cloud'): physical security of data centers (guards, biometrics, surveillance); hardware (servers, networking, storage devices); hypervisor (the software running virtual machines); AWS managed service infrastructure (RDS, Lambda, S3 platform infrastructure); CUSTOMER RESPONSIBILITY ('Security IN the Cloud') — VARIES BY SERVICE MODEL: IAAS (EC2 virtual machines): MOST customer responsibility: OS patching (customer patches Windows/Linux on their EC2); networking configuration (security groups, NACLs — customer configures); application code; data encryption; IAM access management; PAAS (RDS managed databases, Elastic Beanstalk): AWS manages OS and database engine patching; customer manages: application code, data, database access configuration, IAM; SAAS (AWS WorkMail-style services): least customer responsibility; customer manages: data content, user access configuration; COMMON CUSTOMER MISTAKES CAUSING BREACHES: S3 bucket configured as publicly readable (IAM misconfiguration); EC2 security groups allowing all inbound traffic (network misconfiguration); IAM users with excessive permissions; unpatched EC2 instances; hardcoded credentials in code.
explanations.d: The shared responsibility model applies to all commercial cloud deployments regardless of industry.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security architecture review; pre-execution security assessment; critical findings
questions.text: A PMO security review before execution approval finds: no MFA in authentication requirements; customer data stored in a shared multi-tenant database; no security testing in the QA plan; remote developers have no VPN requirement; and one developer has standing admin access to the production database. Rank findings by severity and prescribe corrections.

answers.text: These are minor concerns addressable post-launch — security shouldn't block execution approval

Five findings requiring correction before execution: (1) Developer admin access — CRITICAL: revoke immediately; implement just-in-time privileged access; (2) No MFA — CRITICAL: add MFA to authentication requirements now; (3) Shared database — HIGH: add data isolation requirement; (4) No security testing in QA plan — HIGH: add SAST, DAST, and penetration testing; (5) No VPN requirement — HIGH: add to team security policy. All five must be resolved before execution authorization
Only the admin access finding matters — the others are acceptable baseline practices
Address these after go-live — security concerns add project cost and should be deferred

explanations.a: These five findings represent gaps that, if not corrected, would result in a system that is fundamentally insecure at launch. The cost to fix after launch is 10-100× higher than before.
explanations.b: SECURITY REVIEW — PRIORITIZED REMEDIATION: FINDING 1 — DEVELOPER STANDING ADMIN ACCESS (CRITICAL): RISK: standing admin access to production database; if the developer's account is compromised → attacker has ADMIN access to production data; violates least privilege and (for financial systems) SOX separation of duties; CORRECTION: revoke admin access immediately; implement just-in-time privileged access management (PAM) — submit request → time-limited elevated access granted → automatically revoked → all actions logged. FINDING 2 — NO MFA IN AUTHENTICATION REQUIREMENTS (CRITICAL): RISK: password-only authentication for a customer-facing system; credential stuffing attacks are automated and relentless; one stolen password = full account compromise; CORRECTION: add to authentication requirements: 'All user accounts require MFA (TOTP or hardware key)'; for high-value actions (payment, data export), step-up MFA. FINDING 3 — SHARED MULTI-TENANT DATABASE (HIGH): RISK: a vulnerability or misconfiguration in one tenant's application could expose other tenants' data; data isolation is a fundamental security requirement for multi-tenant systems; CORRECTION: add requirement: 'Customer data stored in dedicated schema/database with isolated credentials and access controls'. FINDING 4 — NO SECURITY TESTING IN QA PLAN (HIGH): RISK: launching without security testing virtually guarantees exploitable vulnerabilities; CORRECTION: add to QA plan: SAST in CI/CD pipeline; DAST against staging environment; penetration test before launch; security exit criteria (no Critical/High open). FINDING 5 — NO VPN REQUIREMENT FOR REMOTE DEVELOPERS (HIGH): RISK: remote developers accessing production source code and systems over unencrypted home networks; CORRECTION: add to team security policy: 'All remote access to project systems requires active VPN. No corporate system access on public WiFi without VPN.'
explanations.c: All five findings are significant. The PMO security review process exists precisely to identify these issues before execution begins — that's the most cost-effective time to address them.
explanations.d: The cost of a data breach post-launch: average $4.45M (IBM 2023); GDPR fine up to 4% of global annual revenue; customer loss, litigation, remediation. All five findings can be addressed in days to weeks before execution — far cheaper than post-launch remediation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — PII test data; data anonymization; synthetic data; HIPAA minimum necessary
questions.text: A healthcare analytics project wants to use real patient data for testing. The privacy officer says this is not allowed. A developer says they need realistic data for proper testing. Who is correct and what alternatives exist?

answers.text: The developer is correct — real patient data is necessary for proper testing

The privacy officer is correct: real PHI (Protected Health Information) in test environments violates HIPAA and GDPR. Test environments have weaker security than production, broader access, and less monitoring. Alternatives: DATA ANONYMIZATION (remove all 18 HIPAA identifiers — result is no longer PHI); PSEUDONYMIZATION (replace identifiers with codes while preserving structure); SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION (statistically realistic but entirely fictional patient data — Synthea, Mostly AI); DATA MASKING (substitute real values with realistic fake values preserving format). The developer's need for realistic data is fully addressable through these methods
Real data can be used if developers promise not to share it — informal controls are sufficient
Only the patient's last name needs to be removed — removing the last name alone is sufficient anonymization

explanations.a: Real patient data in a test environment is a HIPAA violation regardless of the developer's intent. The test environment's weaker security controls, broader access, and less monitoring create exactly the conditions where PHI should not exist.
explanations.b: THE PRIVACY OFFICER IS CORRECT: HIPAA MINIMUM NECESSARY: PHI (Protected Health Information) use limited to the minimum necessary for the task; development testing doesn't require actual patient identity — synthetic data meets the need; GDPR: personal data must be processed with 'appropriate security' — development environments don't qualify; TEST DATA ALTERNATIVES: DATA ANONYMIZATION: remove ALL 18 HIPAA identifiers (name, DOB, address, phone, SSN, medical record number, etc.); result is no longer PHI under HIPAA; LIMITATION: may distort statistical patterns needed for testing; PSEUDONYMIZATION: replace identifiers with codes ('John Smith' → 'Patient-4721'); real identity stored separately in secure key table; test environment has pseudonymous data; preserves data structure and demographics; SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION: completely fictional patients with statistically realistic clinical profiles; tools: Synthea (open-source clinical data generator), Mostly AI, Gretel.ai; meets the developer's 'realistic data' requirement entirely; DATA MASKING: substitute sensitive fields with realistic fake values (real SSN → fake SSN of same format; real name → random census name); preserves format and statistical distribution. DEVELOPER'S CONCERN IS VALID AND ADDRESSABLE: synthetic and pseudonymized data are designed to provide the realism needed for testing without exposing actual patient data.
explanations.c: Informal promises have no legal validity under HIPAA. Technical safeguards are required — not trust-based controls.
explanations.d: HIPAA PHI includes 18 categories of identifiers. Removing only the last name leaves: first name, dates (DOB, admission), geographic data, phone, email, SSN, MRN, insurance numbers, and more. Far from sufficient anonymization.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security runbook; incident response playbook; operations security documentation
questions.text: During project transition, the security team requests a security runbook. The PM thought a general operations runbook covered everything. How does a security runbook differ from a general operations runbook?

answers.text: They are identical — one operations runbook covers all operational and security procedures

The general operations runbook covers routine system administration (start/stop/restart, backup schedules, monitoring dashboards). The SECURITY RUNBOOK covers security-specific procedures: security monitoring and alerting configuration; security incident response playbooks by incident type; access control administration procedures; certificate management and renewal; encryption key rotation; patch management SLAs; vendor access management; security tool configuration. Security runbooks often have restricted access (only authorized security personnel) to prevent adversaries from studying the defense
Security runbooks are only required after a security incident occurs — proactive documentation wastes effort
The security team writes the security runbook independently during operations — the project team has no role

explanations.a: Security procedures are specialized, have different audiences (security team vs. operations team), and often require restricted access. Combining them into a single document reduces security by making incident response procedures accessible to unauthorized parties.
explanations.b: SECURITY RUNBOOK CONTENT: SECURITY MONITORING AND ALERTING: security monitoring tools and dashboards; which security events generate alerts; alert severity levels and escalation paths; how to interpret SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) alerts; INCIDENT RESPONSE PLAYBOOKS (type-specific procedures): PHISHING/CREDENTIAL COMPROMISE: detect → revoke credentials → investigate lateral movement → notify → post-incident review; UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS: detect → isolate affected account → investigate → escalate → notify regulators if required; RANSOMWARE: isolate affected systems immediately → engage IR team → do not pay → restore from backup → forensic investigation; DATA BREACH: contain → assess scope → GDPR 72-hour notification → customer notification → forensics; ACCESS CONTROL ADMINISTRATION: provisioning new user accounts (request → approval → provisioning steps); deprovisioning departing employees (all systems within 24 hours of departure); privilege escalation process (how to request and grant just-in-time elevated access); CERTIFICATE MANAGEMENT: inventory of all SSL/TLS certificates with expiry dates; renewal process (minimum 30 days before expiry); KEY MANAGEMENT: encryption key rotation schedule; key backup procedures; PATCH MANAGEMENT SLAs: Critical: within 7 days; High: within 30 days; RESTRICTED ACCESS: security runbooks should be accessible to authorized security personnel only — adversaries who know the incident response procedures can use that knowledge to evade detection.
explanations.c: Security procedures are MOST needed during active security incidents when there is no time to figure things out. Pre-written, tested playbooks enable rapid, effective response. Regulatory requirements (HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX) often explicitly require documented incident response procedures.
explanations.d: The project team creates the system and knows its security architecture best — they are uniquely qualified to write the initial security runbook. This is handed to security operations as part of the project transition.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — GDPR requirements; data subject rights; breach notification; DPO; privacy by design
questions.text: A project is building a customer management system processing EU personal data. The PM must ensure GDPR compliance is built in from the start. What specific GDPR technical requirements must be addressed in the project?

answers.text: GDPR compliance is achieved by adding a cookie consent banner and a privacy policy page — no technical changes required

GDPR technical requirements include: lawful basis for each data processing activity; consent management system where required; data subject rights implementation (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection); privacy notices; data minimization (collect only required fields); retention limits with automated deletion; Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for high-risk processing; Data Processing Agreements with all vendors; breach detection and 72-hour notification capability; Data Protection Officer engagement
GDPR only applies to organizations headquartered in the EU — others are exempt
A privacy policy on the website covers all GDPR technical requirements

explanations.a: A cookie consent banner addresses only one GDPR requirement. GDPR is a comprehensive regulation requiring dozens of technical implementations. A consent banner without underlying access, deletion, and breach notification capabilities is compliance theater.
explanations.b: GDPR TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: LAWFUL BASIS: document the legal basis for each data category (contract performance, legitimate interest, or explicit consent); CONSENT MANAGEMENT: where consent is the lawful basis: granular per-purpose consent; easy withdrawal mechanism; immutable audit log of consent with timestamps; DATA SUBJECT RIGHTS — all must be technically implemented: RIGHT TO ACCESS: user can download all personal data in machine-readable format (JSON/CSV); RIGHT TO RECTIFICATION: user can correct inaccurate personal data; RIGHT TO ERASURE: deletion of all personal data within 30 days of request (with documented exceptions: legal hold); RIGHT TO DATA PORTABILITY: download data in interoperable format; RIGHT TO OBJECT: opt out of specific processing activities; PRIVACY NOTICES: clear disclosure of data collected, purpose, retention, and third parties; DATA MINIMIZATION: only collect fields with a documented purpose; review every database field — 'do we need this?'; RETENTION LIMITS: automated deletion after defined retention period; retention management module in the system; DPIA: required for high-risk processing (large-scale sensitive data processing); risk analysis and mitigation documented; DATA PROCESSING AGREEMENTS: required with all vendors/processors handling personal data; specifies security requirements and obligations; BREACH NOTIFICATION CAPABILITY: detect breaches and notify supervisory authority within 72 hours; notify affected individuals without undue delay; DPO ENGAGEMENT: engage Data Protection Officer as project stakeholder from initiation; GDPR SCOPE: applies to processing EU residents' personal data regardless of where the processing organization is located.
explanations.c: GDPR applies to processing of EU residents' personal data regardless of where the organization is located. A US company with EU customers is fully subject to GDPR for processing those customers' data.
explanations.d: A privacy policy is a transparency requirement — one of dozens of GDPR obligations. The regulation requires extensive technical controls, not just documentation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security risks in risk register; specific security risk documentation
questions.text: A risk register for a new payment processing system has no security risks. A security architect says this must be corrected. What specific security risks should be added and how should they be documented?

answers.text: Security risks belong in a separate security document — not in the project risk register

Security risks belong in the project risk register like all other risks. Specific entries should include: payment card data breach (probability: Medium, impact: Critical, response: Avoid — use tokenization); authentication bypass via credential stuffing (probability: High, impact: HIGH, response: Mitigate — MFA + rate limiting); critical CVE in authentication library (probability: Medium-High, response: Mitigate — automated dependency scanning, 7-day critical patch SLA); SQL injection in payment endpoint (probability: Low-Medium, response: Mitigate — parameterized queries, SAST). Each documented with probability, impact, response strategy, risk owner, and trigger events
'Security breach' as a single risk entry covers all security concerns adequately
Security risks have zero probability in well-built systems — modern security tools eliminate them

explanations.a: Security risks ARE project risks that affect the project's ability to deliver a compliant, trustworthy system. A payment data breach is one of the most severe possible project outcomes. Security risks belong in the project risk register — not in a separate document that may receive less governance attention.
explanations.b: SECURITY RISKS IN PAYMENT SYSTEM RISK REGISTER: RISK 1 — PAYMENT CARD DATA BREACH: ID: SEC-001; Description: Unauthorized access to credit card numbers stored or processed by the application; Probability: Medium (payment systems are frequent attack targets); Impact: Critical (PCI-DSS fines $5K-$100K/month, card brand fines, litigation, reputational damage); Response: AVOID — use payment tokenization; do not store raw PANs; Risk Owner: Security Architect. RISK 2 — AUTHENTICATION BYPASS (CREDENTIAL STUFFING): ID: SEC-002; Description: Automated attacks using leaked credentials from other breaches; Probability: HIGH (billions of leaked credentials circulate; payment systems are prime targets); Impact: HIGH (customer financial loss, regulatory violation); Response: MITIGATE — MFA; rate limiting on login attempts; account lockout; behavioral anomaly detection; Risk Owner: Development Lead. RISK 3 — CRITICAL CVE IN AUTHENTICATION LIBRARY: ID: SEC-003; Description: Critical vulnerability discovered in authentication library post-launch; Probability: Medium-High (major vulnerabilities discovered regularly); Impact: Critical (may enable authentication bypass or remote code execution); Response: MITIGATE — automated dependency scanning; 7-day critical patch SLA; SBOM maintained; Risk Owner: DevOps Lead. RISK 4 — SQL INJECTION IN PAYMENT FLOW: ID: SEC-004; Probability: Low-Medium; Impact: Critical; Response: MITIGATE — parameterized queries required in all payment SQL; SAST scanning in CI/CD; Risk Owner: Development Lead.
explanations.c: A single 'security breach' entry cannot be effectively managed — no specific response strategy, no specific risk owner, no trigger events defined. Specific risks enable specific monitoring, specific responses, and specific accountability.
explanations.d: New vulnerabilities (CVEs) are discovered in libraries daily. Credential stuffing attacks are constant. No security measure provides 100% protection — risk management acknowledges that residual risk always exists and requires active management.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — vendor access management; third-party access controls; JIT access
questions.text: Four external vendors have remote access to production systems for support. The security team wants a third-party access management program. What controls should be included?

answers.text: Give vendors the same access as internal employees — treating them differently creates friction
A shared 'vendor account' is most efficient — one account for all vendor staff simplifies management

Third-party access management requires: uniquely identified accounts per vendor technician (no shared credentials); MFA for all remote access; vendor-specific VPN segmentation (each vendor can only reach their authorized systems); session recording; time-limited just-in-time access for scheduled maintenance windows; all vendor sessions logged and monitored; periodic access review; formal deprovisioning when vendor engagement ends; security questionnaire and NDA before access provisioned
Vendor access control is unnecessary — contractual obligations are sufficient to prevent misuse

explanations.a: Vendors are third parties with different security standards, motivations, and accountability structures than internal employees. Third-party access compromises are among the most common breach vectors (Target, SolarWinds, Kaseya).
explanations.b: A shared vendor account: provides no audit trail (impossible to determine which person performed which action); cannot be deprovisioned for a specific departing vendor employee; creates unauthorized access risk (any person who knows the shared credentials can log in). Shared accounts are an information security anti-pattern.
explanations.c: THIRD-PARTY ACCESS MANAGEMENT PROGRAM: UNIQUELY IDENTIFIED ACCOUNTS: every vendor technician has their own individual account; audit trail shows which specific person performed which action; no shared credentials ever; MFA: mandatory for all vendor remote access; if vendor credentials are stolen via phishing, MFA prevents unauthorized use; VPN WITH VENDOR-SPECIFIC SEGMENTATION: each vendor connects through dedicated VPN tunnel or VPN group; network access control ensures: Vendor A → can only reach their authorized systems; Vendor B → can only reach their authorized systems; prevents lateral movement if a vendor account is compromised; JUST-IN-TIME (JIT) ACCESS: don't give 24/7 standing access for scheduled maintenance; provide access during maintenance window, auto-revoke after; reduces exposure window; SESSION MONITORING AND RECORDING: all vendor sessions recorded (CyberArk, Delinea); alerts for anomalous behavior (unusual access times, bulk queries); PERIODIC ACCESS REVIEW: quarterly review of all vendor accounts; any engagement change triggers access review; FORMAL OFFBOARDING: vendor contract ends → immediate access deprovisioning within 24 hours; formal process, not informal expectation; VENDOR ONBOARDING: security questionnaire (SOC 2 Type II? ISO 27001?); NDA signed; security awareness acknowledgment; access provisioned ONLY after security requirements verified.
explanations.d: Contractual obligations provide legal recourse AFTER a breach. Technical controls PREVENT the breach. Both are needed — contracts for accountability; technical controls for prevention.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — healthcare project security; priority ranking; critical security findings
questions.text: A new PM takes over a healthcare project 3 months before go-live and discovers: (1) production patient data (PHI) is used in testing; (2) a vendor has remote access with no MFA; (3) application logs all actions but they are unmonitored; (4) all 12 developers have admin access to the production database. Prioritize by urgency and describe immediate actions.

answers.text: Address these post-launch — three months to go-live is too close for security remediation

Priority ranking: (1) PHI in test environment — IMMEDIATE: ongoing HIPAA violation; migrate to synthetic/anonymized data today; conduct breach assessment; (2) Vendor access without MFA — CRITICAL/24 HOURS: active attack surface; enforce MFA within 24 hours or suspend vendor access; (3) 12 developers with admin access — HIGH/THIS WEEK: revoke to least privilege; implement JIT elevated access; (4) Unmonitored logs — MEDIUM/2 WEEKS: configure SIEM alerting. All four must be resolved before go-live
Only the PHI issue matters — the other three findings are low risk
All four are equal priority — address them in any order over the next month

explanations.a: Three months before go-live is entirely sufficient time to address all four issues. Launching with PHI in test environments and no MFA on vendor access would be a serious regulatory violation.
explanations.b: URGENCY-RANKED RESPONSE: PRIORITY 1 — PHI IN TESTING (IMMEDIATE — ONGOING HIPAA VIOLATION): this is a HIPAA violation happening RIGHT NOW; every day of continued testing with PHI is an ongoing unauthorized disclosure; IMMEDIATE ACTION (TODAY): stop all testing using production data; audit what PHI has been accessed and by whom (breach determination); notify Privacy Officer and Legal — breach analysis required; begin migration to synthetic/anonymized test data; if breach criteria met under HIPAA: notify HHS OCR within 60 days. PRIORITY 2 — VENDOR REMOTE ACCESS WITHOUT MFA (CRITICAL — WITHIN 24 HOURS): active attack surface; vendor credentials susceptible to credential stuffing, phishing; if compromised, attacker has remote access to healthcare system; IMMEDIATE ACTION: notify vendor: 'MFA required for all remote access effective immediately'; if vendor cannot implement within 24 hours: SUSPEND remote access until MFA is configured; no exceptions. PRIORITY 3 — 12 DEVELOPERS WITH ADMIN ACCESS (HIGH — THIS WEEK): excessive privilege violates HIPAA minimum necessary; if any of 12 accounts is compromised, attacker has admin access to all production data; ACTIONS: audit what admin access is used for; revoke admin access from all except designated DBA; implement just-in-time privileged access: request → approval → time-limited access → auto-revoke → audit log. PRIORITY 4 — UNMONITORED LOGS (MEDIUM — 2 WEEKS): logs exist but breaches won't be detected; however, this doesn't actively enable an attack unlike priorities 1-3; ACTIONS: configure SIEM or log management; set alerts for: multiple failed logins, admin access outside hours, bulk PHI queries; assign monitoring responsibility. ALL FOUR BEFORE GO-LIVE: 3 months provides 12+ weeks of runway — all four correctable well before launch.
explanations.c: All four are genuine security risks. The PHI breach is most urgent (ongoing violation), vendor MFA gap is actively exploitable, admin access is a major privilege violation, and unmonitored logs prevent breach detection.
explanations.d: Urgency ranking ensures critical issues get immediate attention. Equal treatment would allocate time to configuring log alerts (medium urgency) at the expense of the ongoing PHI violation (immediate urgency).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Information security — security throughout project lifecycle; security governance integration
questions.text: A PMO director asks for a framework integrating security across the full project lifecycle for systems handling sensitive personal data. What is the ideal security integration at each phase?

answers.text: Security is only relevant during the execution phase — other phases have no security implications

Security across the project lifecycle: DISCOVERY (include security/compliance costs in business case; initial regulatory assessment); INITIATION (identify security stakeholders — DPO, CISO, legal; document security constraints in charter); PLANNING (security requirements in requirements doc; threat modeling; security risks in risk register; DPIA; security testing in QA plan; security acceptance criteria); EXECUTION (SAST/DAST in CI/CD pipeline; secure coding standards; security incidents reported immediately; vendor access managed; access reviews); CLOSING (all critical/high vulnerabilities resolved; security runbook complete; access deprovisioned to operational scope; security documentation archived; security lessons learned captured)
Security planning in the planning phase is sufficient — execution and closing have no new security requirements
Security should be handled by a separate security project — it doesn't belong in the main project lifecycle

explanations.a: Security implications exist in every phase: discovery (regulatory costs in business case); initiation (security constraints define scope); planning (requirements, risk, QA); execution (secure development, monitoring, incident response); closing (deprovisioning, runbook, security handover).
explanations.b: SECURITY THROUGHOUT THE PROJECT LIFECYCLE: DISCOVERY/CONCEPT: business case includes: GDPR implementation cost ($50K-$200K for medium system); security certification costs (penetration testing $15K-$50K; SOC 2 Type II $25K-$100K); regulatory penalty risk quantified as avoided cost; initial regulatory assessment: what data is processed? (PII, PHI, financial?); which regulations apply?; INITIATION: SECURITY STAKEHOLDERS IDENTIFIED: Data Protection Officer (DPO); CISO or security architect; legal/compliance; add to stakeholder register; CHARTER SECURITY CONSTRAINTS: 'Must comply with GDPR'; 'Must achieve HIPAA compliance'; 'Must pass penetration testing before go-live'; PLANNING: SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: explicit, testable requirements in requirements document; DPIA: required for high-risk processing (GDPR Article 35); THREAT MODELING: STRIDE analysis for the specific architecture; RISK REGISTER: security risks with probability, impact, response, owner; SECURITY TESTING IN QA PLAN: SAST, DAST, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing; SECURITY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: zero Critical/High vulnerabilities unresolved at go-live; EXECUTION: SECURE DEVELOPMENT: OWASP training for developers; parameterized queries; input validation; CONTINUOUS SCANNING: SAST every code commit; DAST against staging weekly; dependency scanning daily; INCIDENT RESPONSE: any security incident reported to CISO within 1 hour; VENDOR SECURITY: MFA enforced; session recording; quarterly access reviews; CLOSING: SECURITY TESTING SIGN-OFF: all Critical/High vulnerabilities resolved; penetration test passed; SECURITY RUNBOOK: complete and validated; DEPROVISIONING: development and test environment access revoked; production access scoped to operations only; SECURITY DOCUMENTATION: architecture, controls inventory, policies archived; SECURITY LESSONS LEARNED: what was discovered late? what should be done earlier? contribute to organizational security knowledge.
explanations.c: Security must be practiced throughout execution (secure coding, incident response, access control) and formalized in closing (deprovisioning, runbook, security acceptance). Planning alone is insufficient.
explanations.d: Security is an integral component of the main project — not a separate project. Separating it creates coordination failures, missed requirements, and security that doesn't fit the system design.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — HIPAA; Protected Health Information; covered entities; project requirements
questions.text: A project is building a patient portal for a hospital. The security architect says HIPAA applies. What is HIPAA and what basic requirements must the project address?

answers.text: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) is US federal law that protects Protected Health Information (PHI). Project requirements include: technical safeguards (encryption of PHI at rest and in transit; access controls; audit logs); administrative safeguards (policies and procedures; workforce training); physical safeguards (workstation controls; device disposal); minimum necessary standard (access to PHI limited to what's needed for the job function); Business Associate Agreements (BAA) with all vendors handling PHI
HIPAA is a voluntary set of industry guidelines — compliance is optional
HIPAA only applies to paper medical records — electronic systems are exempt
HIPAA compliance is only required after a breach occurs — proactive compliance is optional

explanations.a: HIPAA OVERVIEW AND PROJECT REQUIREMENTS: WHAT IS PHI: individually identifiable health information in any form (electronic, paper, oral) relating to past, present, or future health status, medical care, or payment for care; includes: diagnosis codes, lab results, prescription records, appointment dates combined with patient identity; COVERED ENTITIES: health plans, healthcare providers, healthcare clearinghouses; BUSINESS ASSOCIATES: vendors who handle PHI on behalf of covered entities (IT vendors, cloud providers, billing services); SECURITY RULE TECHNICAL SAFEGUARDS: ENCRYPTION: PHI encrypted at rest and in transit; ACCESS CONTROLS: unique user authentication; automatic logoff; AUDIT CONTROLS: hardware/software activity logs recording access to PHI; INTEGRITY: PHI must not be improperly altered or destroyed; TRANSMISSION SECURITY: encrypted transmission of PHI over networks; MINIMUM NECESSARY STANDARD: users access only the PHI needed for their specific job function (aligns with RBAC); BUSINESS ASSOCIATE AGREEMENTS (BAA): any vendor who touches PHI must sign a BAA; the BAA specifies security obligations; cloud providers offering HIPAA-eligible services: AWS HIPAA BAA, Azure HIPAA BAA, Google Cloud HIPAA BAA; PRIVACY RULE REQUIREMENTS: patient rights to access, amend, and receive accounting of disclosures; notices of privacy practices; BREACH NOTIFICATION RULE: notify affected individuals within 60 days; notify HHS; large breaches (500+ individuals in a state) → notify media.
explanations.b: HIPAA is mandatory federal law with civil penalties ranging from $100 to $50,000 per violation (up to $1.9M per violation category per year) and criminal penalties including imprisonment for willful violations.
explanations.c: HIPAA's Security Rule specifically governs ELECTRONIC Protected Health Information (ePHI). Electronic systems are the primary focus of the Security Rule.
explanations.d: HIPAA compliance is required proactively — before a breach. Proactive compliance is what prevents breaches. Reactive compliance after a breach does not eliminate liability.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — PCI-DSS; payment card data; cardholder data environment; compliance levels
questions.text: A project is adding payment processing to an e-commerce platform. The security team says PCI-DSS applies. What is PCI-DSS and what key requirements must the project address?

answers.text: PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is a security standard for all organizations that store, process, or transmit cardholder data. Key requirements: protect stored cardholder data (don't store CVV codes ever; encrypt PANs if stored); encrypt transmission of cardholder data over public networks (TLS 1.2+); implement strong access controls (MFA, least privilege); maintain vulnerability management (regular patching, penetration testing); maintain an information security policy
PCI-DSS only applies to banks — e-commerce companies are exempt
PCI-DSS only applies to large organizations processing millions of transactions
Using a payment gateway provider means PCI-DSS requirements don't apply to the merchant

explanations.a: PCI-DSS OVERVIEW: WHAT IT COVERS: any organization accepting credit/debit card payments is subject to PCI-DSS; issued by the PCI Security Standards Council (founded by Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, JCB); 12 CORE REQUIREMENTS: Build and maintain a secure network; Protect cardholder data; Maintain a vulnerability management program; Implement strong access control measures; Regularly monitor and test networks; Maintain an information security policy; KEY TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: DO NOT STORE: CVV/CVC codes; full track data; PIN data; these must NEVER be stored — ever; ENCRYPTION: if PANs are stored (which should be avoided via tokenization): encrypt with AES-128/256; mask PANs when displayed (show only last 4 digits: ****1234); TRANSMISSION: TLS 1.2 or higher for all card data transmission; VULNERABILITY MANAGEMENT: quarterly vulnerability scanning; annual penetration testing; anti-malware; COMPLIANCE LEVELS based on annual transaction volume: Level 1: >6M transactions/year (most rigorous — annual QSA audit); Level 4: <20,000 e-commerce transactions/year (self-assessment questionnaire); NON-COMPLIANCE PENALTIES: card brand fines $5,000-$100,000/month; revocation of card acceptance privileges; mandatory forensic investigation after a breach.
explanations.b: PCI-DSS applies to ALL entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data regardless of whether they are a bank, e-commerce company, retailer, or non-profit.
explanations.c: PCI-DSS applies to all organizations regardless of transaction volume. The level of assessment rigor varies by volume (Levels 1-4), but no merchant is exempt.
explanations.d: Using a payment gateway reduces PCI scope but doesn't eliminate it. If the merchant never sees card data (e.g., using Stripe's hosted fields or Stripe Checkout), scope is minimal. But if card data passes through the merchant's systems even briefly, PCI-DSS applies.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — SOX; Sarbanes-Oxley; financial controls; IT general controls
questions.text: A project is implementing a new financial reporting system for a publicly traded company. The compliance team says SOX applies. What is SOX and what IT-specific requirements must the project address?

answers.text: SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley Act) is US federal law requiring accurate financial reporting and internal controls for publicly traded companies. IT General Controls (ITGCs) the project must address: access controls (logical access to financial systems controlled and reviewed); change management (all system changes formally documented and approved); segregation of duties (person entering transactions cannot approve them); audit trail completeness (all financial transactions logged immutably); backup and recovery (financial data can be recovered)
SOX only applies to the finance department — IT projects are exempt from SOX requirements
SOX compliance is achieved by having the CFO sign off on the system — no technical controls required
SOX only applies to the external financial statements — internal systems don't need SOX controls

explanations.a: SOX OVERVIEW AND IT REQUIREMENTS: BACKGROUND: enacted in 2002 after Enron, WorldCom accounting scandals; SECTION 302: CEO/CFO must personally certify accuracy of financial reports; SECTION 404: management must document and assess internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR); external auditors must independently assess these controls; IT GENERAL CONTROLS (ITGCs): logical ACCESS CONTROLS: only authorized users can access financial systems; quarterly access reviews (user accounts certified by access owners); immediate deprovisioning when employees leave; CHANGE MANAGEMENT: all changes to financial systems require formal approval (change request, testing, CAB approval); unauthorized changes create audit findings; emergency changes require retroactive approval; SEGREGATION OF DUTIES (SOD): person who creates a journal entry cannot approve it; person who manages user access cannot access financial data; IT administrators should not be able to bypass application-level controls; AUDIT TRAILS: immutable logs of all financial transactions; who changed what, when, and why; log tampering must be detectable; BACKUP AND RECOVERY: financial data must be recoverable within defined RTO/RPO; backup procedures documented and tested; EXTERNAL AUDITOR IMPLICATIONS: the auditor will test these controls; findings that reveal inadequate controls → management remediation; material weaknesses → potential restatement of financial reports → severe consequences.
explanations.b: IT systems that support financial reporting are subject to SOX IT General Controls. A financial reporting system is one of the most directly SOX-relevant IT systems an organization can build.
explanations.c: SOX requires TECHNICAL controls — not just executive certification. Section 404 requires documented, tested, effective internal controls. Management's signature without underlying technical controls would be a material weakness.
explanations.d: Financial systems that feed into external financial statements are exactly the systems SOX ITGC requirements target. The financial reporting system is the core of SOX technical compliance scope.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — GDPR; CCPA; data privacy regulations; applicability and scope
questions.text: A project manager is not sure whether GDPR or CCPA applies to a new customer analytics platform. The platform will process data from customers in the EU, California, and other US states. What determines which privacy regulations apply?

answers.text: GDPR applies when processing personal data of EU/EEA residents (regardless of where the organization is located); CCPA applies when processing personal data of California residents and the organization meets size thresholds (annual revenue >$25M, or processes data of >100,000 consumers, or derives >50% of revenue from selling personal data). Both may apply simultaneously — the platform must comply with the most restrictive applicable requirement for each data category
Privacy regulations are optional — organizations choose which regulations to comply with
Only one privacy law can apply at a time — organizations choose the most convenient one
Privacy regulations only apply to the country where the company is headquartered

explanations.a: PRIVACY REGULATION APPLICABILITY: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): JURISDICTION: applies to processing personal data of EU/EEA residents; TRIGGER: location of the DATA SUBJECT (the person whose data is processed) — not the organization's location; SCOPE: any organization processing EU residents' personal data must comply; APPLICABILITY TEST: Are any of our customers EU/EEA residents? → YES → GDPR applies; CCPA/CPRA (California Consumer Privacy Act / California Privacy Rights Act): JURISDICTION: applies to California residents' personal data; TRIGGER: location of the data subject; BUSINESS SIZE THRESHOLDS (any ONE of these): annual gross revenue >$25M; buys, sells, or receives data of >100,000 consumers/households annually; derives >50% of annual revenue from selling personal data; SIMULTANEOUS APPLICABILITY: both GDPR and CCPA can apply to the same organization; when they conflict, comply with the MORE RESTRICTIVE requirement; PRACTICAL APPROACH: map each customer's data jurisdiction; apply the most restrictive applicable regulation to that data; the platform must: have GDPR-compliant consent management for EU data; have CCPA-compliant opt-out mechanisms for California data; likely use the strictest standard globally for simplicity.
explanations.b: Privacy regulations are mandatory law with significant penalties. GDPR: up to €20M or 4% of global annual revenue; CCPA/CPRA: up to $7,500 per intentional violation. Compliance is not optional.
explanations.c: Multiple privacy regulations can and do apply simultaneously. An organization processing data from EU and California residents must comply with both GDPR and CCPA.
explanations.d: Privacy regulations are primarily determined by the location of the DATA SUBJECT (the person whose data is processed) — not the company's headquarters. A US company processing EU resident data must comply with GDPR.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — identifying applicable regulations; regulatory landscape analysis; compliance as project requirement
questions.text: A project manager is starting a project to build a patient billing system for a US hospital that also has international patients. Before finalizing requirements, she needs to identify all applicable regulations. What regulatory landscape analysis should she conduct?

answers.text: Regulatory landscape analysis: identify the data types processed (PHI for US patients → HIPAA; payment card data → PCI-DSS; EU patient personal data → GDPR; California patient data → CCPA/CPRA); identify sector-specific requirements (CMS requirements for Medicare/Medicaid billing; state-specific privacy laws); engage legal and compliance team as stakeholders early; document all applicable regulations in the project charter and requirements document; assess compliance costs in the business case
Only ask the legal department after the system is built — compliance requirements can be added at the end
US hospitals only need to comply with HIPAA — international regulations don't apply to US organizations
Compliance requirements are the same for all healthcare systems — no individual analysis is needed

explanations.a: REGULATORY LANDSCAPE ANALYSIS for patient billing system: DATA TYPE MAPPING: PHI (health information): HIPAA Security Rule, Privacy Rule, Breach Notification Rule; Payment Card Data (credit card billing): PCI-DSS; EU Patient Personal Data: GDPR (if any EU/EEA residents are patients); California Patients: CCPA/CPRA (if hospital meets size thresholds); Financial Data (accounting records): SOX (if hospital is publicly traded or government-funded with specific reporting requirements); SECTOR-SPECIFIC REGULATIONS: CMS (Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services): coding accuracy requirements; HIPAA transaction standards (EDI 837 for billing); state Medicaid billing requirements; state medical records retention laws (typically 7-10 years); REGULATORY ENGAGEMENT PROCESS: add compliance/legal team to stakeholder register; schedule regulatory requirements session in planning; map each regulation to specific project requirements; add compliance milestones to the project schedule (e.g., HIPAA review at design gate); include compliance testing in QA plan; BUSINESS CASE UPDATE: each regulation adds cost: HIPAA compliance: $15K-$50K for small systems; GDPR compliance: $50K-$200K; PCI-DSS compliance: $5K-$100K depending on scope; these costs must appear in the business case.
explanations.b: Adding compliance requirements after the system is built is the most expensive possible approach. Privacy and security controls built into architecture from the start cost a fraction of retrofitting them into a completed system.
explanations.c: HIPAA applies because it's a US healthcare facility. GDPR applies because the hospital treats EU residents — GDPR's applicability is determined by the data subject's location, not the organization's. CCPA applies for California patients if thresholds are met. Multiple regulations apply simultaneously.
explanations.d: Every healthcare project has a unique regulatory profile based on: patient demographics; data types processed; geographic scope; organization type (for-profit, non-profit, government); transaction types. Individual analysis is always required.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — HIPAA Business Associate Agreement; third-party PHI handling; vendor compliance
questions.text: A healthcare IT project is selecting a cloud platform to host the patient portal. The compliance officer says a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is required with the cloud provider. What is a BAA, why is it required, and what should the PM verify before selecting the provider?

answers.text: A BAA (Business Associate Agreement) is a legally required contract under HIPAA between a covered entity and any vendor (Business Associate) who accesses, processes, or stores PHI on its behalf. The PM must verify: the cloud provider offers a HIPAA BAA (not all providers do); the BAA covers the specific services being used; the services used are within the provider's HIPAA-eligible service list; the provider's security controls meet HIPAA requirements; without a signed BAA, using that vendor for PHI storage is a HIPAA violation
A BAA is a marketing document — it demonstrates the provider cares about healthcare
BAAs are optional — cloud providers automatically comply with HIPAA by default
The cloud provider's own HIPAA compliance means the customer doesn't need a BAA

explanations.a: HIPAA BUSINESS ASSOCIATE AGREEMENT (BAA): DEFINITION: a legally required contract between: COVERED ENTITY (the hospital, health plan, healthcare provider) and a BUSINESS ASSOCIATE (any vendor who accesses, creates, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of the covered entity); WHY REQUIRED: HIPAA makes covered entities responsible for their business associates' PHI handling; without a BAA, using a vendor for PHI creates HIPAA liability; the BAA transfers some of that responsibility to the vendor contractually; BAA CONTENT: what PHI the Business Associate will access; permitted uses of PHI; security requirements; breach notification obligations (notify covered entity within 60 days of discovering a breach); return or destruction of PHI at contract end; CLOUD PROVIDER BAA VERIFICATION: DOES THE PROVIDER OFFER A BAA? AWS: yes (requires agreement through AWS console); Microsoft Azure: yes; Google Cloud: yes; some smaller providers do NOT offer BAAs — automatically disqualified for PHI; HIPAA-ELIGIBLE SERVICES: not all services from a HIPAA BAA provider are HIPAA-eligible; check the provider's HIPAA eligibility list: AWS: most compute/storage services are HIPAA-eligible; some AI/ML services are not; the services used must all be on the HIPAA-eligible list; BAA EXECUTION: the BAA must be signed BEFORE any PHI is stored or processed on the platform; signing the BAA AFTER data is already in the system means PHI was stored without required safeguards — a HIPAA violation.
explanations.b: A BAA is a legally mandated contract under 45 CFR Part 164 — it is a binding legal document with significant compliance implications, not marketing material.
explanations.c: HIPAA compliance is a shared responsibility between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider's HIPAA controls protect the infrastructure — the customer must still implement application-level controls and execute the BAA. BAAs are not automatic.
explanations.d: The provider's own compliance is necessary but not sufficient. The BAA is required additionally because: it creates explicit contractual obligations specific to the customer's PHI; it establishes breach notification requirements between the parties; HIPAA regulations explicitly require a BAA — compliance without a BAA is a HIPAA violation regardless of the provider's security posture.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — PCI-DSS scope reduction; tokenization; cardholder data environment
questions.text: A PM is designing a new e-commerce checkout system. The security architect recommends 'reducing PCI scope through tokenization.' What does scope reduction mean and how does tokenization achieve it?

answers.text: PCI scope = all systems, people, and processes that store, process, or transmit cardholder data. Scope reduction means minimizing the systems that touch card data. Tokenization achieves this: when a customer enters card details, the card data goes directly to a PCI-compliant payment processor (Stripe, Braintree); the processor stores the card number and returns a token (random string) to the merchant; the merchant stores only the token — not the card number; result: the merchant's systems never receive or store actual card data, drastically reducing PCI scope
PCI scope cannot be reduced — all payment systems require the same level of compliance
Tokenization means encrypting card numbers — the encrypted numbers still require full PCI compliance
Scope reduction only applies to small merchants — large merchants must maintain full PCI scope

explanations.a: PCI SCOPE REDUCTION THROUGH TOKENIZATION: WHAT IS PCI SCOPE: the Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) includes all components that store, process, or transmit cardholder data AND all connected systems; PCI compliance requirements apply to ALL in-scope systems; wider scope = more compliance burden; SCOPE REDUCTION GOAL: minimize the CDE to minimize compliance cost and risk; TOKENIZATION MECHANISM: CUSTOMER CHECKOUT: customer enters card number in the browser; DIRECT-TO-PROCESSOR: using iframe or JavaScript library (Stripe.js, Braintree SDK), card data is sent DIRECTLY from the browser to the processor's servers; the card number NEVER touches the merchant's servers; PROCESSOR STORES CARD: the processor stores the actual card number in their PCI-compliant vault; TOKEN RETURNED: the processor returns a token (e.g., 'tok_1234567890abcdef') to the merchant; MERCHANT STORES TOKEN: merchant stores only the token; for future purchases, passes the token to the processor; RESULT: merchant's servers, databases, and applications never receive or store actual card numbers; these systems are now OUT OF PCI SCOPE (or in very limited scope); COMPLIANCE BENEFIT: A large e-commerce company processing 2 million transactions/year: WITHOUT tokenization: Level 1 PCI compliance requiring annual QSA audit ($50,000-$200,000/year); WITH tokenization: potentially Level 4 or reduced Level 1 scope significantly reducing compliance burden; MERCHANT STILL IN SCOPE FOR: security of the tokenization implementation; authentication to the payment processor's API; fraud monitoring and chargebacks.
explanations.b: PCI scope reduction is not only possible — it is the recommended best practice for e-commerce merchants. The PCI DSS explicitly supports and encourages scope reduction through architecture choices.
explanations.c: Tokenization is fundamentally different from encryption. Encryption: the card number exists in encrypted form — the system is still in PCI scope; Tokenization: a meaningless token replaces the card number — no card data exists on the system.
explanations.d: Scope reduction through tokenization is available to merchants of all sizes. In fact, small merchants benefit most because full PCI compliance is proportionally more burdensome for them.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — SOX IT General Controls; change management for financial systems; segregation of duties
questions.text: An external auditor is reviewing IT General Controls (ITGCs) for a publicly traded company's new financial reporting system. The auditor identifies three SOX deficiencies: developers can deploy code directly to production without change management approval; no quarterly access reviews are being conducted; and the same person who enters journal entries can also approve them. How should each be remediated?

answers.text: These findings don't need remediation — IT controls are advisory, not mandatory under SOX
Only finding 3 (same person enters and approves) requires remediation — the others are IT operational issues

Three SOX ITGC remediations: (1) Developer direct deployment: implement formal change management (all deployments require change request, testing documentation, change advisory board approval, and separate deployment team); (2) No access reviews: implement quarterly access certification (system owners review and certify each user's access is still appropriate); (3) Same person enters and approves: implement segregation of duties (separate the entry role from the approval role — no user can have both)
Ask the external auditor to not report these findings — negotiating with auditors resolves SOX findings

explanations.a: SOX IT General Control findings are serious compliance deficiencies. Material weaknesses can require: financial statement restatements; regulatory enforcement; executive criminal liability (Section 302 certification); management cannot certify effective internal controls when material weaknesses exist.
explanations.b: All three findings are material SOX ITGC deficiencies. The auditor will report all three. Ignoring two of three would result in an adverse ICFR opinion.
explanations.c: SOX ITGC REMEDIATION: FINDING 1 — DEVELOPER DIRECT PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT (CHANGE MANAGEMENT DEFICIENCY): RISK: unauthorized code changes to financial systems without approval; a developer could modify financial calculation logic without oversight; REMEDIATION: FORMAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT PROCESS: all code changes require a Change Request (CR); CR must document: what changed, why, testing performed, risk assessment; CR requires approval from: development manager, IT security, business owner; separate deployment team (not the developer who wrote the code) performs production deployment; Emergency changes require retroactive approval within 24 hours; all changes logged in change management system (ServiceNow, Jira); FINDING 2 — NO QUARTERLY ACCESS REVIEWS (ACCESS CONTROL DEFICIENCY): RISK: former employees retain access; users have access beyond their current job function; REMEDIATION: QUARTERLY ACCESS CERTIFICATION: every system owner receives a report of all users with access; owner actively reviews and certifies each user: still employed? still needs this access level?; certifications documented in the access review tool; accounts flagged as 'no longer needed' deprovisioned within 5 business days; results reported to internal audit; FINDING 3 — SAME PERSON ENTERS AND APPROVES (SEGREGATION OF DUTIES DEFICIENCY): RISK: a single user could create fraudulent journal entries and self-approve them; classic SOX fraud vector (Enron); REMEDIATION: SEGREGATION OF DUTIES: separate ENTRY role from APPROVAL role in the application; technical enforcement: the system must prevent a user with the entry role from approving; workflow: journal entry creator → automatically routes to a different approver; the system CANNOT allow self-approval; document the role matrix showing SOD enforcement.
explanations.d: External auditors operate independently — they have a professional obligation to report findings accurately. Asking an auditor not to report a finding is an attempt to interfere with an audit — potentially illegal.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — regulatory change management; new regulation impact on existing projects
questions.text: A project team is 8 months into a 12-month development effort when a new data privacy regulation is announced with an 18-month compliance deadline. The regulation requires data localization (customer data cannot leave the customer's home country). The project was designed for a single global data center. What should the project manager do?

answers.text: Ignore the new regulation — it applies only to systems built after the compliance deadline
Complete the original system and build compliance into a Phase 2 project

Treat the regulation as a scope change: immediately assess the technical impact of data localization on the current architecture; consult legal to confirm applicability and timeline; submit a formal change request for the required architectural changes (regional data centers or data residency features in the cloud platform); update the risk register with the regulatory compliance risk; reschedule if needed — with 18 months until the compliance deadline and 12 months of planned project duration, a 4-6 month architecture change may still be achievable before the deadline
Simply add a legal disclaimer to the privacy policy acknowledging the regulation

explanations.a: New regulations with explicit compliance deadlines apply to all systems operating at the deadline date — not just new systems built after the announcement. Systems in development that launch before the deadline must be compliant.
explanations.b: 'Phase 2' for regulatory compliance is a high-risk strategy. If the regulation's effective date is before Phase 2 launches, the organization operates non-compliantly — facing fines, enforcement actions, and reputational damage. Legal must evaluate whether this risk is acceptable.
explanations.c: REGULATORY CHANGE IMPACT MANAGEMENT: IMMEDIATE ASSESSMENT: APPLICABILITY: does this regulation apply to our customers? (which countries? which data types?); TECHNICAL IMPACT: data localization = customer data stays in the customer's country; current single global data center architecture = non-compliant; technical options: AWS/Azure/GCP data residency features (store data in specific regions); build or procure regional data centers in required jurisdictions; architectural changes required: multi-region deployment; customer country-based data routing; legal assessment: compliance deadline (18 months); when will the project launch? (4 months from now); does the system need to be compliant at launch or at the regulation's effective date?; FORMAL CHANGE REQUEST: document the required architectural changes; scope impact (additional work); schedule impact (4-6 months for architecture changes?); cost impact (multi-region infrastructure is more expensive); DECISION OPTIONS: EXTEND THE PROJECT: delay launch to incorporate localization architecture; DESCOPE: launch without the affected regions initially; ACCEPT RISK: launch globally and pursue compliance as Phase 2 (legal must evaluate this risk); RESCHEDULE IF NEEDED: with 18-month compliance deadline and 4 months of project remaining, there may still be time to incorporate changes and launch compliant; RISK REGISTER UPDATE: add 'regulatory non-compliance' risk with revised probability and impact.
explanations.d: A privacy policy disclaimer does not achieve regulatory compliance. Regulators evaluate technical implementation, not policy language. Saying 'we acknowledge the regulation' while processing data in violation of it provides no legal protection.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — audit readiness; internal controls documentation; compliance evidence
questions.text: A PM is preparing for an internal audit of the project's compliance with ISO 27001 (information security management). The auditor will review documentation and test controls. What should the PM do to ensure audit readiness?

answers.text: Create documentation just before the audit — auditors only review what's presented on audit day
Only the IT security team needs to prepare — the PM has no role in IT compliance audits

Audit readiness requires evidence of actual, consistently operating controls. Ensure controls have been operating throughout the audit period. Organize existing evidence (access review records, change logs, scan reports, incident logs). Identify and close control gaps before the audit. Brief team members on what auditors will ask and how to demonstrate the controls they own
Ask the auditor to skip testing and only review policy documentation — policies demonstrate intent

explanations.a: Creating documentation just before the audit (often called 'audit-washing') is fraudulent when presented as evidence of controls operating throughout the period. Auditors check timestamps, corroborating evidence, and interview team members — manufactured documentation is often detected.
explanations.b: The PM oversees the project's compliance posture and ensures team members are prepared. Audit preparation is a cross-functional responsibility the PM coordinates.
explanations.c: AUDIT READINESS for ISO 27001: CONTINUOUS CONTROL OPERATION: audits assess controls operating EFFECTIVELY over the audit period (typically 12 months); evidence must span the entire period — not just the week before; EVIDENCE ORGANIZATION: ACCESS CONTROL EVIDENCE: quarterly access review records (dates, reviewers, certifications); provisioning/deprovisioning request logs; CHANGE MANAGEMENT: change request logs with approval chains and testing documentation; VULNERABILITY MANAGEMENT: weekly scan reports; remediation tracking with dates; INCIDENT MANAGEMENT: incident log with dates, classifications, resolutions; SECURITY TRAINING: training completion records with timestamps; CONTROL GAP IDENTIFICATION: pre-audit internal review to find gaps; implement missing controls immediately; gather some evidence before audit date; document the gap and remediation; TEAM BRIEFING: auditors interview team members; each person should know: what control they own; how they perform it; where evidence is stored; RESPOND PROMPTLY: answer auditor requests within 24 hours; organize evidence clearly.
explanations.d: Auditors test OPERATING EFFECTIVENESS of controls — not just the existence of policies. 'We have a policy' without evidence that the policy is followed is an audit finding.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — data retention and deletion; records management compliance; retention schedules
questions.text: A project manager is designing a customer data platform. The legal team provides a data retention schedule: customer transaction records must be retained for 7 years (tax regulations); personal profile data must be deleted within 2 years of account inactivity (GDPR data minimization); payment card data must be deleted immediately after transaction completion (PCI-DSS). How should these requirements be built into the system?

answers.text: Retain all data indefinitely — storage is cheap and more data is always better for analytics
Manual review processes can handle retention — automated enforcement is unnecessary

Build automated retention enforcement into the system architecture: implement a retention management module that automatically applies different retention periods to different data types; classify data at ingestion (transaction record vs. profile vs. payment); automated deletion workflow triggered by retention schedule; deletion audit logs (proof of deletion for regulatory inspectors); legal hold capability (pause automated deletion for litigation); test the automated deletion in the QA plan
One retention period for all data simplifies compliance — choose 7 years and apply it to everything

explanations.a: Retaining all data indefinitely directly violates: GDPR data minimization principle ('not kept in a form which permits identification for longer than is necessary'); GDPR storage limitation ('kept for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed'); PCI-DSS prohibition on storing sensitive authentication data; organizations that retain data longer than required have MORE regulatory exposure — they hold more data that can be breached.
explanations.b: At scale (millions of records), manual deletion processes fail: inconsistent application; missed deletions; no audit trail; unmanageable labor cost. Regulators specifically look for automated, systematic enforcement with evidence.
explanations.c: AUTOMATED RETENTION ENFORCEMENT: WHY AUTOMATED (NOT MANUAL): manual deletion is error-prone and inconsistent; regulatory inspectors want evidence that deletion ACTUALLY happened; manual processes break down at scale; RETENTION MANAGEMENT MODULE: DATA CLASSIFICATION AT INGESTION: tag each data record with its type (transaction record, customer profile, payment data); RETENTION CLOCK: start the retention clock from a defined trigger event (transaction date for tax records; last account activity for profile data; transaction completion for card data); AUTOMATED DELETION WORKFLOW: when the retention period expires, automatically schedule for deletion; soft delete (flag as 'deleted') then hard delete (actual removal) with configurable timing; DELETION EVIDENCE: audit log recording: data type, quantity of records deleted, deletion date, deletion method; this is the proof of deletion required by regulators; DIFFERENT PERIODS FOR DIFFERENT DATA: transaction records: 7 years from transaction date (tax compliance); customer profile: 2 years from last account activity (GDPR minimization); payment card data: immediate deletion after transaction authorization (PCI-DSS — never store sensitive authentication data); LEGAL HOLD: capability to pause automated deletion for specific records under litigation hold; TESTING: include retention/deletion automation tests in the QA plan; verify records are actually deleted, not just hidden.
explanations.d: Applying the 7-year retention period to all data violates: GDPR: personal profile data must be deleted within 2 years of inactivity; PCI-DSS: payment card data must be deleted immediately after transaction; applying inappropriate retention periods to regulated data categories creates regulatory violations.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — CCPA consumer rights; opt-out mechanisms; data sale definition
questions.text: A project is adding CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) compliance to a consumer app. The product manager says: 'We don't sell customer data so CCPA doesn't apply.' The legal team disagrees. Who is correct and what CCPA requirements must the app address?

answers.text: The product manager is correct — CCPA only applies to organizations that sell customer data
CCPA only applies when data is sold for direct monetary compensation — ad network sharing is excluded

The legal team is correct: CCPA's definition of 'selling' is broader than direct payment for data and may include sharing data with third-party ad networks for targeted advertising. CCPA requirements the app must address: right to know (what data is collected and how it's used); right to delete (consumers can request deletion of personal data); right to opt-out of 'sale' of personal data (including ad network sharing); right to non-discrimination (consumers who opt out can't be denied service); required privacy disclosures
CCPA compliance only requires updating the privacy policy — no technical changes needed

explanations.a: CCPA's definition of 'selling' is expansive and specifically designed to prevent organizations from evading the regulation by calling data transfers something other than 'selling.'
explanations.b: This is exactly the misconception CCPA was designed to address. Sharing data with ad networks for advertising services IS considered a 'sale' under CCPA's broad definition.
explanations.c: CCPA REQUIREMENTS AND BROAD DEFINITION OF 'SALE': BROAD DEFINITION OF 'SELLING' PERSONAL DATA: CCPA defines 'sell' as: 'selling, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer's personal information by the business to another business or third party for monetary or other valuable consideration'; 'VALUABLE CONSIDERATION' includes: direct payment (traditional data sale); receiving advertising services in exchange for sharing data (ad network tracking pixels); receiving enhanced functionality from a third party in exchange for data; THE PRODUCT MANAGER IS WRONG: sharing data with ad networks (Google Ads, Facebook Ads) in exchange for ad targeting capabilities IS a 'sale' under CCPA; CCPA TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: RIGHT TO KNOW: privacy disclosure listing all categories of personal data collected and how it's used; RIGHT TO DELETE: consumer can request deletion of personal data; technical implementation: deletion workflow; audit log; 30-day response window; RIGHT TO OPT-OUT: 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' link prominently displayed; technical implementation: mechanism to stop data sharing with ad networks for opted-out consumers; RIGHT TO CORRECT (CPRA): consumer can request correction of inaccurate personal data; RIGHT TO NON-DISCRIMINATION: consumers who exercise rights cannot be denied goods/services; CPRA ENHANCEMENTS: CPRA (California Privacy Rights Act) strengthened CCPA in 2023: added right to limit use of sensitive personal information; created California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) for enforcement; COMPLIANCE APPROACH: implement consent management platform that handles CCPA opt-out; configure ad networks to exclude opted-out consumers from targeting.
explanations.d: CCPA requires technical implementation of consumer rights (deletion workflows, opt-out mechanisms) — a privacy policy update without technical controls does not achieve compliance.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — compliance frameworks; NIST CSF; ISO 27001; SOC 2; choosing a framework
questions.text: A startup is building a B2B SaaS platform. Enterprise customers require the company to demonstrate information security maturity. The PM asks: 'Should we pursue ISO 27001 certification, SOC 2 Type II attestation, or NIST CSF alignment?' How should the PM choose?

answers.text: All three are identical — choose the cheapest option
Startups should avoid security frameworks — they add cost without value

Choose based on customer requirements and geography: SOC 2 Type II is preferred by US enterprise customers (established standard for SaaS); ISO 27001 is recognized globally and preferred by international customers; NIST CSF is a self-assessment framework without third-party attestation (useful internally but less recognized externally). For a US-focused B2B SaaS startup, SOC 2 Type II is typically the most valuable starting point, with ISO 27001 added for international expansion
NIST CSF always provides the highest external assurance for enterprise customers

explanations.a: The three frameworks have fundamentally different structures, audiences, and assurance mechanisms. They are not interchangeable.
explanations.b: Security frameworks are competitive advantages for SaaS startups — enterprise customers increasingly require them as a procurement condition. Lack of SOC 2 can be a disqualifier in enterprise sales.
explanations.c: SECURITY FRAMEWORK COMPARISON: SOC 2 TYPE II: ISSUING BODY: AICPA (American Institute of CPAs); WHAT IT IS: an audit of a service organization's controls related to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy; TYPE II: tests controls over a period (typically 6-12 months) demonstrating sustained operation; AUDIENCE: US enterprise customers in SaaS, cloud, and managed services; RECOGNITION: highly recognized by US enterprise procurement; many enterprise SaaS contracts require SOC 2; COST: $20,000-$80,000 for initial Type II audit; ISO 27001: ISSUING BODY: International Organization for Standardization; WHAT IT IS: an international standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS); CERTIFICATION: external auditor certifies that the ISMS meets the standard; AUDIENCE: globally recognized; required by international enterprise customers; European and APAC customers often require ISO 27001; COST: $30,000-$100,000 for certification; NIST CSF (Cybersecurity Framework): ISSUING BODY: US National Institute of Standards and Technology; WHAT IT IS: a voluntary framework for managing cybersecurity risk (5 functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover); AUDIENCE: primarily US government and critical infrastructure; useful for internal maturity assessment; NO THIRD-PARTY CERTIFICATION: organizations self-assess or use the framework for internal guidance; limited external recognition as a standalone attestation; RECOMMENDATION for US B2B SaaS: START with SOC 2 Type II (most enterprise customers request it); ADD ISO 27001 when international expansion begins; USE NIST CSF internally to guide security program maturity.
explanations.d: NIST CSF doesn't provide third-party attestation — it's a self-assessment framework. External assurance requires SOC 2 (audited by CPA firm) or ISO 27001 (certified by accredited certification body).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — HIPAA breach notification; breach analysis; breach response timeline
questions.text: During a healthcare project's warranty period, a developer discovers a misconfiguration that may have exposed patient records to unauthorized access for 3 weeks. The PM is notified. What is the correct compliance response sequence under HIPAA?

answers.text: Fix the misconfiguration quietly — no notification is required if the access was accidental
Wait 6 months before notifying anyone — investigate fully before making any disclosures

HIPAA breach response: immediately contain the exposure (fix misconfiguration); conduct a breach analysis to determine if a breach actually occurred (4-factor test: nature of PHI involved, who accessed it, whether accessed, risk to individuals); if breach is confirmed, notify HHS within 60 days of discovery and notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay; if 500+ individuals in a state are affected, also notify prominent local media outlets; document the entire incident and response
Only notify patients if they complain — passive disclosure is sufficient for small breaches

explanations.a: HIPAA's Breach Notification Rule has mandatory notification requirements. Accidental unauthorized access is not automatically exempt — the breach analysis determines whether notification is required. Willful suppression of a known breach is a serious violation with criminal penalties.
explanations.b: HIPAA notification deadlines are absolute: 60 days from discovery for HHS (large breaches); without unreasonable delay for individuals. Waiting 6 months is a violation of the notification rule even if the investigation is still ongoing.
explanations.c: HIPAA BREACH NOTIFICATION RESPONSE: STEP 1 — IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT: fix the misconfiguration immediately; preserve logs and evidence for investigation; STEP 2 — BREACH ANALYSIS (4-FACTOR RISK ASSESSMENT): NATURE AND EXTENT OF PHI: what specific PHI was potentially exposed? (diagnosis, treatment, payment?); severity scale: sensitive categories (mental health, HIV, substance use) = higher risk; WHO ACCESSED: was it another healthcare entity (lower risk) or unknown/unauthorized person (higher risk)?; WAS PHI ACTUALLY ACCESSED: server logs showing the misconfigured endpoint was accessed; were records actually viewed vs. just accessible?; RISK TO INDIVIDUALS: likelihood that the exposure created meaningful risk to the individual's privacy; IF RISK IS LOW: document the analysis; no notification required (but document why); IF BREACH IS CONFIRMED (significant risk): STEP 3 — NOTIFICATION TIMELINE: INDIVIDUALS: notify without unreasonable delay, no later than 60 days after discovery; include: description of breach, PHI involved, steps to protect yourself, what we're doing; HHS (SECRETARY): notify within 60 days if breach affects 500+ individuals; if <500 individuals in a state: log and report annually within 60 days of calendar year end; MEDIA (if 500+ in a state): notify prominent local media outlets without unreasonable delay; DOCUMENTATION: complete records of the breach, analysis, and notifications required for 6 years.
explanations.d: HIPAA notification is proactive — organizations must identify and notify affected individuals, not wait for complaints. 'Passive disclosure' is not a HIPAA compliance mechanism.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — compliance monitoring in project execution; ongoing compliance assurance
questions.text: A project PM is 6 months into executing a regulated system development. A compliance officer asks: 'How are you monitoring compliance throughout execution, not just at the end?' The PM realizes compliance is being treated as a go-live checkpoint only. What should ongoing compliance monitoring look like during execution?

answers.text: Compliance verification only happens at go-live — ongoing monitoring during development adds no value
Compliance requirements are addressed once in planning — no ongoing monitoring is needed during execution
Hire a compliance officer to monitor independently — PM is not responsible for compliance
