Ongoing compliance monitoring during execution: integrate compliance checkpoints into sprint reviews (are compliance requirements being implemented?); track compliance requirements in the backlog (treat them like any other user story); conduct periodic compliance self-assessments (monthly for high-risk projects); include compliance-specific testing in each sprint (not just functional testing); monitor the regulatory environment for changes; track any compliance risks in the risk register and update status

explanations.a: Compliance discovered only at go-live produces: last-minute architectural changes (expensive); delayed launches; or launching non-compliant systems. Early, continuous compliance monitoring prevents these outcomes.
explanations.b: Compliance requirements evolve during execution: new regulatory guidance may be published; requirements may be misunderstood and need correction; technology choices may create compliance implications not anticipated in planning. Continuous monitoring catches these issues early.
explanations.c: The PM is responsible for overall project compliance. The compliance officer is a subject matter expert and stakeholder — but the PM coordinates compliance integration into the project, not the compliance officer.
explanations.d: ONGOING COMPLIANCE MONITORING during execution: SPRINT-LEVEL COMPLIANCE INTEGRATION: compliance requirements treated as acceptance criteria in user stories; sprint review includes compliance demonstration (not just functional demo); Example sprint story: 'As a user, I can request deletion of my account data (GDPR right to erasure)'; acceptance criteria include: 'All personal data deleted within 24 hours of request; deletion logged in audit trail; confirmation email sent'; COMPLIANCE BACKLOG: dedicated compliance epics/features in the backlog; compliance items have the same priority as functional items; when compliance items are de-prioritized sprint after sprint, they never get done; PERIODIC COMPLIANCE SELF-ASSESSMENT (monthly for high-risk projects): 'Which requirements are implemented and tested?'; 'Which are still pending?'; 'Are any requirements at risk based on current design decisions?'; COMPLIANCE-SPECIFIC TESTING: each sprint includes tests for compliance requirements implemented that sprint; SAST scanning runs every sprint (don't wait for the final pentest); dependency scanning runs continuously; REGULATORY MONITORING: subscribe to regulatory update services; assign someone to monitor for relevant regulatory changes; assess impact of changes on the project; RISK REGISTER: compliance risks tracked with probability, impact, and mitigation status; any new regulatory interpretation or enforcement action reviewed for impact.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — PCI-DSS penetration testing requirements; compliance-driven testing
questions.text: A project is launching a payment processing application. PCI-DSS Requirement 11 mandates regular penetration testing. The PM asks: 'Why does PCI require penetration testing and what must the test cover?'

answers.text: Penetration testing is optional under PCI-DSS — it is a recommendation, not a requirement
PCI penetration testing can be performed by internal developers — no external assessor is required
Penetration testing only needs to cover the web application — the network infrastructure is excluded

PCI-DSS mandates penetration testing because automated vulnerability scanning finds known vulnerabilities but cannot identify complex attack chains that simulate real attacker behavior. PCI Req 11 requires: annual internal and external penetration testing; testing after significant infrastructure changes; testing of all system components and access points; testing for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities; retesting to confirm remediation. Results must be retained as compliance evidence

explanations.a: PCI-DSS Requirement 11 explicitly mandates penetration testing as a required control — not a recommendation. Non-compliance with any PCI-DSS requirement results in compliance failure.
explanations.b: PCI allows qualified internal security staff to perform penetration testing — but the tester must be separate from the people who manage the systems being tested (independence requirement). An organization's own developers who built the application should not test their own code.
explanations.c: PCI penetration testing scope includes: cardholder data environment (CDE); all network segmentation controls; application layer AND network layer; web applications AND APIs handling card data.
explanations.d: PCI-DSS PENETRATION TESTING REQUIREMENT 11: WHY PCI REQUIRES PEN TESTING: automated vulnerability scanning identifies KNOWN CVEs in software components; penetration testing simulates a skilled attacker — finding complex attack chains, business logic vulnerabilities, and access control bypasses that automated tools miss; real attackers think creatively — pen testers replicate this; PCI REQUIREMENT 11 SPECIFICS: FREQUENCY: at minimum annually; after any significant infrastructure or application changes; SCOPE (all system components): EXTERNAL penetration testing: from the perspective of an internet attacker; application-layer (OWASP Top 10) AND network-layer testing; INTERNAL penetration testing: from within the network perimeter; simulates an attacker who has already breached the perimeter; NETWORK SEGMENTATION TESTING: confirm that systems outside the Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) cannot reach inside the CDE; OWASP TOP 10: SQL injection, XSS, broken authentication, insecure deserialization, etc.; REMEDIATION AND RETESTING: all exploitable vulnerabilities remediated; retest to confirm remediation before compliance sign-off; DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS: penetration test methodology documented; results retained; remediation status tracked; evidence available for PCI QSA (Qualified Security Assessor) review; ASSESSOR QUALIFICATIONS: no specific external requirement in PCI v4.0 for Level 2-4 merchants; Level 1 merchants should use qualified internal security staff or qualified third-party; independence from the assessed systems is important.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — privacy impact assessment; DPIA; risk-based privacy approach
questions.text: A project is implementing AI-powered facial recognition to automate building access for employees. The legal team says a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is required under GDPR. What is a DPIA and what should it evaluate?

answers.text: A DPIA is optional paperwork — only required for massive breaches
Facial recognition for internal employee access doesn't require a DPIA — it's not consumer-facing
DPIAs are only required when a breach has already occurred — they are post-incident assessments

A DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) is a formal analysis required under GDPR Article 35 for processing likely to result in high risk to individuals. For facial recognition access control, the DPIA must evaluate: the nature and purpose of the processing (what biometric data is collected, why, how long retained); necessity and proportionality (is facial recognition the least privacy-invasive way to achieve access control?); risks to individuals (consent challenges; biometric data breach consequences; potential discrimination); mitigation measures planned; whether a DPO consultation is required

explanations.a: A DPIA under GDPR Article 35 is MANDATORY — not optional — for certain high-risk processing activities. Failure to conduct a required DPIA is itself a GDPR violation, separate from any violations in the processing itself.
explanations.b: GDPR's special category protection for biometric data applies regardless of whether processing is consumer-facing or internal. Employee biometric data receives the same protection as consumer biometric data.
explanations.c: DPIAs are PROSPECTIVE assessments conducted BEFORE high-risk processing begins. They identify risks in advance so mitigation can be built into the system design.
explanations.d: DPIA FOR FACIAL RECOGNITION ACCESS CONTROL: WHY A DPIA IS REQUIRED: GDPR Article 35 mandates a DPIA when processing 'is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons'; HIGH-RISK TRIGGERS including facial recognition: systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects using automated processing (including profiling); processing on a large scale of special categories of personal data (BIOMETRICS are a 'special category' under GDPR Article 9 — highest protection level); DPIA STRUCTURE AND CONTENT: DESCRIPTION OF PROCESSING: what biometric data is captured (facial geometry); how it is stored; where it is processed; how long it is retained; NECESSITY AND PROPORTIONALITY: why is facial recognition chosen over less privacy-invasive alternatives (key cards, PIN codes, employee badges)?; is it proportionate to the access control purpose?; if less invasive means can achieve the same goal, facial recognition may not be justified; RISKS TO INDIVIDUALS: BIOMETRIC DATA BREACH: biometric data cannot be 'reset' like a password — if the facial geometry template is stolen, the individual is permanently compromised; DISCRIMINATION: facial recognition systems have documented accuracy disparities across demographic groups (race, gender); CONSENT ISSUES: are employees truly free to refuse? (employment context undermines free consent); MITIGATION MEASURES: technical: on-device processing (no central database of facial templates); storage of mathematical templates, not images; strict access controls; retention limits; ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS: what alternatives were considered? KEY MANAGEMENT: which data controller is responsible? who is the DPO? has the DPO been consulted? OUTCOME: GDPR Article 35(7) requires conclusion on whether processing can proceed and under what conditions.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — cross-border data transfers; GDPR international transfers; standard contractual clauses
questions.text: A project is developing a global HR platform that will transfer employee personal data from EU subsidiaries to a US parent company for centralized processing. The privacy officer says GDPR restricts cross-border transfers. What must the project address?

answers.text: Data can flow freely within a multinational corporation — internal transfers are not subject to GDPR
The US has an adequacy agreement with the EU so no special mechanism is needed for all US-EU transfers
Intra-company transfers within a multinational are excluded from GDPR transfer restrictions

GDPR restricts transfers of personal data outside the EU/EEA to non-adequate countries (including the US) unless an approved transfer mechanism is in place. For EU-to-US transfers, the options include: EU-US Data Privacy Framework (adequacy decision, 2023); Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) between the EU entity and the US entity; Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) for multinational corporations. The project must implement one of these mechanisms before transferring any EU employee data to the US

explanations.a: GDPR transfer restrictions apply to transfers to any recipient outside the EU/EEA — including intra-company transfers to subsidiaries, parent companies, or affiliates in third countries. The controller-processor or controller-controller relationship within a corporate group does not exempt transfers from GDPR Chapter V requirements.
explanations.b: The US does not have a blanket adequacy decision. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework provides a mechanism for certified US companies — but only those who self-certify under the framework are covered.
explanations.c: GDPR Chapter V explicitly applies to intra-group transfers. The same legal requirements apply whether the recipient is a wholly owned subsidiary or an independent company.
explanations.d: GDPR CROSS-BORDER TRANSFER MECHANISMS: GDPR RESTRICTION: personal data transfers outside the EU/EEA to countries without an 'adequate level of protection' require an approved mechanism; the US is NOT automatically considered adequate (prior Safe Harbor and Privacy Shield frameworks were invalidated); CURRENT TRANSFER MECHANISMS FOR EU-US: EU-US DATA PRIVACY FRAMEWORK (DPF): adequacy decision adopted July 2023; US companies certified under DPF can receive EU personal data without additional mechanisms; verify the US entity is DPF-certified; STANDARD CONTRACTUAL CLAUSES (SCCs): standard contract templates adopted by the European Commission; executed between the EU data exporter and the non-EU data importer; legally binding on both parties; most commonly used mechanism; BINDING CORPORATE RULES (BCRs): for multinational corporations; company-wide privacy rules approved by a lead EU supervisory authority; enables intra-group transfers without SCCs for each relationship; expensive to implement ($200K-$500K for approval) but efficient for large multinationals; SUPPLEMENTARY MEASURES: transfer impact assessment (TIA): evaluate whether the destination country's laws undermine the protections in the SCC; implement supplementary technical measures if needed (encryption, pseudonymization); PROJECT IMPLICATIONS: identify which EU entities transfer data to the US; confirm the US parent company's transfer mechanism (DPF certification? BCRs in place? If neither, implement SCCs); execute SCCs between EU subsidiaries and US parent before any data transfer; document the legal basis for each transfer.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — industry-specific regulations; FDA 21 CFR Part 11; GxP compliance; validated systems
questions.text: A pharmaceutical company is replacing its clinical trial data management system. The compliance team says the new system must comply with FDA 21 CFR Part 11. What is 21 CFR Part 11 and what technical requirements does it create for the project?

answers.text: 21 CFR Part 11 is an optional FDA guideline for pharmaceutical companies
Part 11 compliance is achieved by adding user passwords — no other technical controls are required
21 CFR Part 11 only applies to physical laboratory equipment — software systems are exempt

21 CFR Part 11 is FDA regulation requiring that electronic records and electronic signatures in systems used for regulated activities be trustworthy, reliable, and equivalent to paper records. Technical requirements: closed system controls (only authorized users can access); audit trail (complete, computer-generated, unalterable record showing all data creation, modification, deletion); authority checks (who can do what); operational system checks; system validation (documented evidence that the system does what it's supposed to do); electronic signature controls (unique to each individual, non-repudiable)

explanations.a: 21 CFR Part 11 is a binding FDA regulation — non-compliance can result in: FDA warning letters; clinical trial data rejection; consent decree; import alerts for pharmaceutical manufacturers.
explanations.b: Passwords alone do not achieve Part 11 compliance. The regulation requires: unique IDs per user; immutable audit trails; system validation; electronic signature controls — all of which require significant technical implementation beyond just passwords.
explanations.c: 21 CFR Part 11 specifically targets electronic records and electronic signatures in COMPUTER SYSTEMS used for FDA-regulated activities. Software systems are the primary target.
explanations.d: FDA 21 CFR PART 11 — TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: WHAT IT COVERS: electronic records and electronic signatures in systems used to create, modify, maintain, archive, retrieve, or transmit records required by FDA regulations (clinical trial data, manufacturing records, quality records, laboratory data); CLOSED SYSTEM CONTROLS: ACCESS CONTROLS: uniquely identify each user; computer-generated audit trails showing who accessed what and when; authority checks (validate access rights before allowing actions); AUDIT TRAIL REQUIREMENTS (most technically demanding): COMPLETE: every record creation, modification, and deletion must be captured; UNALTERABLE: the audit trail cannot be modified or deleted — immutable log; COMPUTER-GENERATED: automatically generated by the system, not human-entered; TIMESTAMP: accurate date and time of each event; CONTENT: who made the change, what the original value was, what the new value is, when, and (optionally) why; electronic records must show all changes; SYSTEM VALIDATION: the most resource-intensive Part 11 requirement; VALIDATION DOCUMENTATION: Installation Qualification (IQ): system installed correctly; Operational Qualification (OQ): system operates as designed; Performance Qualification (PQ): system performs correctly in the actual operating environment; CHANGE CONTROL: all changes to validated systems require formal validation impact assessment and re-validation if needed; ELECTRONIC SIGNATURES: must be linked to the signer's records; must be unique to the individual; biometrics or username/password combinations meeting Part 11 requirements; non-repudiable — the signer cannot deny signing; RETENTION: records retained for the duration specified by the applicable FDA regulation (often 15+ years for clinical trials).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — compliance as project success criterion; go/no-go compliance checklist
questions.text: A project PM is preparing the go/no-go decision criteria for a regulated financial system launch. What compliance-specific go/no-go criteria should be included?

answers.text: Compliance criteria are separate from go/no-go decisions — launch first and verify compliance later
The compliance team independently decides go/no-go — the PM has no role
Only functional and performance criteria belong in go/no-go checklists — compliance is verified post-launch

Compliance-specific go/no-go criteria: all applicable regulatory requirements implemented and tested (SOX ITGCs operating, PCI-DSS controls in place); penetration test completed with no critical/high findings open; compliance documentation complete (policies, procedures, evidence ready for audit); legal approval obtained (legal team has reviewed and approved the system); regulatory filing made if required (e.g., notification to regulators of new system); BAAs signed with all relevant vendors; access controls and audit logging verified operational

explanations.a: Launching a regulated system non-compliantly 'to verify compliance later' is a violation in itself. Regulators do not accept 'we launched and will fix it' — they expect compliance at launch.
explanations.b: The PM owns the overall go/no-go decision and coordinates all inputs including compliance. The compliance team is an essential stakeholder providing expertise and formal approval — but the PM orchestrates the comprehensive go/no-go review.
explanations.c: Compliance failure at launch creates immediate regulatory exposure. Functional success with compliance failure is not a project success — it's a regulatory incident.
explanations.d: COMPLIANCE-SPECIFIC GO/NO-GO CRITERIA for regulated financial system: REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS IMPLEMENTATION: all identified regulatory requirements (SOX ITGCs, PCI-DSS, GDPR) implemented; each requirement has a corresponding test result showing it works; compliance backlog at zero — no deferred compliance items; SECURITY TESTING: penetration test completed by qualified assessor; no Critical or High findings left open; SAST and DAST scans completed with acceptable results; PCI-DSS vulnerability scans passed (Level 1 merchants: external scanning quarterly); COMPLIANCE DOCUMENTATION: security policies and procedures finalized; user access control matrix documented; change management procedure documented; audit trail operation demonstrated; LEGAL APPROVAL: legal/compliance team has formally reviewed and approved the system; any legal questions about compliance approach resolved; DATA PROCESSING AGREEMENTS: all vendor DPAs signed; HIPAA BAAs executed (if applicable); PCI DSS service provider agreements signed; VENDOR COMPLIANCE VERIFICATION: all in-scope vendors have provided current compliance certifications (SOC 2 report, PCI DSS certificate); REGULATORY NOTIFICATIONS: any required advance notifications to regulators submitted (some jurisdictions require notification before launching new financial systems); AUDIT READINESS: compliance evidence organized and accessible; audit log operation verified; EXAMPLE FORMAT: Compliance Gate Criterion | Status | Evidence; SOX ITGC controls implemented and tested | PASS | Test results Q3-2024; PCI penetration test completed, no open findings | PASS | Pen test report 10/1/2024.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — children privacy; COPPA; age verification; parental consent
questions.text: A project is building a social media app that allows users age 13+. The legal team says COPPA may apply. What is COPPA and how does it affect the project's design?

answers.text: COPPA doesn't apply to social media apps — it only covers children's educational platforms
COPPA only applies to operators of websites directed to children — general-audience apps are exempt regardless of user age
Allowing ages 13+ means COPPA doesn't apply — COPPA only covers ages 12 and under

COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) restricts collection of personal information from children under 13. The app must implement: age verification mechanism (prevent under-13 users from registering); if the service might be used by under-13s, parental consent required before data collection; limited data collection from minors (13-17 in some states); privacy policy describing data practices for children; the project requirements must include age gate design and data handling procedures for verified minors

explanations.a: COPPA applies to operators of online services directed to children under 13 AND to general-audience services when they have actual knowledge that a child under 13 is using the service. Social media apps with a minimum age of 13 must implement effective age gates to prevent children under 13 from accessing the service.
explanations.b: General-audience apps have 'mixed-audience' COPPA obligations — when they have actual knowledge that a child under 13 is using the service, COPPA applies to the personal data of that specific child.
explanations.c: 'Age 13+' minimum age means the app must implement an effective age verification mechanism to prevent under-13 users from accessing the service. The minimum age claim doesn't create exemption — it creates an obligation to verify and enforce it.
explanations.d: COPPA OVERVIEW AND PROJECT REQUIREMENTS: WHAT COPPA REQUIRES: prohibits operators from collecting personal information from children under 13 without verifiable parental consent; DIRECTED-TO-CHILDREN TEST: subject matter, visual content, use of animated characters, celebrities that appeal to children, advertising aimed at children; GENERAL AUDIENCE WITH KNOWLEDGE: apps with minimum age 13 that have actual knowledge a child under 13 is using → COPPA applies to that child; AGE VERIFICATION REQUIREMENTS: implement an effective age gate during registration; 'date of birth' entry that blocks under-13 users; for under-13 users who attempt to register: do not collect any personal information; do not use the birthday data entered by the rejected user for marketing or analytics; AGE APPROPRIATE DESIGN: UK Age Appropriate Design Code (Children's Code): applies to services 'likely to be accessed' by children under 18; by default, highest privacy settings for child users; DATA MINIMIZATION for users under 18; PARENTAL CONSENT (if under-13 users will be allowed with parental consent): verifiable parental consent mechanism; limited data collection even with consent; parental right to review and delete child's data; STATE REQUIREMENTS: California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act (AB 2273): similar to UK Children's Code; requires data protection impact assessment for services likely to be accessed by minors; PROJECT REQUIREMENTS: age gate as required user registration flow; data handling procedures differentiating minor vs. adult users; privacy policy covering child data practices; FTC enforcement: significant fines for COPPA violations.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — compliance cost in project business case; total cost of compliance; ROI of compliance
questions.text: A project sponsor asks: 'All this compliance work costs money. What's the business case for investing in compliance versus accepting the risk of non-compliance?' How should the PM respond?

answers.text: Compliance has no business case — it's mandatory so cost doesn't need justification

The business case for compliance investment: quantify the cost of non-compliance (regulatory fines, data breach costs, legal fees, reputational damage, customer loss); compare to compliance investment cost; present the expected value analysis. Non-compliance expected costs typically far exceed compliance investment. Additionally, compliance enables business growth (enterprise customers require SOC 2; international expansion requires GDPR compliance) and builds organizational trust
Non-compliance risk is theoretical — most non-compliant organizations are never caught
Compliance is a cost center with no return — accept non-compliance risk to save costs

explanations.a: While compliance is mandatory in many cases, executives benefit from understanding the quantified business rationale — not just 'the law requires it.' A well-constructed business case builds commitment and appropriate resource allocation.
explanations.b: COMPLIANCE BUSINESS CASE FRAMEWORK: COST OF NON-COMPLIANCE: REGULATORY FINES: GDPR: up to €20M or 4% of global annual revenue (whichever is higher); PCI-DSS: $5,000-$100,000/month plus potential loss of card acceptance privileges; HIPAA: $100-$50,000 per violation (up to $1.9M per violation category); SOX: personal criminal liability for executives; DATA BREACH COSTS: average data breach cost: $4.45M (IBM 2023); healthcare breaches: average $10.9M; financial services: $5.9M; LEGAL COSTS: class action litigation; regulatory defense; remediation legal fees; $10M-$100M+ for major incidents; REPUTATIONAL DAMAGE: customer churn after a high-profile breach: typically 10-30% customer loss; BUSINESS DISRUPTION: suspended card processing (PCI); system shutdown orders (FDA); operational disruption during breach response; COST OF COMPLIANCE INVESTMENT: GDPR: $50K-$500K for medium-sized organization; SOC 2 Type II: $30K-$150K annually; PCI-DSS Level 1: $50K-$200K annually; HIPAA security program: $50K-$200K annually; EXPECTED VALUE ANALYSIS: if non-compliance probability of significant incident = 10% per year; if incident cost = $5M; expected cost of non-compliance = $500K/year; if compliance cost = $200K/year; expected value of compliance investment: $300K/year saved; COMPLIANCE AS BUSINESS ENABLER: enterprise SaaS sales require SOC 2 — non-compliant companies lose contracts; international expansion requires GDPR compliance; healthcare market entry requires HIPAA compliance; compliance enables revenue opportunities that non-compliance closes.
explanations.c: Regulatory enforcement has increased dramatically: GDPR fines since 2018 total over €4 billion; FTC enforcement of COPPA is active; OCR (HIPAA enforcement) fines reached $28M in 2023. The probability of being caught is not theoretical.
explanations.d: Compliance has measurable positive returns through: avoided breach costs; enabled enterprise sales; customer trust; international market access. Characterizing it as pure cost center misses these revenue-enabling dimensions.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — compliance documentation in project records; maintaining compliance evidence
questions.text: A project is implementing a GDPR-compliant data processing system. The PM asks: 'What compliance documentation must we create and maintain and for how long?'

answers.text: Compliance documentation is created once for the audit and then discarded — ongoing maintenance wastes effort

GDPR compliance documentation that must be created and maintained: Records of Processing Activities (ROPA — GDPR Article 30, required for most organizations); Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs for high-risk processing); Data Processing Agreements with all vendors; consent records (who consented to what, when); breach notification records (any breaches and responses); training records (staff trained on data protection); these must be available for supervisory authority inspection on request and maintained for the life of the processing activity plus additional regulatory retention periods
Only the privacy policy needs to be maintained — other compliance documents are optional
Delete all compliance documentation after 1 year — older records create more regulatory risk

explanations.a: GDPR Article 5(2) establishes the 'accountability principle' — controllers must be able to demonstrate compliance. Without ongoing documentation, an organization cannot demonstrate compliance when the supervisory authority requests evidence.
explanations.b: GDPR COMPLIANCE DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS: RECORDS OF PROCESSING ACTIVITIES (ROPA — Article 30): required for organizations processing large scale or sensitive data; contains: categories of data subjects; categories of personal data; purposes of processing; data recipients; cross-border transfers; retention periods; technical and organizational measures; maintained and kept up to date; must be provided to supervisory authority on request; DATA PROTECTION IMPACT ASSESSMENTS (DPIAs): for high-risk processing; retained as evidence of proactive risk assessment; updated if processing changes significantly; DATA PROCESSING AGREEMENTS (DPAs): contracts with all processors handling personal data; retained for the duration of the relationship plus applicable limitation period; CONSENT RECORDS: evidence that valid consent was obtained; who, what, when, mechanism used; retained for as long as consent is relied upon (plus limitation period for challenges); BREACH NOTIFICATION RECORDS: details of any personal data breach; breach notification sent; supervisory authority communication; retained for 5 years minimum (GDPR Article 33(5)); TRAINING RECORDS: evidence that staff training on data protection was conducted; dates, content, attendees; retained for employment period plus limitation period; RETENTION STRATEGY: documentation related to active processing: retain while processing continues; after processing ends: retain for applicable statute of limitations period (typically 3-6 years for most jurisdictions); START DOCUMENTATION AT PROJECT INITIATION — not as an afterthought at go-live.
explanations.c: GDPR requires many documents beyond the privacy policy: the ROPA alone requires detailed processing documentation that is far more comprehensive than a public privacy policy.
explanations.d: Deleting compliance documentation creates an accountability gap. Supervisory authorities can investigate incidents and compliance for years after they occurred — documentation from 2+ years ago may be needed.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — state privacy laws; patchwork regulation; multi-state compliance
questions.text: A US-based company processes consumer data from all 50 states. In addition to federal regulations, 15+ states have passed their own privacy laws (California, Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, etc.). How should the project approach multi-state privacy compliance?

answers.text: Follow only California's CCPA — it's the most comprehensive and complying with it covers all other states

Implement a comprehensive privacy program based on the most restrictive applicable requirements: map all state privacy laws applicable to the customer base; implement capabilities required by the most demanding state requirements (typically California CPRA); verify that these satisfy other states' requirements; where states have unique requirements not covered by the most restrictive standard, add specific compliance for those provisions; maintain a regulatory monitoring process for new state laws
Ignore state laws — only federal regulations are legally enforceable
Build separate compliance versions of the system for each state — one system per state jurisdiction

explanations.a: CCPA/CPRA is comprehensive — but other states have specific requirements that may not be covered: Virginia VCDPA: data protection assessments for high-risk processing (similar to GDPR DPIA); Colorado CPA: opt-out of profiling; Connecticut CTDPA: sensitive data category protections; some states have different thresholds for applicability; a 'CCPA covers everything' assumption may miss state-specific requirements.
explanations.b: MULTI-STATE PRIVACY COMPLIANCE STRATEGY: REGULATORY MAPPING: compile the applicable state privacy laws for all states where consumers are located; key questions for each state law: applicability thresholds (number of consumers, revenue); consumer rights granted; obligations imposed on controllers; unique requirements not in other laws; 'HIGHEST STANDARD' APPROACH: implement technical capabilities required by the most demanding state laws; for most US companies, CPRA (California Privacy Rights Act) sets the baseline for comprehensive rights implementation; UNIVERSAL CAPABILITIES TO IMPLEMENT: right to know (all states with privacy laws); right to delete (all states); right to opt-out of data sale/sharing (most states); right to correct (most states); sensitive data protections (some states have broader sensitive categories than others); STATE-SPECIFIC ADDITIONS: data protection assessments: Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut; profiling opt-out: Colorado; specific employee data protections: California; REGULATORY MONITORING: privacy legislation is expanding rapidly; 15+ states as of 2024; 10+ more states with pending legislation; subscribe to IAPP (International Association of Privacy Professionals) regulatory tracker; assess each new law for impact on existing compliance program within 30 days of enactment; ALTERNATIVE TO STATE-BY-STATE SYSTEMS: geolocation-based feature flags rather than separate systems; a single privacy infrastructure that applies different rules based on consumer location; simpler to maintain than 50 separate system versions.
explanations.c: State privacy laws are fully enforceable — states have their own attorneys general and enforcement agencies. California has the CPPA (California Privacy Protection Agency) with dedicated enforcement authority.
explanations.d: Building separate system versions per state is impractical and expensive. A unified compliance framework with jurisdiction-sensitive logic (based on consumer location) is the standard industry approach.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — SOX material weakness; control deficiency classification; remediation priority
questions.text: An internal auditor reports two SOX findings for a new financial system: Finding 1: access control documentation is incomplete (no formal access matrix); Finding 2: the same individual can enter and approve journal entries over $1M (no SOD). How should the PM prioritize and remediate these?

answers.text: Both findings are equally urgent — address them in any order over the next 6 months

Finding 2 (SOD failure for $1M+ transactions) is a material weakness requiring immediate remediation — it creates actual fraud risk; Finding 1 (incomplete documentation) is a significant deficiency requiring prompt remediation but lower urgency than the SOD gap. Immediate remediation of Finding 2: configure the system to prevent self-approval of transactions over $1M; separate the entry and approval roles technically; document who is authorized for each role. Finding 1 remediation within 30 days: create and document the formal access control matrix
Finding 1 is more critical — documentation problems are always higher priority than control gaps
Inform the CEO and let them decide without further analysis — SOX findings require executive decision

explanations.a: The two findings have very different risk profiles: Finding 2 (SOD failure) represents actual fraud risk today; Finding 1 (documentation gap) is a governance weakness but doesn't enable immediate fraudulent activity.
explanations.b: SOX FINDING CLASSIFICATION AND REMEDIATION: FINDING CLASSIFICATION: CONTROL DEFICIENCY: a control doesn't exist or is not designed adequately; SIGNIFICANT DEFICIENCY: a deficiency that is less severe than a material weakness but important enough to merit attention by those responsible for oversight; MATERIAL WEAKNESS: a deficiency where there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected on a timely basis; FINDING 2 — SOD FAILURE ($1M JOURNAL ENTRIES) — MATERIAL WEAKNESS: RISK: one person can create and approve fraudulent journal entries over $1M; a single individual could manipulate financial statements for amounts that would be 'material' (significant) to the financial statements; CLASSIFICATION: likely Material Weakness — meets the 'reasonable possibility of material misstatement' threshold; IMMEDIATE REMEDIATION: configure the application workflow: Step 1: journal entry created by data entry user (Entry role); Step 2: automatically routes to a different user for approval (Approval role); the system CANNOT allow a user with both Entry and Approval permissions for the same transaction; implement compensating control while technical fix is being built: manual supervisory review of all transactions where SOD cannot be technically enforced; document the compensating control; FINDING 1 — INCOMPLETE ACCESS DOCUMENTATION — SIGNIFICANT DEFICIENCY: RISK: without a formal access matrix, it's impossible to confirm that access is appropriately limited; doesn't inherently mean access is wrong — just undocumented; CLASSIFICATION: Significant Deficiency (documentation gap, not a control failure itself); REMEDIATION (within 30 days): create the access control matrix (role, system, access level, approver, date last reviewed); document approval chain for each access level; implement quarterly review and certification.
explanations.c: A SOD failure enabling potential material financial fraud is a higher urgency than documentation incompleteness. Documentation must be fixed, but active fraud risk must be mitigated immediately.
explanations.d: The PM should diagnose and recommend remediation — not escalate to the CEO without having done the analysis. The CEO will ask 'what is the risk and what should we do?' — the PM must have those answers.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — vendor compliance risk; third-party audit rights; compliance contractual terms
questions.text: A project uses a third-party cloud analytics vendor that will process customer personal data. The compliance team says the vendor's compliance must be verified before use. What due diligence should the PM conduct and what contractual protections should be in place?

answers.text: Trust the vendor's claims about compliance — self-reported compliance is sufficient

Vendor compliance due diligence: obtain and review the vendor's SOC 2 Type II report (or ISO 27001 certificate); review the vendor's security questionnaire responses; confirm the vendor has signed the Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with appropriate GDPR terms; confirm the vendor's own subprocessors are disclosed and compliant; verify the vendor's breach notification commitment. Contractual protections: DPA with specific technical/organizational measures; audit right clause; breach notification requirements; data deletion upon contract end; penalty provisions for non-compliance
Only the contract's price terms need to be reviewed — compliance terms are standard boilerplate
Vendor compliance is the vendor's problem — the project team has no responsibility for vendor compliance

explanations.a: Self-reported compliance without evidence is insufficient for regulatory purposes. GDPR Article 28 requires that controllers 'only use processors providing sufficient guarantees' — the controller must verify, not just trust.
explanations.b: VENDOR COMPLIANCE DUE DILIGENCE AND CONTRACTUAL PROTECTIONS: DUE DILIGENCE PROCESS: SOC 2 TYPE II REPORT: issued by an independent CPA firm; covers actual control operation over a period (typically 6-12 months); review the report's findings and any exceptions noted; confirm the Trust Services Criteria covered (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Privacy); ALTERNATIVELY: ISO 27001 CERTIFICATION: third-party certification of the ISMS; check the scope of certification (does it include the analytics service?); check expiry date (annual renewal); SECURITY QUESTIONNAIRE: detailed questionnaire about specific controls (encryption, access control, incident response, subprocessors); compare answers to requirements; SUBPROCESSOR REVIEW: analytics vendors often use subprocessors (AWS, GCP, data processing tools); confirm subprocessors are disclosed; confirm they are under equivalent compliance obligations; CONTRACTUAL PROTECTIONS: DATA PROCESSING AGREEMENT (DPA — required by GDPR Article 28): must include: processing instructions; subject matter, duration, nature, purpose; categories of data subjects; data controller's rights and obligations; technical and organizational security measures; assistance with data subject rights; breach notification (to controller: without undue delay, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware); deletion or return of data at end of contract; audit cooperation; AUDIT RIGHT CLAUSE: 'Controller has the right to conduct audits or request audit results demonstrating compliance'; BREACH NOTIFICATION: 'Processor must notify Controller within 24-48 hours of discovering a personal data breach'; SUBPROCESSOR MANAGEMENT: prior written consent before engaging new subprocessors; DATA DELETION: upon contract termination, all personal data deleted and deletion certified in writing.
explanations.c: Compliance terms in a DPA are legally binding and critically important — they determine the organization's ability to demonstrate GDPR compliance and recover damages if the vendor causes a breach.
explanations.d: Organizations are responsible for ensuring their processors comply with GDPR. GDPR Article 82 can make both the controller and the processor jointly liable for damages resulting from non-compliance. 'It's the vendor's problem' is not a legal defense under GDPR.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — industry standards vs. regulations; mandatory vs. voluntary compliance
questions.text: A project sponsor asks: 'Some of the compliance requirements our team is working on appear to be industry standards (like SOC 2) rather than laws. Do we really need to comply with voluntary standards?' How should the PM explain the distinction and practical importance?

answers.text: Voluntary standards have no compliance value — ignore them and focus only on mandatory regulations

Voluntary standards like SOC 2 are market-driven requirements: while not legally mandated, enterprise customers require SOC 2 attestation as a condition of procurement; without SOC 2, the organization is disqualified from enterprise customer opportunities; the 'voluntary' standard effectively becomes mandatory for business viability. Distinction: regulations (HIPAA, GDPR, SOX) carry legal penalties; standards (SOC 2, ISO 27001) carry market consequences. Both create real compliance obligations — just through different enforcement mechanisms
SOC 2 is irrelevant for B2B SaaS companies — it only matters for consumer-facing applications
Standards always supersede regulations — if SOC 2 is complied with, legal regulations are automatically satisfied

explanations.a: Ignoring voluntary standards that are market requirements effectively disqualifies the organization from business opportunities. Many sales are lost not to better competitors but to compliance requirements: 'We can't use your product without SOC 2' is a common procurement response.
explanations.b: MANDATORY VS. VOLUNTARY COMPLIANCE FRAMEWORK: LEGALLY MANDATED REGULATIONS: HIPAA: federal law; criminal and civil penalties; GDPR: EU regulation; fines up to €20M or 4% of global revenue; SOX: federal law; criminal penalties for executives; PCI-DSS: technically a contractual obligation of card network agreements, not a law; but card acceptance is practically mandatory; MARKET-DRIVEN STANDARDS: SOC 2 TYPE II: AICPA attestation standard; not a law; BUT enterprise customers (banks, healthcare organizations, public companies) contractually require SOC 2 as a vendor condition; WITHOUT SOC 2: disqualified from enterprise SaaS market; loses competitive bids; 'voluntary' in legal theory; 'mandatory' in practice; ISO 27001: international certification standard; required by many multinational enterprise customers; required for certain government contracts (UK G-Cloud, US DoD suppliers); NIST CSF: voluntary framework; effectively required for US federal contractors and critical infrastructure companies; PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE APPROACH: assess the organization's target market and customer base; identify which standards customers require as purchase conditions; treat customer-required standards as effectively mandatory; build a compliance program that satisfies both legal and market requirements; CONVERGENCE BENEFIT: SOC 2 controls address many of the same control objectives as GDPR technical measures and HIPAA Security Rule; building SOC 2 controls often satisfies multiple compliance requirements simultaneously.
explanations.c: SOC 2 is most commonly required in B2B technology sales — not consumer applications. Enterprise B2B customers (financial institutions, healthcare organizations, large corporations) routinely require SOC 2 from their software vendors.
explanations.d: Standards and regulations are not hierarchically related — they operate independently. Complying with SOC 2 doesn't satisfy GDPR (GDPR has specific legal requirements that SOC 2 doesn't fully address); similarly, HIPAA compliance doesn't automatically satisfy SOC 2 requirements.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Compliance — comprehensive compliance scenario; multi-regulation project; integrated compliance approach
questions.text: A PM is leading a new telehealth platform serving patients in the US (including California) and the EU. The platform processes PHI, payment cards, and EU personal data. A compliance consultant identifies 4 applicable frameworks: HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR, and CCPA. Describe an integrated compliance approach that addresses all four efficiently.

answers.text: Address each regulation separately with independent compliance projects — one regulation at a time

Integrated compliance through control mapping: many controls satisfy multiple frameworks simultaneously (encryption satisfies HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and GDPR; access controls satisfy all four; audit logging satisfies HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and SOX); build a unified control framework addressing the union of requirements from all frameworks; map each control to the specific framework requirement it satisfies; avoid redundant work by implementing shared controls once; create a compliance matrix showing all requirements and which controls satisfy them
Implement only GDPR — it's the most comprehensive and satisfies all other requirements
Hire four separate compliance teams — one per regulation — to ensure specialization

explanations.a: Separate compliance projects per regulation create: duplicate implementation of overlapping controls; inconsistent security posture (control implemented differently for each regulation); inefficient resource use; coordination challenges between compliance projects.
explanations.b: INTEGRATED COMPLIANCE APPROACH for multi-regulation telehealth platform: CONTROL MAPPING — SHARED REQUIREMENTS: ENCRYPTION AT REST AND IN TRANSIT: HIPAA Security Rule: ePHI must be encrypted; PCI-DSS Req 3/4: cardholder data encrypted; GDPR Article 32: appropriate technical measures including encryption; IMPLEMENT ONCE: AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit — satisfies all three simultaneously; ACCESS CONTROLS AND MFA: HIPAA: unique user identification, access controls; PCI-DSS Req 7/8: least privilege, MFA for admin; GDPR: access to personal data limited to authorized personnel; CCPA: security measures protecting personal information; IMPLEMENT ONCE: RBAC + MFA — satisfies all four; AUDIT LOGGING: HIPAA: audit trail of all PHI access; PCI-DSS Req 10: logging of all system components; GDPR: processing activity records; CCPA: ability to demonstrate compliance; IMPLEMENT ONCE: comprehensive immutable audit log — satisfies all frameworks; UNIQUE REQUIREMENTS PER FRAMEWORK: HIPAA ONLY: Business Associate Agreements; 60-day breach notification to HHS; covered entity-specific administrative safeguards; PCI-DSS ONLY: Cardholder Data Environment scoping; quarterly ASV vulnerability scans; annual penetration test with specific PCI scope; GDPR ONLY: Data Subject Rights implementation (access, delete, port, object); Data Processing Agreements with all processors; 72-hour breach notification to supervisory authority; DPIA for high-risk processing; CCPA/CPRA ONLY: 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' opt-out mechanism; annual data inventory and privacy notice; COMPLIANCE MATRIX: create a spreadsheet listing: Control → HIPAA Req → PCI Req → GDPR Art. → CCPA Sec.; this shows which controls satisfy which requirements and identifies gaps; EFFICIENCY BENEFIT: a shared control framework implementing overlapping requirements once reduces total compliance implementation effort by 30-50% vs. sequential single-regulation approaches.
explanations.c: GDPR is a privacy regulation — it doesn't satisfy HIPAA (clinical security requirements), PCI-DSS (payment security requirements), or CCPA (California-specific consumer rights). Each framework has unique requirements not covered by others.
explanations.d: Four separate compliance teams create: redundant implementations of shared controls (encryption implemented four different ways); inconsistent approaches (different access control models for different regulations); expensive coordination; potential conflicts between implementations. An integrated team with cross-framework expertise is more efficient.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — ITIL; change management purpose; controlled changes
questions.text: What is the PRIMARY purpose of IT change management in ITIL and why is it necessary?

answers.text: IT change management ensures changes to IT services and infrastructure are implemented in a controlled, coordinated manner that minimizes the risk of disruption to live services — it balances the need to make changes (new features, patches, fixes) against the risk that changes introduce new failures
IT change management exists to prevent all changes — the goal is stability through zero change
IT change management is only required for hardware changes — software deployments don't need change control
IT change management replaces project management — all IT work is managed through the change process

explanations.a: ITIL CHANGE MANAGEMENT PURPOSE: CORE PROBLEM ADDRESSED: uncontrolled changes are the leading cause of IT service failures; 70-80% of availability problems are caused by changes (Gartner); when multiple teams make changes simultaneously without coordination, changes conflict and cascade into outages. WHAT CHANGE MANAGEMENT PROVIDES: VISIBILITY: all planned changes documented and communicated; no surprises for operations teams; RISK ASSESSMENT: every change evaluated for potential impact before implementation; high-risk changes require more scrutiny; COORDINATION: changes scheduled to avoid conflicts; change calendar prevents simultaneous high-risk changes; APPROVAL: appropriate authority approves changes based on risk level; ROLLBACK: every change has a tested back-out plan; REVIEW: post-implementation review captures lessons learned. KEY METRIC VALUE: organizations with mature change management processes have: 50-75% fewer unplanned outages; faster mean time to restore (MTTR) when outages occur; better regulatory compliance (SOX, PCI-DSS require change control). CHANGE MANAGEMENT DOES NOT: prevent all changes; require months of process for simple changes; replace project management for delivering new systems.
explanations.b: The goal of change management is NOT zero change — organizations must update systems to deliver value and stay secure. The goal is CONTROLLED change that minimizes service disruption.
explanations.c: Software deployments are among the highest-risk IT changes — they directly affect service functionality and can introduce defects. Software change control is often MORE important than hardware change control.
explanations.d: IT change management (ITSM) and project management serve different purposes: project management delivers NEW capabilities; change management controls how those capabilities are deployed into the live environment. Both are needed.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — change types; standard normal emergency; change classification
questions.text: ITIL defines three types of changes. What are they and what characterizes each?

answers.text: The three ITIL change types are: Standard Change (pre-approved, low-risk, documented procedure — performed without individual CAB approval; examples: password reset, applying a pre-approved patch template); Normal Change (requires full change management process — RFC submitted, risk assessed, CAB reviewed, scheduled; most project-delivered changes use this type); Emergency Change (urgent change needed to restore service or prevent imminent failure — expedited process with ECAB or on-call CAB; full documentation completed retrospectively)
ITIL has only one change type — all changes go through the same process
The three types are: Small, Medium, and Large — sized by the number of servers affected
Change types are: Approved, Pending, and Rejected — they describe the change status, not the type

explanations.a: THREE ITIL CHANGE TYPES: STANDARD CHANGE: PRE-APPROVED: the change type itself is approved; no individual RFC approval needed for each occurrence; LOW RISK: well-understood risk profile from previous implementations; DOCUMENTED PROCEDURE: a tested procedure exists; execution is repeatable; EXAMPLES: adding a user to a pre-approved security group; applying a standard security patch using the approved process; restarting a service using the documented procedure; resetting a user password; BENEFIT: fast execution without bureaucracy for routine low-risk changes. NORMAL CHANGE: REQUIRES FULL PROCESS: Request for Change (RFC) submitted; impact and risk assessed; CAB review (or manager approval for minor normal changes); scheduled in the change calendar; RISK RANGE: low to high; complex changes are normal changes; EXAMPLES: deploying a new application release; modifying network firewall rules; migrating a database; implementing project deliverables into production; TIMING: typically scheduled 1-2 weeks ahead to allow review. EMERGENCY CHANGE: URGENCY: immediate action needed; delaying would cause or extend significant service disruption; PROCESS: expedited approval (Emergency CAB or on-call authority); implementation proceeds before normal documentation is complete; RETROSPECTIVE: full documentation completed after the change; EXAMPLES: emergency security patch for a zero-day exploit being actively exploited; rollback of a change that caused an outage; RISK: higher risk of error due to speed — therefore requires post-implementation review.
explanations.b: ITIL specifically defines three change types precisely because a single process for all changes would be either too slow (for pre-approved routine changes) or too fast (for risky complex changes).
explanations.c: Change types in ITIL are categorized by risk, urgency, and authorization level — not by the size of infrastructure affected.
explanations.d: Approved/Pending/Rejected describe the STATE of a change request — not the type. All three ITIL change types (standard, normal, emergency) can be in any of these states (though standard changes skip the approval step).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — CAB; Change Advisory Board; change approval governance
questions.text: What is a Change Advisory Board (CAB) and who typically participates?

answers.text: The CAB is a governance body that reviews, evaluates, and approves or rejects proposed IT changes; typical participants include: change manager (chairs the meeting), representatives from IT operations, application teams, security, business relationship managers for affected services, and infrastructure teams — composition varies based on which changes are on the agenda
The CAB is a software development team that builds the changes being deployed
The CAB is a project steering committee — it serves the same function as a project's steering committee
The CAB only approves emergency changes — standard and normal changes are self-approved

explanations.a: CHANGE ADVISORY BOARD (CAB): PURPOSE: a group that supports the change management process by advising the change manager on the authorization of changes and by assisting in their assessment and prioritization. COMPOSITION (varies by organization and by what's on the agenda): CORE MEMBERS: Change Manager (chairs; leads the meeting; records decisions); IT Operations Manager (represents service stability); ADDITIONAL MEMBERS BASED ON AGENDA: Application Team representatives (for software change items); Infrastructure/Network/Security representatives (for infrastructure changes); Business Relationship Managers (represent business impact); Vendor representatives (for vendor-delivered changes that affect production); QUORUM: typically defined in the change management policy (e.g., must have change manager + at least 2 technical representatives); HOW CAB WORKS: RFC submitted 48-72 hours before the CAB meeting; change manager pre-screens RFCs; CAB reviews each RFC: what is the change? risk assessment? rollback plan? when is it scheduled?; CAB recommends approval, approval with conditions, or rejection; change manager makes the final authorization decision; CAB MEETING FREQUENCY: typically weekly; some organizations have daily CAB for high-change environments; VIRTUAL CAB: electronic review via email or workflow tool for low-risk normal changes; IN-PERSON CAB: for high-risk or complex changes.
explanations.b: The CAB reviews and evaluates changes that were built by development teams — it is a governance body, not a development team.
explanations.c: CAB and steering committee serve different purposes: CAB = operational governance of IT changes into live service; steering committee = project governance (scope, schedule, budget decisions). They may have overlapping membership for large projects but serve distinct functions.
explanations.d: Standard changes do not require CAB approval for each instance — but the standard change type itself was approved by the CAB (or equivalent authority) when it was first defined. Normal changes require CAB approval. Emergency changes use an expedited process (ECAB), not full CAB.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — RFC; Request for Change; change request process; change record
questions.text: What is a Request for Change (RFC) and what information does it typically contain?

answers.text: An RFC (Request for Change) is a formal proposal to make a change to an IT system or service; it typically contains: change description and business justification; affected systems and services; risk assessment (impact/probability); rollback/back-out plan; implementation schedule; testing approach; resource requirements; change owner/requestor
An RFC is a Request for Contract — a procurement document for vendor services
An RFC is only needed for emergency changes — normal changes don't require formal documentation
An RFC is the same as a project change request — both follow the same process and template

explanations.a: REQUEST FOR CHANGE (RFC) CONTENT: CHANGE IDENTIFICATION: unique change ID; date submitted; requestor name and team; DESCRIPTION: what is changing? what specific systems, configurations, or services are affected?; BUSINESS JUSTIFICATION: why is this change needed? what business problem does it solve? (e.g., 'This change deploys version 3.2 of the billing module, implementing the approved pricing update required for Q1 billing cycle'); IMPACT ASSESSMENT: which services are affected? expected user impact (none, degraded, unavailable)?; RISK ASSESSMENT: probability that the change causes an unintended failure; severity if the change fails; overall risk rating (Low/Medium/High/Critical); ROLLBACK / BACK-OUT PLAN: if the change fails, how will the environment be restored? how long will the rollback take? has the rollback been tested?; IMPLEMENTATION SCHEDULE: proposed change window; start time; estimated duration; who is performing the change?; TEST PLAN: how will successful implementation be verified? what tests will confirm the change worked correctly?; RESOURCES: who needs to be available during the change? (implementer, tester, support)  CHANGE OWNER: accountable person for the change; APPROVALS: change manager approval; any additional approvals required; RFC LIFECYCLE: Draft → Review → Approved → Scheduled → Implementing → Closed.
explanations.b: RFC in IT change management stands for Request for Change — not Request for Contract. RFC in procurement contexts does mean something different, but in ITIL/ITSM, RFC = Request for Change.
explanations.c: Normal changes require an RFC — it is the fundamental document of the change management process. Emergency changes also require an RFC, though it may be submitted concurrently with implementation and completed retrospectively.
explanations.d: Project change requests (scope/schedule/cost changes) and IT change management RFCs serve different purposes and follow different processes: project CR = changes to the project plan; IT RFC = changes to live IT systems. A project may submit a change request internally AND then separately submit an RFC to deploy the approved project change into production.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — CAB vs. ECAB; emergency change process; expedited approval
questions.text: At 11 PM on a Friday, a critical security vulnerability is disclosed (CVSS 9.8). The vendor has released an emergency patch. Production systems are actively being scanned for the vulnerability. The normal CAB meeting isn't until Tuesday. What process should be followed?

answers.text: Invoke the Emergency Change process: convene the Emergency CAB (ECAB) — a smaller, on-call subset of CAB members available 24/7; present the RFC for the emergency patch; get expedited approval; implement the patch; document fully retrospectively; ECAB is specifically designed for situations where delaying until the next normal CAB meeting would cause unacceptable risk
Wait until Tuesday's CAB meeting — no change should be made outside the normal CAB process
Implement the patch immediately without any approval — security emergencies override change management
Have the security team implement the patch and tell the CAB about it at next Tuesday's meeting — security supersedes change control

explanations.a: EMERGENCY CHANGE PROCESS for CVSS 9.8 patch: WHY ECAB, NOT 'SKIP CHANGE CONTROL': even in emergencies, change management provides value: coordinated notification (operations teams know a change is happening at 11 PM); risk assessment (what is the patch's own risk profile? any known issues with this patch?); rollback planning (if the patch causes issues, what is the rollback plan?); documentation (creates a record of what was changed when, for compliance and future reference); ECAB PROCESS: STEP 1 — DECLARE EMERGENCY CHANGE: change manager or security lead declares the change an emergency; STEP 2 — CONVENE ECAB: ECAB = on-call subset of CAB (typically: change manager + security lead + operations lead); can be convened by phone/video in minutes (not a 2-hour meeting); STEP 3 — EXPEDITED RFC: submit a brief RFC covering: what change (patch X), why (CVSS 9.8, active exploitation), affected systems, rollback plan (remove patch), test plan (verify service after patching); STEP 4 — APPROVAL: ECAB reviews and approves (typically minutes); STEP 5 — IMPLEMENT: implementation proceeds under approved change window; STEP 6 — RETROSPECTIVE DOCUMENTATION: full RFC completed retroactively within 24-48 hours; presented at next normal CAB for review; REAL EXAMPLE: Log4Shell (Dec 2021) — virtually every organization invoked emergency change processes to patch; those without emergency processes had to choose between unacceptable delay or unsanctioned changes.
explanations.b: Waiting until Tuesday for a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability being actively exploited is an unacceptable risk. The emergency change process exists precisely for this scenario — urgent action required to prevent or resolve significant service impact.
explanations.c: Implementing without any approval creates: no audit trail; no coordination (other teams unaware); no rollback plan documented; for regulated systems, an undocumented change may be a compliance violation (SOX, PCI-DSS). 'Security emergency' doesn't eliminate the need for coordination — it requires EXPEDITED coordination.
explanations.d: Retrospective reporting (implementing first, telling CAB later with no advance process) is the least safe option: no coordination during implementation; no rollback plan; compliance violation for regulated systems. ECAB provides the same speed with minimally required governance.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — standard change; pre-approval; change model; routine changes
questions.text: A project manager asks: 'Why does my team need to submit an RFC every time they apply a routine security patch? It takes 2 weeks to get approval.' What ITIL mechanism exists to streamline recurring, low-risk changes?

answers.text: Standard changes — pre-approved change types that don't require individual RFC approval; once the CAB approves a 'change model' (the procedure for a specific type of change), the procedure can be executed without individual CAB review each time; for security patches, a 'Monthly Security Patch Standard Change' model is defined and pre-approved; the team executes it per the procedure without individual CAB review
All changes must follow the same RFC-to-CAB process — no exceptions exist for routine work
Ask the security team to implement patches instead — different teams have different approval thresholds
Emergency change process is the solution — declare all patches as emergencies to bypass CAB

explanations.a: STANDARD CHANGE MECHANISM: WHAT IT IS: a pre-approved change type where: the change procedure is well-documented; the risk is low and well-understood; the procedure has been successfully executed many times; individual CAB review is not required for each occurrence. HOW IT'S ESTABLISHED: the team proposes the change model to the CAB: 'We propose a standard change for monthly security patching with the following procedure: [step-by-step]; rollback plan: [remove patch]; testing: [verify service after patching]'; CAB reviews and approves the change MODEL (not each individual execution); CHANGE REGISTER: the standard change is registered in the change management system; EXECUTION: when a monthly patch cycle arrives, the team logs a standard change instance (records what was done) and follows the pre-approved procedure without individual CAB review; POST-IMPLEMENTATION RECORD: the standard change execution is still recorded for audit purposes. COMMON STANDARD CHANGE EXAMPLES: monthly OS security patching (following the approved procedure); adding a user to a predefined security group; restarting a service using documented procedure; applying a pre-approved configuration template to a new server; replacing a failed hard drive in a RAID array. WHAT MAKES A GOOD STANDARD CHANGE CANDIDATE: well-defined, repeatable procedure; consistently low risk in practice; performed frequently; clear rollback available. PERIODIC REVIEW: standard changes are reviewed periodically (annually) to confirm they remain low-risk and the procedure remains current.
explanations.b: A 2-week approval cycle for routine monthly patches is exactly the dysfunctional change management pattern that the standard change mechanism was designed to fix. Applying the same process to all changes regardless of risk defeats the purpose of tiered change management.
explanations.c: Routing work to a different team to bypass change control is not a solution — it's a workaround that creates governance gaps and inconsistency.
explanations.d: Declaring routine patches as emergencies to bypass CAB is an abuse of the emergency process: it dilutes the emergency process for genuine emergencies; it prevents proper coordination; it creates compliance risks for regulated environments.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — change freeze; blackout periods; holiday freeze; project planning impact
questions.text: A project manager plans to deploy a major new e-commerce platform on December 18. The IT change management policy specifies a 'change freeze' from December 15 to January 5 (the holiday retail peak). What is a change freeze and how should the PM respond?

answers.text: A change freeze is a defined period where non-emergency changes to production systems are prohibited or heavily restricted to protect service stability during high-risk periods; the PM should: recognize the December 18 deployment falls within the freeze; evaluate options (move deployment to December 12 before the freeze, or to January 6 after it); engage the change manager immediately; evaluate whether any exception process exists for the deployment; update the project schedule accordingly
Ignore the change freeze — project delivery timelines override operational change control policies
Submit the RFC anyway — the CAB will make an exception for project delivery dates
Proceed with the deployment as planned — the freeze only applies to infrastructure changes, not application deployments

explanations.a: CHANGE FREEZE MANAGEMENT: WHAT IS A CHANGE FREEZE: a defined period where the change management policy prohibits or heavily restricts production changes; protects service stability during HIGH-RISK PERIODS: retail holiday peak (Black Friday through New Year); financial year-end processing; tax filing seasons; academic enrollment periods; post-major-release stability periods; RATIONALE: statistics show that changes cause 70-80% of availability problems; during the holiday peak, an e-commerce outage is catastrophically expensive; the risk-reward of a new deployment doesn't justify the availability risk during peak revenue period. PM OPTIONS: OPTION 1 — MOVE DEPLOYMENT EARLIER: deploy December 12 (3 days before freeze); provides 3 days of stabilization before peak; best option if development is complete; OPTION 2 — DEPLOY AFTER FREEZE: January 6 deployment; project closes in the new year; safest for production stability; OPTION 3 — EXCEPTION REQUEST: some organizations allow freeze exceptions for: critical security patches (emergency change); business-critical deployments with executive sign-off; if exception is requested: requires justification ('this cannot wait because...'); elevated approval (CIO-level); detailed rollback plan; SCHEDULE IMPACT: either option affects the project schedule; inform sponsor immediately; update the schedule baseline through change control. KEY PM LEARNING: identify change freeze periods in the PLANNING phase — not 2 weeks before go-live.
explanations.b: Change management policies apply to all IT changes — project delivery timelines don't override operational governance. A PM who ignores the change freeze may face: change being rejected by operations; emergency rollback during peak business period if the deployment fails; regulatory compliance violation (for organizations with documented change control).
explanations.c: CAB exceptions during change freezes are rare and require extraordinary justification. A project delivery date is generally not sufficient justification for breaking a freeze — the freeze exists precisely because the risk is too high during this period.
explanations.d: Application deployments are among the highest-risk changes — a new e-commerce platform deployment carries more stability risk than a routine infrastructure task. Freeze periods apply especially to application deployments.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — change risk assessment; impact analysis; change risk rating
questions.text: A CAB member asks the change requester: 'How did you assess the risk of this change?' The requester submitted 'Low risk' without explanation. What factors should a proper change risk assessment cover?

answers.text: Risk is assessed by how long the change takes — longer changes are always higher risk

A proper change risk assessment covers: number and criticality of services affected; number of users impacted; change complexity (tested before? new code? configuration-only?); change window timing (business hours vs. off-peak); change frequency/familiarity (first time vs. hundredth time); availability of rollback; testing completed in lower environments; dependencies on other concurrent changes; risk rating matrix (probability × impact)
Only the change requestor's opinion is needed — they know their system best
Risk assessment is done after implementation — only then is the actual risk known

explanations.a: Change duration is one input to risk assessment (longer windows have more exposure) but is not the sole or primary determinant. A 2-minute change that touches a payment processing service is higher risk than a 4-hour maintenance window on a low-traffic internal tool.
explanations.b: CHANGE RISK ASSESSMENT FACTORS: SERVICES AND USERS AFFECTED: BREADTH: how many services are affected? (1 application vs. entire network segment); CRITICALITY: what is the affected service's business criticality? (P1 service = high risk; internal tooling = lower risk); USER COUNT: how many users are affected by an outage? (1,000 vs. 50,000 users); REVENUE IMPACT: is this a revenue-generating service? (e-commerce checkout = extremely high criticality). CHANGE COMPLEXITY: TESTED: has this change been tested in dev and staging environments? (tested = lower risk); NOVEL: is this the first time this change type has been made? (novel = higher risk); CHANGE TYPE: code change vs. configuration change vs. data migration? (code changes typically higher risk); SCOPE: how many system components are modified? (more components = more potential failure points). TIMING: BUSINESS HOURS: changes during business hours have more users affected if something goes wrong; PEAK PERIODS: changes during high-traffic periods (Black Friday, payroll processing) are extremely high risk; DEPENDENCY CONFLICTS: are other changes happening at the same time? (concurrent changes complicate rollback). ROLLBACK CAPABILITY: HOW LONG: if the change fails, how quickly can it be rolled back? (2 minutes = lower risk than 2 hours); TESTED ROLLBACK: has the rollback procedure been tested? (untested rollback = higher risk). RISK MATRIX OUTPUT: PROBABILITY: how likely is the change to cause an unintended failure? (based on complexity, testing, familiarity); IMPACT: how severe would a failure be? (based on service criticality, user count, revenue impact); RISK RATING: P × I matrix → Low/Medium/High/Critical; REVIEW PERIOD: the CAB reviews the risk assessment; a self-assessed 'Low' that doesn't align with the factors above will be challenged.
explanations.c: Self-assessment by the requestor is one input — but the CAB provides independent validation. Requestors are motivated to underestimate risk (lower risk = easier approval). Independent CAB review provides a check on optimistic risk assessments.
explanations.d: Risk assessment BEFORE implementation is the entire point — to identify and mitigate risks BEFORE they become outages. Post-implementation risk assessment is a post-mortem, not a risk management tool.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Change Control — project change vs. operational change; project go-live as IT change; RFC for project deployment
questions.text: A project manager is preparing for production deployment of a new inventory management system. The IT change management team tells her: 'You need to submit an RFC for the deployment.' The PM is confused — she has a project change request process. Why is a separate IT RFC required and how do they differ?

answers.text: An IT RFC is not needed if a project change request was already approved — one process covers both
IT change management only applies to infrastructure changes — application deployments are exempt

Project change requests and IT RFCs serve different purposes: the project CR manages changes to the project plan (scope, schedule, cost); the IT RFC manages the change to the live production environment (operational risk, service impact, coordinated deployment); both are needed — the project CR ensures the delivery is authorized; the IT RFC ensures the deployment is coordinated with operations, scheduled appropriately, and has a rollback plan
Submit the IT RFC only after the production deployment is complete — the RFC documents what was done

explanations.a: Project change requests and IT RFCs are separate governance mechanisms for different purposes. A project CR being approved doesn't mean the deployment can happen without change management coordination.
explanations.b: Application deployments are among the most common and highest-impact IT changes. Application change requests represent the majority of IT RFC volume in most organizations.
explanations.c: PROJECT CHANGE REQUEST vs. IT RFC — COMPLEMENTARY GOVERNANCE: PROJECT CHANGE REQUEST: WHAT IT MANAGES: changes to the PROJECT PLAN; scope changes (adding or removing project deliverables); schedule changes (moving milestone dates); budget changes (authorizing additional spend); AUTHORITY: approved by the project sponsor, CCB, or PM (depending on thresholds); TIMING: throughout the project lifecycle; QUESTION ANSWERED: 'Is this delivery authorized and has it been approved by the business?'. IT RFC (REQUEST FOR CHANGE): WHAT IT MANAGES: changes to LIVE PRODUCTION SYSTEMS; implementation risk during the deployment window; coordination with operations, infrastructure, and other teams; scheduling in the change calendar (avoiding conflicts with other changes); AUTHORITY: approved by the CAB; TIMING: submitted before production deployment; QUESTION ANSWERED: 'How will this change be safely deployed into production with minimal service disruption?'.
