explanations.a: THREE CLOUD SERVICE MODELS: IaaS (INFRASTRUCTURE AS A SERVICE): PROVIDER MANAGES: physical data centers; physical servers and storage; networking hardware; hypervisor and virtualization layer; CUSTOMER MANAGES: operating system installation and patching; middleware (web servers, databases); runtime environments; applications; data; EXAMPLES: AWS EC2; Azure Virtual Machines; Google Compute Engine; USE WHEN: you need full control over the OS and software stack; CUSTOMER TECHNICAL EXPERTISE NEEDED: high. PaaS (PLATFORM AS A SERVICE): PROVIDER MANAGES: everything in IaaS PLUS operating system; middleware; runtime environments (Java, Python, Node.js); database engines; CUSTOMER MANAGES: application code; application configuration; data; EXAMPLES: AWS Elastic Beanstalk; Google App Engine; Azure App Service; Heroku; USE WHEN: you want to focus on application development without managing infrastructure; CUSTOMER TECHNICAL EXPERTISE NEEDED: medium (application development focused). SaaS (SOFTWARE AS A SERVICE): PROVIDER MANAGES: everything; physical infrastructure through application; software updates and maintenance; CUSTOMER MANAGES: user configuration and data within the application; EXAMPLES: Salesforce; Microsoft 365; Google Workspace; ServiceNow; Workday; USE WHEN: you need standard software functionality without hosting it yourself; CUSTOMER TECHNICAL EXPERTISE NEEDED: low (business user focused). PM DECISION FRAMEWORK: SaaS first (does a commercial product solve the need?); PaaS if custom development needed without infrastructure management; IaaS if specialized infrastructure control is required.
explanations.b: The three service models (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) represent fundamentally different levels of managed service — each has distinct customer responsibilities and use cases.
explanations.c: Cloud service models are classified by the level of managed service — not by deployment speed. Deployment speed varies independently within each model.
explanations.d: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS have fundamentally different customer responsibilities, total cost profiles, and control levels. They are not interchangeable.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — cloud deployment models; public private hybrid community cloud
questions.text: A project manager is recommending a cloud deployment model for a regulated financial services company. What are the four cloud deployment models and when is each appropriate?

answers.text: The four models are: Public cloud (shared infrastructure owned by a cloud provider, accessible over the internet — best for scalable, cost-effective workloads with no strict data residency requirements); Private cloud (cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization — best for regulated industries with strict data control requirements); Hybrid cloud (combination of public and private — production data in private, burst capacity or dev/test in public); Community cloud (shared among organizations with similar requirements — e.g., government cloud, healthcare cloud)
There is only one cloud deployment model — all organizations use the same type of cloud
Cloud deployment models are: Cheap, Medium, and Premium — classified by cost tier
All four models provide identical data control and cost — the choice is purely aesthetic

explanations.a: FOUR CLOUD DEPLOYMENT MODELS: PUBLIC CLOUD: DEFINITION: infrastructure owned, operated, and managed by a third-party provider (AWS, Azure, GCP); shared among multiple organizations; accessible over the internet; ADVANTAGES: pay-as-you-go (no capital expense); unlimited scalability; global geographic reach; DISADVANTAGES: data sovereignty concerns; shared infrastructure; BEST FOR: web-facing applications; development/test environments; workloads requiring elasticity; organizations without strict data residency requirements. PRIVATE CLOUD: DEFINITION: cloud infrastructure exclusively for one organization; may be on-premises or hosted by a third party; ADVANTAGES: full control; data stays within organizational boundaries; customizable to exact needs; DISADVANTAGES: capital expense; requires technical expertise to operate; BEST FOR: regulated industries (financial services, healthcare, government); highly sensitive data; strict compliance requirements. HYBRID CLOUD: DEFINITION: combination of public and private cloud, connected with technology allowing data and applications to be shared between them; EXAMPLES: production data and customer PII in private cloud; dev/test and non-sensitive analytics in public cloud; burst workloads scale from private to public during peak demand; ADVANTAGES: flexibility; cost optimization; compliance for sensitive data with scalability for others; BEST FOR: organizations with mixed workload sensitivity (e.g., financial services firm — ideal for the scenario). COMMUNITY CLOUD: DEFINITION: infrastructure shared among organizations with similar compliance requirements; EXAMPLES: FedRAMP-compliant government cloud; healthcare cloud meeting HIPAA; financial services cloud meeting SOX; ADVANTAGES: shared compliance cost; pre-certified for community's regulatory requirements; BEST FOR: government agencies; regulated industry consortiums.
explanations.b: Organizations choose deployment models based on specific requirements: regulatory constraints, cost optimization, data sovereignty, and scalability needs. A single universal model doesn't serve all these diverse needs.
explanations.c: Cloud deployment models are classified by ownership, access, and control characteristics — not by cost tier.
explanations.d: The four models have fundamentally different data control levels, cost structures, and performance characteristics. For a regulated financial services company, the choice between public and private cloud determines regulatory compliance capability.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — OSI model; network layers; networking concepts for project managers
questions.text: A project manager needs basic networking literacy to communicate with the infrastructure team. What is the OSI model and why does it matter for project planning?

answers.text: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer conceptual framework describing how network communications work; for project managers, the most relevant layers are: Layer 3 (Network — IP addressing, routing); Layer 4 (Transport — TCP/UDP, ports); Layer 7 (Application — HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, email protocols); understanding layers helps PMs scope network security requirements, communicate with infrastructure teams, and understand where security controls like firewalls (Layer 3-4) and WAFs (Layer 7) operate
The OSI model is a project management framework for organizing project phases — unrelated to networking
The OSI model only applies to physical network hardware — software applications don't use the OSI model
Project managers don't need to understand networking — infrastructure teams handle all technical concepts

explanations.a: OSI MODEL — PROJECT MANAGER'S VIEW: 7 LAYERS (mnemonic: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'): LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL: cables, fiber optic, wireless signals; hardware that transmits raw bits; LAYER 2 — DATA LINK: MAC addresses, switches; local network framing; LAYER 3 — NETWORK: IP addresses, routing, routers; determines path from source to destination; PROJECT RELEVANCE: IP address planning (how many IPs needed for the new system?); LAYER 4 — TRANSPORT: TCP (reliable, connection-oriented) and UDP (fast, connectionless); port numbers (HTTP = port 80, HTTPS = 443, SSH = 22); PROJECT RELEVANCE: firewall rules specify which ports to open; LAYER 5 — SESSION: establishes and manages sessions between applications; LAYER 6 — PRESENTATION: data formatting, encryption/decryption (SSL/TLS); PROJECT RELEVANCE: TLS encryption for data in transit operates here; LAYER 7 — APPLICATION: user-facing protocols — HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMTP, FTP; PROJECT RELEVANCE: WAF operates at Layer 7 (filters malicious HTTP); application security testing focuses here. WHY PMs NEED THIS: SCOPE CONVERSATIONS: infrastructure team says 'we need to open a port on the Layer 4 firewall' — PM understands this means a network security rule change; SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: 'Layer 7 WAF protection' means the PM should include WAF in requirements; SYSTEM DEPENDENCIES: understanding that DNS (Layer 7) resolves application names to IP addresses helps the PM understand why DNS configuration is a deployment prerequisite; BASIC LITERACY: enables productive conversations with technical teams without being an expert.
explanations.b: OSI stands for Open Systems Interconnection — a networking standard, not a project management framework.
explanations.c: The OSI model describes how ALL networked communications work — from physical hardware to application protocols. Software applications communicate using Layer 7 protocols.
explanations.d: Project managers who lack basic IT literacy face: inability to understand technical requirements; communication gaps with infrastructure teams; scope gaps (missing technical requirements); unrealistic timelines (not accounting for infrastructure provisioning steps). Basic IT literacy is a project management competency.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — containers; Docker; Kubernetes; VMs vs. containers; microservices
questions.text: A development team proposes using containers (Docker) instead of traditional VMs for a new microservices application. The project manager needs to understand the difference to evaluate the proposal. What are containers and how do they differ from VMs?

answers.text: Containers package an application and its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit that shares the host OS kernel (unlike VMs which each have their own OS); containers start in seconds (vs. minutes for VMs), use less resource overhead, and are ideal for microservices; VMs provide stronger isolation (each has its own OS) and are better for running different operating systems; containers add complexity in orchestration (Kubernetes) and security configuration
Containers and VMs are identical technologies with different names
Containers are only for web applications — VMs are required for databases and infrastructure
Containers provide complete hardware isolation — each container has its own dedicated physical CPU and RAM

explanations.a: CONTAINERS vs. VMs: VIRTUAL MACHINES: ISOLATION: each VM has its own complete OS (kernel + OS libraries); HYPERVISOR: manages resource allocation between VMs; STARTUP TIME: minutes (OS must boot); RESOURCE OVERHEAD: significant — each VM needs dedicated RAM for its OS (typically 1-4 GB overhead per VM); IMAGE SIZE: typically gigabytes (full OS included); SECURITY ISOLATION: strongest (kernel separation between VMs); BEST FOR: running different operating systems; applications requiring kernel-level isolation; legacy applications; long-running services. CONTAINERS: ISOLATION: application-level; containers share the HOST OS KERNEL (only application code and dependencies are isolated, not the kernel); CONTAINER RUNTIME: Docker (builds and runs containers); Kubernetes (orchestrates many containers); STARTUP TIME: seconds (no OS boot — just the application starts); RESOURCE OVERHEAD: minimal (no duplicate OS per container; 10-100 MB per container vs. gigabytes per VM); IMAGE SIZE: megabytes (app + dependencies, no OS); SECURITY ISOLATION: weaker than VMs (kernel is shared — kernel vulnerability affects all containers on the host); requires additional security hardening; BEST FOR: microservices (each service in its own container); CI/CD pipelines (fast startup/shutdown); applications requiring high density and portability. KUBERNETES (K8s): orchestrates thousands of containers; handles: container scheduling across nodes; automatic scaling (scale out when load increases); self-healing (restart failed containers); load balancing; PM RELEVANCE: container-based projects need: Docker/Kubernetes expertise (specialized skill, may require contractor); security configuration for containers; monitoring/logging infrastructure (containers are ephemeral — centralized logging needed).
explanations.b: Containers and VMs use fundamentally different isolation mechanisms and have different performance characteristics, resource usage, and security profiles.
explanations.c: Containers are used for virtually all application types: web servers, APIs, databases (PostgreSQL, Redis run in containers in production), data processing, and infrastructure services.
explanations.d: Containers share the HOST OS kernel and are scheduled by the container runtime — they don't have dedicated physical hardware.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — cloud migration; lift-and-shift; re-platform; re-architect; 6 Rs
questions.text: A project manager is leading a cloud migration project for 15 applications. The cloud architect explains there are different migration strategies. What are the main cloud migration strategies and how does the PM use this to plan the project?

answers.text: The main migration strategies (6 Rs) are: Rehost (Lift-and-Shift — move as-is to cloud VMs; fastest, lowest cost, least cloud-optimized); Replatform (move and optimize for cloud — e.g., migrate to managed database service; moderate effort, some cloud benefit); Refactor/Re-architect (redesign to be cloud-native — microservices, serverless; most expensive/time-consuming, greatest long-term cloud value); Retire (decommission unused applications); Retain (keep on-premises — too complex or regulated); Replace (switch to SaaS); different applications use different strategies based on complexity and cloud benefit
There is only one cloud migration strategy — move all applications to the cloud the same way
All applications should be re-architected — maximum cloud optimization is always worth the cost
Cloud migration is a single-step project — all applications move simultaneously on one date

explanations.a: THE 6 Rs OF CLOUD MIGRATION: REHOST (LIFT-AND-SHIFT): WHAT: copy the application from on-premises server to a cloud VM with minimal or no changes; ANALOGY: picking up a house and setting it down in a new location unchanged; EFFORT: lowest; TIMELINE: fastest; CLOUD BENEFIT: lowest (same app, just in a different location — not using cloud-native features); BEST FOR: applications that must be migrated quickly; legacy applications hard to modify; initial migration phase (can optimize later); EXAMPLE: take a web server running on physical hardware and run it on an EC2 instance. REPLATFORM (LIFT-TINKER-AND-SHIFT): WHAT: make modest optimizations during the migration (without changing the core architecture); EXAMPLES: migrate database from on-premises SQL Server to Amazon RDS (managed database service — eliminates OS patching); move file storage to S3; EFFORT: moderate; CLOUD BENEFIT: moderate (managed services reduce operational burden); REFACTOR/RE-ARCHITECT: WHAT: fundamentally redesign the application to be cloud-native; EXAMPLES: break monolith into microservices; replace on-premises batch processing with serverless Lambda functions; EFFORT: highest (essentially rebuilding the application); CLOUD BENEFIT: maximum (scalability, resilience, cost optimization); BEST FOR: business-critical applications where cloud-native capabilities provide substantial business value. RETIRE: WHAT: identify applications that are no longer needed and decommission them; EFFECT: reduces migration scope and licensing costs; RETAIN: WHAT: keep on-premises — regulatory requirements, high latency sensitivity, or replatform/refactor not currently feasible; REPLACE: WHAT: replace the application with a SaaS alternative (e.g., replace on-premises CRM with Salesforce); PM PLANNING IMPLICATIONS: assess each of 15 applications and assign a migration strategy; different strategies have different costs, timelines, and risks; the portfolio of strategies drives the overall project plan; typically: 40-60% rehost; 20-30% replatform; 10-20% refactor; 10-15% retire/retain/replace.
explanations.b: Different applications have different characteristics (age, complexity, regulatory requirements, business value) that make different migration strategies appropriate. A single approach wastes opportunity or wastes investment.
explanations.c: Re-architecting all applications would be massively expensive and time-consuming. For most organizations, a mix of strategies (primarily rehost and replatform) provides the right balance of cost and benefit.
explanations.d: Migrating all 15 applications simultaneously is extremely high risk — a single failed migration could affect all applications. A phased approach (wave-based migration) is standard: less critical, lower-risk applications first; critical applications last.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — RTO RPO; disaster recovery objectives; recovery planning
questions.text: A project is building a payment processing system. The business requires: 'If there's a disaster, we cannot be down for more than 4 hours, and we cannot lose more than 15 minutes of transactions.' Translate these requirements into RTO and RPO and explain their implications for DR design.

answers.text: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = 4 hours — maximum acceptable downtime before service is restored; RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = 15 minutes — maximum acceptable data loss (transactions processed in the last 15 minutes before a disaster might be lost); implications: the 15-minute RPO requires near-continuous database replication (not daily backups which would produce up to 24 hours of data loss); the 4-hour RTO requires automated failover capability or a pre-provisioned DR site (not a cold site that takes days to bring up)
RTO and RPO are the same metric — both measure how quickly a system recovers
RTO = 15 minutes; RPO = 4 hours — time objectives are interchangeable
RTO and RPO are only relevant for on-premises systems — cloud systems don't need DR planning

explanations.a: RTO AND RPO DEFINITIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: RTO (RECOVERY TIME OBJECTIVE): DEFINITION: the maximum acceptable time from a disaster occurring to service being restored; REQUIREMENT: 4 hours — service must be restored within 4 hours of a disaster; IMPLICATION FOR DR DESIGN: determines the type of DR site needed: COLD SITE (12+ hours): pre-built data center with power and connectivity but no servers running; must provision servers from scratch → RTO of days; TOO SLOW for 4-hour RTO; WARM SITE (2-8 hours): infrastructure partially provisioned; systems can be started and configured from recent backups → RTO of 2-8 hours; POSSIBLE for 4-hour RTO if execution is efficient; HOT SITE (<1 hour): fully provisioned, mirror of production; automated failover; RTO of minutes to 1 hour; BEST for 4-hour RTO requirement (provides margin); CLOUD DR: cloud enables hot-site DR without the physical cost of maintaining a standby data center. RPO (RECOVERY POINT OBJECTIVE): DEFINITION: the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time; REQUIREMENT: 15 minutes — transactions processed up to 15 minutes before the disaster may be lost; transactions more than 15 minutes old must be recoverable; IMPLICATION FOR DR DESIGN: determines backup/replication frequency: DAILY BACKUP: up to 24 hours of data loss → FAILS 15-minute RPO; HOURLY BACKUP: up to 60 minutes of data loss → FAILS 15-minute RPO; 15-MINUTE INCREMENTAL BACKUP: achieves the RPO; SYNCHRONOUS DATABASE REPLICATION: zero data loss (each transaction replicated to DR before acknowledged to user) → EXCEEDS RPO requirement (better than needed). COMBINED IMPLICATION: a hot DR site with 15-minute incremental replication (or near-synchronous replication) satisfies both RTO (4 hours) and RPO (15 minutes); PROJECT COST IMPLICATION: hot site with continuous replication is significantly more expensive than a daily backup approach — the PM must include this DR infrastructure cost in the business case.
explanations.b: RTO and RPO measure different things: RTO is about TIME TO RESTORE SERVICE; RPO is about acceptable DATA LOSS. They have different implications for DR architecture and cost.
explanations.c: RTO = Recovery TIME Objective (downtime); RPO = Recovery POINT Objective (data loss). The 4-hour requirement refers to downtime (RTO) and the 15-minute requirement refers to data loss (RPO). Swapping them produces an incorrect DR design.
explanations.d: Cloud systems absolutely require DR planning — cloud providers can have regional outages (AWS us-east-1 has had multiple significant outages). A multi-region DR architecture using cloud services is a common solution for cloud-hosted systems.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — DNS; DHCP; IP addressing; networking fundamentals for PMs
questions.text: A project team is deploying a new application that requires DNS configuration, IP address planning, and DHCP setup. A developer asks the PM: 'Why do we need to plan DNS, IP, and DHCP separately?' How should the PM explain each and why all three are required?

answers.text: DNS, DHCP, and IP are the same thing — one configuration covers all three
Only DNS is needed — DHCP and IP planning are legacy concepts not relevant to modern applications

All three serve different but interdependent roles: IP addresses (unique numerical identifiers for devices — must be planned to avoid conflicts); DNS (Domain Name System — translates human-readable names like 'api.company.com' to IP addresses — required for service discovery and application connectivity); DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — automatically assigns IP addresses to clients — required for end-user devices and workstations); all three must be configured correctly for the application to be reachable by its domain name
IP addressing, DNS, and DHCP are all the same concept — they all refer to how computers find each other on a network

explanations.a: DNS, DHCP, and IP addressing are three distinct, interdependent networking concepts that each require separate configuration.
explanations.b: DHCP is essential for user devices to get IP addresses automatically; IP planning is essential to avoid conflicts and design subnets; both remain critical concepts in modern networks including cloud environments.
explanations.c: DNS, DHCP, AND IP — THREE DISTINCT ROLES: IP ADDRESSING: WHAT: every device and service on a network has a unique IP address; IPV4: e.g., 192.168.1.100 (4 octets, 0-255 each); IPv6: longer format (e.g., 2001:0db8::1) for the expanded address space; PLANNING REQUIREMENTS: allocate IP address ranges (subnets) for each environment (production, staging, test); plan IP addresses for servers (typically static — assigned and never changing); avoid IP conflicts (two devices with the same IP = network failure); PM IMPLICATION: IP planning is an infrastructure design task that must be completed before deployment; DHCP (DYNAMIC HOST CONFIGURATION PROTOCOL): WHAT: a server that automatically assigns IP addresses to client devices when they connect to the network; WHO NEEDS IT: end-user workstations, laptops, mobile devices — they don't have fixed IPs; they request an IP from DHCP on connection; WHAT IT PROVIDES: IP address (temporary lease), subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server addresses; PM IMPLICATION: DHCP server must be available before workstations connect; DHCP scope must cover expected number of devices; note that servers typically use STATIC IPs (not DHCP) — only client devices typically use DHCP. DNS (DOMAIN NAME SYSTEM): WHAT: translates human-readable names to IP addresses; USER TYPES 'api.company.com' → DNS resolves to IP 10.20.30.40 → browser connects to 10.20.30.40; PLANNING REQUIREMENTS: DNS record creation for every service hostname: A record: api.company.com → 10.20.30.40; CNAME: alias records; MX records for email; CONFIGURATION TIMING: DNS records must be created BEFORE go-live (if DNS isn't configured, no one can reach the new application by name); DNS propagation takes 0-48 hours depending on TTL settings; PM IMPLICATION: include DNS record creation as a deployment readiness criterion; HOW THEY CONNECT: DHCP tells workstations 'your DNS server is at 10.1.0.1'; DNS tells applications 'api.company.com is at 10.20.30.40'; IP addressing makes the actual connection from workstation to the server at 10.20.30.40; all three must be configured for the user to successfully reach the new application.
explanations.d: All three concepts are distinct: IP = the address; DNS = the name directory; DHCP = the address assignment service.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — storage types; SAN NAS DAS; storage tiers; RAID concepts
questions.text: A project is designing storage for a new financial database that requires: high performance (IOPS), high availability (no single point of failure), and large capacity. What storage concepts should the PM understand and how do different storage options map to these requirements?

answers.text: All storage is the same — capacity is the only relevant storage metric
Only SSD storage matters — no other storage concepts are relevant for modern systems

Key storage concepts: DAS (Direct-Attached Storage — fast, simple, but no sharing); SAN (Storage Area Network — high-performance block storage for databases, connected via high-speed fiber; excellent for the IOPS and HA requirements); NAS (Network-Attached Storage — file-level storage for shared access; lower performance than SAN); RAID (provides redundancy — RAID 1 = mirroring; RAID 5/6 = distributed parity; RAID 10 = mirror + stripe; prevents data loss if a drive fails); for a financial database: SAN with RAID 10 or RAID 6 provides the right combination of performance and redundancy
Storage planning is post-project work — it doesn't need to be addressed in project requirements

explanations.a: Storage has multiple critical dimensions: performance (IOPS — input/output operations per second); capacity (how much data can be stored); availability (what happens when a drive fails?); access patterns (block storage for databases; file storage for documents); cost (SSDs cost more than HDDs).
explanations.b: SSDs are one storage media type (solid-state, high-performance) — the storage architecture concepts (SAN, NAS, RAID) apply to both SSDs and traditional HDDs. SSDs on a SAN is the best combination for a high-performance financial database.
explanations.c: STORAGE CONCEPTS FOR FINANCIAL DATABASE: DAS (DIRECT-ATTACHED STORAGE): WHAT: storage physically connected directly to the server (internal SATA/SAS drives, external USB/eSATA); PERFORMANCE: good (direct connection, no network overhead); SHARING: cannot be shared between servers (each server sees only its own storage); USE FOR: single-server applications; development workstations; LIMITATION: no high availability across servers (if the server fails, storage is inaccessible). SAN (STORAGE AREA NETWORK): WHAT: dedicated high-speed network connecting servers to storage arrays; uses Fibre Channel (FC) or iSCSI protocols; PERFORMANCE: excellent — specifically designed for high-IOPS workloads; BLOCK STORAGE: server sees SAN storage as if it's a local disk; SHARING: multiple servers can access the same storage array (though typically only one server mounts a given volume at a time); HIGH AVAILABILITY: SAN arrays support RAID configurations; multiple paths between server and storage (multipathing — if one FC connection fails, alternate path activates); BEST FOR: production databases; financial transaction systems; any workload requiring consistent, high IOPS. NAS (NETWORK-ATTACHED STORAGE): WHAT: storage accessible over a standard IP network (Ethernet); FILE STORAGE: servers access storage as a network file share (SMB, NFS protocols); PERFORMANCE: lower than SAN (IP network overhead); SHARING: multiple servers can read/write simultaneously (file sharing); BEST FOR: shared file storage; document management; home directories; backup targets. RAID CONFIGURATIONS: RAID 1 (MIRRORING): data written to two drives simultaneously; if one fails, the other has a complete copy; WRITE PERFORMANCE: slightly lower (must write to both); READ PERFORMANCE: higher (can read from either); CAPACITY: 50% efficiency (2 drives = 1 drive of storage); RAID 5 (DISTRIBUTED PARITY): data + parity spread across ≥3 drives; can survive 1 drive failure; CAPACITY: (N-1)/N efficiency; RAID 6: can survive 2 simultaneous drive failures; RAID 10 (MIRROR + STRIPE): mirrors the data AND stripes across multiple pairs; best performance + 2-drive failure tolerance; RECOMMENDATION for financial database: SAN with RAID 10 (or RAID 6) — maximizes performance and provides drive failure protection.
explanations.d: Storage planning is a critical infrastructure project requirement: storage must be procured (lead time 4-8 weeks for hardware); sized correctly (database size × growth rate × 3-year plan); configured before the application is deployed. Missing storage planning from requirements is a significant project risk.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — disaster recovery tiers; hot warm cold site; DR vs. HA; business continuity
questions.text: A project manager is designing the disaster recovery strategy for a new ERP system. The business continuity team says the ERP requires Tier 2 DR. What are the DR tiers and how do they differ from high availability (HA)?

answers.text: Disaster recovery and high availability are the same concept
DR tiers only apply to government organizations — commercial businesses use HA instead

DR tiers represent different recovery speed/cost trade-offs: Cold site (Tier 1 — empty facility with power/cooling; servers must be provisioned; RTO days-weeks; lowest cost); Warm site (Tier 2 — partially provisioned; servers exist but must be configured and restored from backup; RTO hours-days; moderate cost); Hot site (Tier 3 — fully provisioned mirror of production; automated failover; RTO minutes-hours; highest cost). DR protects against site-level disasters. HA protects against component failures WITHIN a site (redundant servers, load balancers, clustering — keeps service running during hardware failures but doesn't protect against site-wide disasters)
A cold site provides the fastest recovery — the simpler the site, the faster the recovery

explanations.a: HA (High Availability) and DR (Disaster Recovery) operate at different scales: HA = redundancy within a site (survives component failure); DR = recovery at a different location (survives site failure). Both are needed for comprehensive resilience.
explanations.b: DR tiers apply to all organizations with critical IT systems — government, commercial, healthcare, and financial organizations all use DR planning. The terminology and investment scale may differ, but the concept is universal.
explanations.c: DR TIERS AND HA: COLD SITE (TIER 1): WHAT IS AVAILABLE: physical space; power and cooling; network connectivity; WHAT IS NOT AVAILABLE: servers (must be procured or shipped from primary site); application software (must be installed); data (must be restored from offsite backup); RTO: DAYS to WEEKS (hardware procurement + setup + data restore); COST: lowest (facility cost only); BEST FOR: applications with flexible recovery requirements; non-critical systems; archival systems; RISK: if your hardware vendor can't ship in 3 days during a regional disaster, RTO extends. WARM SITE (TIER 2): WHAT IS AVAILABLE: facility; power/cooling; servers (already installed, possibly powered down); network connectivity; WHAT MUST BE DONE: power on and configure servers; restore data from backup (could be up to 24 hours of data depending on backup frequency); deploy and configure applications; RTO: HOURS to DAYS; COST: moderate (facility + hardware standing by); BEST FOR: important business applications (ERP, CRM) that need recovery within 24-48 hours; the ERP Tier 2 requirement aligns here; HOT SITE (TIER 3+): WHAT IS AVAILABLE: fully operational mirror of production; all servers running; data replicated (near-real-time); applications deployed and operational; FAILOVER: automated or manual with very fast procedure; RTO: MINUTES to HOURS; COST: highest (full duplicate of production); BEST FOR: business-critical systems where extended downtime is catastrophic (payment processing, healthcare monitoring, stock trading). HIGH AVAILABILITY (HA) — DIFFERENT CONCEPT: PROTECTS AGAINST: individual component failures (server, network card, storage controller); MECHANISM: redundant components within the same site (active-active clusters, load balancers, RAID storage); RTO: ZERO or SECONDS (automatic failover within the site); DOES NOT PROTECT AGAINST: fire, flood, power grid failure, earthquake (whole-site events); HA + DR TOGETHER: HA handles component failures (no downtime for hardware failure); DR handles site failures (recovery in hours for major disasters).
explanations.d: Cold sites provide the SLOWEST recovery (most manual work required) and LOWEST cost. Hot sites provide the FASTEST recovery and HIGHEST cost. Speed and cost are inversely correlated in DR tier design.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — API; REST; integration; API-first; PM understanding of APIs
questions.text: A project manager is planning an integration between a new HR system and an existing payroll system. The technical team says: 'We'll use the payroll system's REST API.' What is a REST API and what project planning considerations does API integration introduce?

answers.text: A REST API is a type of server hardware — API servers are physical machines dedicated to integration
REST APIs only work for simple data retrieval — complex operations require different integration methods

A REST API (Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface) is a standard way for two software systems to communicate over HTTP/HTTPS; one system makes requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to the other's endpoints; project planning considerations: API documentation review; rate limits (how many calls per minute?); authentication requirements (API key, OAuth); error handling design; API versioning (will the payroll API change during the project?); API testing in lower environments; vendor API availability and reliability
API integration requires no special project planning — developers handle all API decisions independently

explanations.a: API (Application Programming Interface) is a SOFTWARE concept — a specification for how two software systems communicate. It has nothing to do with physical server hardware.
explanations.b: REST APIs handle complex multi-step operations: creating records; updating nested data; triggering workflows; processing financial transactions. REST is suitable for complex integrations.
explanations.c: REST API CONCEPTS FOR PROJECT MANAGERS: WHAT IS A REST API: an architectural style for building APIs using HTTP methods; STANDARD HTTP METHODS (CRUD operations): GET: retrieve data ('GET /employees/123' returns employee 123's record); POST: create new data ('POST /employees' creates a new employee); PUT/PATCH: update existing data ('PUT /employees/123' updates employee 123); DELETE: remove data ('DELETE /employees/123' removes employee 123); REST API USES: integration between internal systems; mobile app back-ends; third-party service integration; microservices communication; PROJECT PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS: API DOCUMENTATION: does the payroll vendor provide complete API documentation? (what endpoints exist? what data formats? what authentication is required?); RATE LIMITS: most APIs limit calls per minute or per hour (e.g., 1,000 calls/minute); the integration design must stay within limits or use batching; AUTHENTICATION: how does the HR system authenticate to the payroll API? (API key; OAuth 2.0; JWT tokens); the authentication design must be included in the security requirements; ERROR HANDLING: what happens when the API returns an error? (retry logic; notification; fallback process); API VERSIONING: is the payroll API versioned? (v1 vs. v2); if the vendor updates the API during the project, is there backward compatibility?; API TESTING ENVIRONMENT: does the vendor provide a sandbox/test environment? (test integration without affecting real payroll data); RATE LIMIT RISK: if the HR system processes 10,000 employee record updates simultaneously but the API allows only 1,000/minute, the synchronization takes 10+ minutes — a design constraint; CONTRACTS/SLAs: what is the vendor's API availability SLA? (what is the impact if the payroll API is down?).
explanations.d: API integration has significant project planning implications: scope (what data flows in which direction?); design (rate limits, error handling, batching); testing (API test environment required); risk (vendor API changes; API downtime).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — bandwidth; latency; network performance; WAN connectivity
questions.text: A project will deploy a real-time video collaboration tool for a global team with offices in New York, London, and Singapore. The infrastructure team flags 'bandwidth and latency concerns.' What are bandwidth and latency and why do they matter for this project?

answers.text: Bandwidth and latency are the same network metric — both measure network speed
Bandwidth and latency only matter for file downloads — real-time applications are not affected

Bandwidth is the maximum data throughput (Mbps/Gbps) — how much data can flow simultaneously; latency is the delay (milliseconds) for data to travel from source to destination; for real-time video collaboration, latency matters most (high latency causes audio/video sync issues and meeting disruption); bandwidth also matters (HD video requires 5-10 Mbps per participant); NY-Singapore latency is approximately 200ms+ which approaches the threshold for acceptable video quality (target <150ms); this may require: routing optimization; CDN for media relay; regional video servers
Latency is the same across all locations — geography doesn't affect network latency

explanations.a: Bandwidth and latency are distinct metrics: bandwidth measures CAPACITY (how much); latency measures DELAY (how long). For real-time applications, latency is the more critical constraint.
explanations.b: Real-time applications are the MOST sensitive to latency — a 200ms latency that's imperceptible in file download makes real-time voice/video conversation noticeably delayed.
explanations.c: BANDWIDTH vs. LATENCY for real-time video: BANDWIDTH: DEFINITION: the maximum rate of data transfer across a network connection; UNIT: Mbps (megabits per second) or Gbps (gigabits per second); ANALOGY: the width of a highway (more lanes = more cars simultaneously); REAL-TIME VIDEO REQUIREMENTS: 1080p HD video stream: 5-10 Mbps per participant; a 10-person video call: 50-100 Mbps total bandwidth needed; corporate WAN links are typically 100 Mbps – 1 Gbps (generally sufficient); LATENCY: DEFINITION: the time for a data packet to travel from source to destination; UNIT: milliseconds (ms); ANALOGY: the length of the highway (longer road = more time to travel regardless of how many lanes); GEOGRAPHIC LATENCY (APPROXIMATE): New York to London: ~70-80ms (acceptable for video); New York to Singapore: ~170-200ms (approaching the upper limit); Singapore to London: ~180-220ms; IMPACT ON VIDEO COLLABORATION: <150ms: good video quality; 150-300ms: noticeable delay; audio/video sync issues begin; >300ms: satellite-level delay; conversations feel unnatural; speakers talk over each other; SOLUTIONS FOR HIGH LATENCY: CDN FOR MEDIA RELAY: video conferences route through regional media relays (instead of direct peer-to-peer); reduces effective latency (NYC → Singapore peer-to-peer vs. NYC → AWS CloudFront relay → Singapore); REGIONAL VIDEO SERVERS: meeting hosted on a regional server closest to most participants; CODEC OPTIMIZATION: video compression algorithms that are tolerant of higher latency; PM IMPLICATION: the NY-Singapore latency concern is legitimate — the project should: test video quality between all office pairs; evaluate CDN/relay solutions; include network performance testing in the QA plan; the infrastructure team's flag should be investigated and addressed in project design.
explanations.d: Geography directly determines latency — light travels at a finite speed through fiber optic cables; the physical distance between New York and Singapore creates a minimum unavoidable latency of ~170ms.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — VPN; Site-to-Site VPN; Remote Access VPN; encryption tunnel
questions.text: A project manager is planning network connectivity between a company's headquarters and a new cloud environment, AND needs secure remote access for 50 remote workers. The infrastructure team proposes two different VPN solutions. What are the two main VPN types and which suits each need?

answers.text: There is only one type of VPN — all VPNs work the same way
VPNs only encrypt internet traffic — internal corporate network traffic doesn't need encryption

Site-to-Site VPN creates a persistent encrypted tunnel between two fixed locations (HQ to cloud environment — always-on, no user configuration required; traffic between the sites is automatically encrypted); Remote Access VPN allows individual users to connect their device to the corporate network from anywhere (each remote worker installs a VPN client; connects on-demand when working remotely; encrypts all traffic between their device and the corporate network); HQ-to-cloud connectivity = Site-to-Site; remote workers = Remote Access VPN
Site-to-Site VPN requires users to manually connect each day — it's the same as Remote Access VPN

explanations.a: Site-to-Site and Remote Access VPNs have fundamentally different architectures, use cases, and management requirements.
explanations.b: VPNs encrypt traffic between specified endpoints — Site-to-Site VPNs encrypt traffic between two internal corporate networks; Remote Access VPNs encrypt traffic between an external device and the corporate network.
explanations.c: TWO VPN TYPES: SITE-TO-SITE VPN: PURPOSE: connect two physical locations (or cloud environments) with a persistent encrypted tunnel; ARCHITECTURE: VPN gateway device at each end (on-premises router/firewall and cloud VPN gateway); traffic between the two networks is automatically encrypted — no user action required; TYPICAL USES: HQ to branch office connectivity; on-premises data center to cloud VPC (Virtual Private Cloud); EXAMPLE for this project: HQ firewall ↔ AWS/Azure VPN Gateway creates an encrypted tunnel; traffic from HQ servers to cloud resources flows through the tunnel automatically; no individual configuration needed by end users; 24/7 always-on connection; MANAGEMENT: managed by network administrators; ALTERNATIVES: AWS Direct Connect or Azure ExpressRoute (dedicated private connection, faster and more reliable than internet-based VPN but more expensive — for higher-traffic requirements). REMOTE ACCESS VPN (also called 'client VPN'): PURPOSE: allow individual users to securely connect to the corporate network from anywhere; ARCHITECTURE: VPN client software on user's device; connects to a VPN server/concentrator at the corporate network; creates an encrypted tunnel between the user's device and the corporate network; USER EXPERIENCE: user opens VPN client; authenticates (username + password + MFA); encrypted tunnel established; user can now access corporate resources as if in the office; TYPICAL USES: remote workers accessing internal applications; traveling employees; contractors accessing specific systems; EXAMPLE for this project: 50 remote workers install corporate VPN client (e.g., Cisco AnyConnect, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, OpenVPN); each connects individually when working remotely; SPLIT TUNNELING vs. FULL TUNNEL: FULL TUNNEL: all internet traffic routes through corporate VPN (maximum security); SPLIT TUNNEL: only corporate-bound traffic goes through VPN; internet traffic goes direct (better performance; reduces VPN bandwidth load).
explanations.d: Site-to-Site VPN is automatically always-on — once configured, it requires no user action. Remote Access VPN requires users to actively connect.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — load balancing; high availability; redundancy; failover clustering
questions.text: A project is building an e-commerce application that requires 99.95% uptime. The architecture team recommends 'load balancing and high availability clustering.' What are these concepts and how do they contribute to the uptime requirement?

answers.text: Load balancing means adding faster servers — speed is the equivalent of high availability
99.95% uptime is achieved by having one very powerful server — a single large server is more reliable than multiple smaller servers

Load balancing distributes incoming requests across multiple servers (if one server fails or becomes overwhelmed, others continue serving traffic); high availability clustering pairs servers so that if the active server fails, a standby server automatically takes over (failover); together they eliminate single points of failure; 99.95% uptime means a maximum of 4.4 hours of downtime per year — this requires eliminating single server failures, which HA and load balancing accomplish
Load balancing and high availability are only needed for systems with more than 1 million users

explanations.a: Faster servers are still single points of failure — if one fast server fails, the application goes down. High availability requires redundancy (multiple servers), not just higher-performing servers.
explanations.b: A single server — however powerful — is a single point of failure. Hardware failures, OS crashes, and updates all create downtime. Multiple servers with redundancy are required for high uptime targets.
explanations.c: LOAD BALANCING AND HIGH AVAILABILITY: UPTIME CALCULATION: 99.95% uptime means: downtime allowed = (1 - 0.9995) × 8,760 hours/year = 4.38 hours/year; this must account for: planned maintenance windows; hardware failures; software crashes; LOAD BALANCER: WHAT IT DOES: sits in front of multiple application servers; distributes incoming requests across all healthy servers (round-robin, least-connections, or other algorithms); HEALTH CHECKS: continuously monitors each server; if a server fails the health check, it's removed from rotation; TRAFFIC DISTRIBUTION: no single server is overwhelmed; if one server fails, the load balancer routes all traffic to the remaining servers; EXAMPLE: 3 app servers behind a load balancer; each handles 33% of requests; if Server 2 fails: load balancer detects failure (health check); routes traffic to Servers 1 and 3 (50% each); users may notice a brief delay (one request may fail during failover, ~seconds); 99.99%+ uptime achievable for application layer; HIGH AVAILABILITY CLUSTERING: WHAT IT DOES: pairs servers in active-passive or active-active configuration; ACTIVE-PASSIVE (for databases/stateful services): one server is active, processing all requests; one server is standby, synchronized; if the active server fails, the passive server detects the failure and takes over automatically (failover); failover time: seconds to minutes; ACTIVE-ACTIVE: both servers handle requests simultaneously; provides both HA AND load distribution; COMBINING LOAD BALANCER + HA: application tier: 3 servers behind load balancer (HA + load distribution); database tier: active-passive HA cluster (if primary DB fails, standby takes over); both tiers have no single point of failure; 99.95%+ uptime achievable; PM IMPLICATION: HA adds cost (duplicate servers, licenses) but is required to meet the uptime SLA; include in infrastructure budget and scope.
explanations.d: 99.95% uptime requirements apply to any business-critical application where extended downtime causes significant revenue loss or user impact — regardless of user count. E-commerce losing $10,000/minute during an outage justifies HA regardless of whether it has 1,000 or 1 million users.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — database types; relational vs. NoSQL; ACID; SQL vs. NoSQL use cases
questions.text: A project is building a new analytics platform. The data architect says: 'We need both a relational database for transactional data and a NoSQL database for analytics.' A PM needs to understand the difference. What are relational and NoSQL databases and what are their respective strengths?

answers.text: Relational and NoSQL databases are the same — the term 'NoSQL' just means a newer relational database
The choice of database doesn't affect project requirements — any database can do any job equally well
NoSQL databases are always better — relational databases are outdated technology

Relational databases store data in structured tables with relationships (SQL — ACID transactions — strong consistency — ideal for financial and transactional data where data integrity is critical); NoSQL databases sacrifice strict consistency for scale and flexibility (document stores like MongoDB; key-value stores like Redis; columnar stores; graph databases — ideal for large-scale analytics, variable data structures, and high-volume reads/writes at scale)

explanations.a: Relational and NoSQL databases use fundamentally different data models, consistency models, and query languages. 'NoSQL' means 'Not Only SQL' — it's a category of databases that don't use the traditional relational model.
explanations.b: Database choice has significant project requirements implications: data model design; query performance; consistency requirements; migration complexity; skill requirements (developers need different expertise for SQL vs. MongoDB); operational tooling.
explanations.c: Both database types excel in their respective use cases. Replacing all relational databases with NoSQL would lose ACID transaction guarantees needed for financial systems. Replacing all NoSQL with relational would sacrifice scalability for analytics workloads.
explanations.d: RELATIONAL vs. NoSQL DATABASES: RELATIONAL DATABASES (SQL): DATA MODEL: structured tables with defined schemas; rows and columns; relationships between tables (foreign keys); QUERY LANGUAGE: SQL (Structured Query Language) — standardized; ACID PROPERTIES: ATOMICITY: transaction completes entirely or not at all; CONSISTENCY: data always in a valid state; ISOLATION: transactions don't interfere with each other; DURABILITY: committed transactions survive failures; STRENGTHS: strong data integrity (financial, accounting, order processing); complex queries with JOIN operations; well-understood technology with mature tooling; regulatory compliance (auditable data model); EXAMPLES: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle; BEST FOR: transactional data (orders, payments, user accounts); systems requiring strong consistency. NoSQL DATABASES: DATA MODEL: various — document (JSON), key-value, columnar (wide-column), graph; schema-flexible (no rigid table structure); QUERY LANGUAGES: various (MongoDB uses MQL; Cassandra uses CQL; others use different APIs); CONSISTENCY: often eventual consistency (data may be temporarily inconsistent across nodes — reconciles over time); CAP THEOREM: NoSQL databases typically optimize for Availability and Partition tolerance (AP) vs. relational databases which optimize for Consistency (CP); STRENGTHS: HORIZONTAL SCALING: can distribute data across thousands of servers (relational databases scale more complex); HIGH WRITE THROUGHPUT: can handle millions of writes per second; FLEXIBLE SCHEMAS: add new fields without schema migration; TYPES AND USE CASES: DOCUMENT STORES (MongoDB, Couchbase): JSON-like documents; product catalogs, content management; KEY-VALUE (Redis, DynamoDB): simple lookups; caching, session storage; COLUMNAR (Cassandra, HBase): time-series data; analytics; IoT; GRAPH (Neo4j): relationship-centric data; social networks, fraud detection. ANALYTICS PLATFORM — BOTH NEEDED: RELATIONAL DATABASE: transactional records (accurate, consistent, ACID-compliant financial transactions); NoSQL ANALYTICS DATABASE: high-volume analytics queries across billions of records (columnar store optimized for aggregation queries).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — backup types; full incremental differential; backup rotation; 3-2-1 rule
questions.text: A project manager is defining backup requirements for a new application that generates 100 GB of new data daily. The data team proposes a backup strategy. What backup types should the PM understand and what is the 3-2-1 backup rule?

answers.text: All data should be fully backed up every hour — more frequent backups always mean better protection
Backup types don't affect RTO/RPO — all backup methods provide identical recovery time
Only one backup is needed — multiple backups waste storage

Key backup types: Full backup (copy of ALL data — complete but time/storage intensive — typically done weekly); Incremental backup (backs up only data changed since the LAST BACKUP of any type — faster, less storage, but slower restore); Differential backup (backs up only data changed since the LAST FULL BACKUP — medium speed/storage, faster restore than incremental). The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite

explanations.a: Hourly FULL backups for 100 GB/day of new data would generate: 2,400 GB of backup data per day (24 × 100 GB); astronomically expensive; potentially slow enough to impact production performance; the right strategy is a mix of backup types based on RTO/RPO requirements.
explanations.b: Backup type directly affects RTO and RPO: FULL BACKUP: fast restore (low RTO); slow backup creation; HIGH STORAGE COST; INCREMENTAL: slow restore (high RTO); fast backup; low storage cost; the RPO is determined by backup frequency (daily backups = RPO of up to 24 hours); organizations choose backup types based on their RTO/RPO requirements.
explanations.c: 'Only one backup' violates the 3-2-1 rule. If the single backup is corrupted or the backup media fails (which happens regularly), data is irrecoverably lost. Multiple copies are essential.
explanations.d: BACKUP TYPES AND STRATEGY: FULL BACKUP: WHAT: complete copy of all data; TIME: longest (must copy everything); STORAGE: largest (all data); RESTORE: fastest (one tape/file restores everything); FREQUENCY: typically weekly (due to time and storage cost). INCREMENTAL BACKUP: WHAT: copies only data changed since the LAST backup of ANY type (full or incremental); TIME: fastest (only daily changes — 100 GB in our example); STORAGE: smallest (only daily changes); RESTORE: slowest (need full + every incremental since the last full); EXAMPLE RESTORE: need full backup tape + 6 incremental tapes for a weekly cycle. DIFFERENTIAL BACKUP: WHAT: copies data changed since the LAST FULL backup; grows larger each day (Day 2 = 2 days of changes; Day 7 = 7 days of changes); TIME: medium; STORAGE: medium; RESTORE: need only the FULL backup + the LATEST differential (just 2 tapes); EXAMPLE ROTATION (common strategy): Sunday: Full backup (100 GB base); Monday-Saturday: Differential backups (Monday: 100 GB; Saturday: 700 GB). 3-2-1 BACKUP RULE: 3 COPIES: the original + 2 backup copies (never rely on a single backup — backup failures happen); 2 DIFFERENT MEDIA: protects against media-specific failures (if HDDs fail, tape still has backup; if tape fails, HDD still has backup); media types: local disk, tape, cloud storage; 1 OFFSITE COPY: protects against site-level disasters (fire, flood, theft); offsite copies: geographic replication, cloud backup, tape in secure offsite vault; PRACTICAL IMPLEMENTATION: LOCAL: weekly full + daily incremental on local backup disk; CLOUD: copies to cloud storage (Amazon S3, Azure Blob); this satisfies 3-2-1: 3 copies (production + local backup + cloud backup); 2 media (disk + cloud); 1 offsite (cloud).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — cloud cost models; CapEx vs. OpEx; cloud billing; cost optimization
questions.text: A project manager is presenting the business case for migrating from on-premises data centers to cloud. The CFO asks: 'How does cloud billing differ from our current capital expense model and what cost management practices are needed?' How should the PM explain cloud cost economics?

answers.text: Cloud costs are always lower than on-premises — no cost management practices are needed
Cloud costs are fixed monthly — usage level doesn't affect the bill
Cloud billing is identical to on-premises CapEx — the only difference is who owns the hardware

On-premises uses CapEx (Capital Expenditure — upfront hardware purchase, depreciated over years); cloud uses OpEx (Operational Expenditure — pay monthly for resources consumed); cost management practices needed: right-sizing (don't over-provision); auto-scaling (scale down during off-peak hours); reserved instances for predictable workloads (commit 1-3 years for 30-60% discount); unused resource cleanup; cost tagging for budget visibility; monitoring and alerting on cost anomalies

explanations.a: Cloud CAN be more cost-effective — but it requires active cost management. Organizations that migrate to cloud without cost governance often experience 'cloud shock' — higher costs than expected due to over-provisioning, idle resources, and unoptimized architectures.
explanations.b: Cloud billing is entirely usage-based for most services — cost varies with the number of servers running, data stored, API calls made, and data transferred. Mismanaged cloud environments can generate unexpectedly high bills.
explanations.c: Cloud billing is fundamentally different from on-premises CapEx: cloud is consumption-based; on-premises is capacity-based. The economic model, accounting treatment, and planning approach all differ.
explanations.d: CLOUD COST ECONOMICS: ON-PREMISES CapEx MODEL: WHAT IT IS: large upfront capital purchases for servers, storage, networking; ACCOUNTING: capitalized as an asset; depreciated over 3-5 years; PLANNING: based on PEAK CAPACITY (must buy hardware for your biggest expected workload — idle capacity wastes money); CFO PERSPECTIVE: predictable multi-year cost; appears on balance sheet; limited flexibility. CLOUD OpEx MODEL: WHAT IT IS: pay-per-use; monthly billing for resources consumed; ACCOUNTING: operational expense (P&L impact each month, not balance sheet); PLANNING: based on ACTUAL USAGE (scale up for peak; scale down during quiet periods); CFO PERSPECTIVE: variable monthly cost; no capitalized assets; flexible. COST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES: RIGHT-SIZING: analyze actual CPU/RAM utilization; if a VM uses 10% of CPU and 20% of RAM, it's over-provisioned; downsize to a smaller instance type; TYPICAL FINDING: 30-40% of cloud resources are over-provisioned; RIGHT-SIZING savings: 20-30% of cloud spend. AUTO-SCALING: automatically add resources during peak load; automatically reduce resources during off-peak (evenings, weekends for business apps); SAVINGS: pay only for compute when needed. RESERVED INSTANCES / SAVINGS PLANS: commit to 1 or 3 years of usage for a 30-60% discount vs. on-demand; ideal for predictable, steady-state workloads (production databases, core application servers). SPOT INSTANCES: discounted (50-90% cheaper) instances that can be reclaimed by the cloud provider; for interruptible workloads (batch processing, CI/CD pipelines). UNUSED RESOURCE CLEANUP: stopped instances still cost money for attached storage; unused Elastic IPs, orphaned snapshots, idle load balancers all cost money; MONTHLY CLEANUP: use cloud cost management tools (AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, GCP Cloud Billing) to identify and eliminate waste. COST TAGGING: tag all resources with: project name; environment (prod/staging/test); team; business unit; enables cost allocation reporting.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — serverless; Function as a Service; FaaS; Lambda; event-driven architecture
questions.text: A developer proposes using AWS Lambda (serverless) for a new data processing pipeline. The PM asks: 'What does serverless mean and what are its benefits and limitations?' How should the developer explain serverless architecture?

answers.text: Serverless means the application runs without any computers — data is processed by the internet itself
Serverless eliminates all cloud costs — serverless is free to use
Serverless means code runs faster because it avoids server hardware overhead — performance is the main benefit

Serverless (Function as a Service — FaaS) means the developer writes only the application code (functions); the cloud provider manages all server infrastructure; code runs only when triggered by an event (HTTP request, file upload, scheduled timer); billing is per-invocation (not for idle servers); benefits: no server management; automatic scaling; pay only for actual usage; limitations: cold start latency (first invocation slower); maximum execution time (15 minutes for Lambda); stateless (no persistent memory between invocations)

explanations.a: 'Serverless' doesn't mean no servers — servers exist and process the code. 'Serverless' means the developer and operations team don't MANAGE servers — the cloud provider handles all server provisioning, scaling, and maintenance.
explanations.b: Serverless billing is per-invocation — for high-volume workloads, serverless can be MORE expensive than reserved instances. It's cost-effective for variable/intermittent workloads; may be expensive for consistently high-volume continuous processing.
explanations.c: Serverless doesn't necessarily run faster — cold starts can actually be slower than always-on servers for latency-sensitive applications.
explanations.d: SERVERLESS / FUNCTION AS A SERVICE (FaaS): CONCEPT: developer writes discrete FUNCTIONS (small units of code that do one thing); cloud provider handles all infrastructure (server provisioning, scaling, OS patching, load balancing); code ONLY runs when triggered — no servers sitting idle waiting; EVENT TRIGGERS: HTTP request (API Gateway trigger); file upload (S3 upload trigger); database event (DynamoDB stream); scheduled timer (cron-like); message queue event (SQS, SNS); HOW IT WORKS: function is dormant (no cost); event occurs (user uploads a file); cloud provider provisions infrastructure in milliseconds; function code executes; processing completes; infrastructure scales back to zero; EXAMPLES: AWS Lambda; Google Cloud Functions; Azure Functions; BENEFITS: NO SERVER MANAGEMENT: no OS patching; no capacity planning; no infrastructure provisioning; reduces operational burden; AUTOMATIC SCALING: Lambda scales from 0 to thousands of concurrent executions automatically; handles traffic spikes without pre-provisioning; COST MODEL: pay only for actual execution time (milliseconds × memory GB); idle time costs nothing (vs. always-on VMs that cost money even when idle); EXCELLENT FOR: event-driven processing (image processing after upload); API backends with variable traffic; scheduled batch processing; lightweight integrations. LIMITATIONS: COLD START LATENCY: first invocation (or after idle period) takes 100ms-1s longer (infrastructure provisioning); MAXIMUM EXECUTION TIME: Lambda: 15 minutes per invocation; long-running processes can't run serverless; STATELESS: no persistent memory between invocations (must use external storage like DynamoDB for state); DEBUGGING COMPLEXITY: harder to debug distributed functions than a traditional monolith; VENDOR LOCK-IN: Lambda code is not easily portable to other cloud providers. PM IMPLICATION: serverless projects need: FaaS expertise on the team; monitoring strategy (functions are ephemeral — centralized logging required); cost modeling (usage-based billing needs volume projections); understanding of execution time limits.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — DevOps; CI/CD pipeline; continuous integration; continuous deployment
questions.text: A project team practices DevOps and uses a CI/CD pipeline for deployments. The PM needs to understand what a CI/CD pipeline is to incorporate it into project planning. What is CI/CD and how does it change project execution?

answers.text: CI/CD stands for Construction and Installation or Commissioning and Decommissioning — construction project terms
CI/CD pipelines eliminate the need for QA testing — the pipeline handles all quality assurance
CI/CD means developers manually test and deploy code continuously — CI/CD replaces automated testing with human review

CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code every time a developer commits code changes; CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automatically deploys tested code to staging or production environments; CI/CD pipelines shorten the delivery cycle from months to days/hours; project planning implications: automated testing is built into the development process; deployments are frequent (not one big go-live); the pipeline is itself a project deliverable that must be designed, built, and maintained

explanations.a: CI/CD is a software development practice: Continuous Integration (automated build and test) and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (automated deployment). It's not related to construction project terms.
explanations.b: CI/CD ENABLES automated testing — it doesn't eliminate the need for quality assurance. QA engineers write the automated tests that run in the pipeline; the pipeline executes them automatically.
explanations.c: CI/CD AUTOMATES the build, test, and deployment process — the opposite of manual. Human review (code review, UAT) remains, but repetitive tasks are automated.
explanations.d: CI/CD PIPELINE FOR PROJECT MANAGERS: CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION (CI): TRIGGER: every time a developer pushes code to the version control system (Git); WHAT THE PIPELINE DOES AUTOMATICALLY: Compile/build the code; Run unit tests; Run SAST security scanning; Check code quality (linting, code coverage); Build a deployable artifact (Docker image, JAR file); RESULT: developer gets immediate feedback (within minutes) if their code change broke something; BENEFIT: bugs detected immediately after introduction (cheapest time to fix) rather than discovered weeks later in testing; CONTINUOUS DELIVERY (CD — manual approval to production): pipeline automatically deploys to STAGING after passing CI; the production deployment requires a human approval step; CONTINUOUS DEPLOYMENT (CD — fully automated): pipeline automatically deploys to PRODUCTION without human approval (every commit that passes all tests goes to production); TYPICAL PIPELINE STAGES: 1. Code Commit → 2. Build → 3. Unit Tests → 4. SAST Security Scan → 5. Code Quality Check → 6. Deploy to Dev → 7. Integration Tests → 8. Deploy to Staging → 9. UAT/Manual Review → 10. Deploy to Production; PM PLANNING IMPLICATIONS: PIPELINE IS A DELIVERABLE: design, build, and maintain the CI/CD pipeline must be in scope; development cannot fully begin until the pipeline exists; TESTING SHIFTS LEFT: automated tests are built alongside the features (not at the end); QA team focuses on test automation (not manual testing); FREQUENT DEPLOYMENTS: no 'big bang' go-live; features deploy continuously; CHANGE MANAGEMENT: frequent deployments mean frequent RFCs (see Q744 — standard change model for Agile releases); ROLLBACK STRATEGY: with frequent deployments, automated rollback capability is essential; TEAM SKILLS: CI/CD requires DevOps expertise (pipeline configuration, Docker, cloud deployment); may require additional team member or training.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — Infrastructure as Code; IaC; Terraform; CloudFormation; reproducible environments
questions.text: A project team uses Terraform (Infrastructure as Code) to manage cloud infrastructure. The PM asks: 'What is Infrastructure as Code and how does it benefit the project?' How should the team explain IaC?

answers.text: Infrastructure as Code means writing the code that runs on infrastructure — the same as application development
IaC eliminates the need for infrastructure planning — code creates any infrastructure automatically without design
IaC only works for local development environments — production infrastructure must be manually configured

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines and manages infrastructure through code files instead of manual clicking in cloud consoles; benefits: reproducibility (identical environments created from the same code — dev/staging/production are identical); version control (infrastructure changes tracked like application code; rollback to previous state is possible); automation (environments provisioned in minutes not days); consistency (eliminates 'it works on my machine' — all environments configured identically); documentation (code IS the documentation — self-describing infrastructure)

explanations.a: IaC (Infrastructure as Code) is the practice of defining and managing infrastructure (servers, networks, databases, load balancers) through code — not application code that runs ON the infrastructure.
explanations.b: IaC requires thorough infrastructure design before the code is written. The code implements the design — it doesn't replace the design process. An IaC project still needs: architecture design; capacity planning; security design.
explanations.c: IaC is primarily used for PRODUCTION infrastructure — consistent, repeatable, auditable production environments are the primary benefit. Local development environments may also use IaC, but production is the key use case.
explanations.d: INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE (IaC): WHAT IT IS: instead of manually clicking through cloud console to create a server, IaC describes the desired infrastructure in a code file: Terraform example: resource 'aws_instance' 'web_server' { ami = 'ami-0abcd1234' instance_type = 't3.medium' vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id] }; run 'terraform apply' → Terraform creates the server exactly as specified; POPULAR IaC TOOLS: Terraform (cloud-agnostic; works with AWS, Azure, GCP); AWS CloudFormation (AWS-specific); Azure Resource Manager (Azure-specific); Pulumi (IaC using general-purpose programming languages); BENEFITS FOR PROJECTS: REPRODUCIBILITY: the same Terraform code creates identical environments; development, staging, and production are defined by the SAME code; eliminates the 'but it worked in staging!' problem caused by environment differences; VERSION CONTROL: infrastructure code lives in Git (same as application code); every change is tracked; who changed what, when, and why; rollback to previous infrastructure configuration if a change causes problems; AUTOMATION AND SPEED: creating a new environment takes minutes (running the code) instead of days (manual configuration by a human); critical for CI/CD pipelines that need environments on-demand; CONSISTENCY: no manual configuration errors; a junior engineer running the code creates the same infrastructure as a senior engineer; DOCUMENTATION: the code IS the documentation; anyone reading the Terraform files knows exactly what infrastructure exists and how it's configured; PM IMPLICATIONS: IaC SKILLS REQUIRED: the project team needs IaC skills (Terraform, CloudFormation); may require training or hiring; IaC IS A DELIVERABLE: the infrastructure code itself is a project deliverable (not just the infrastructure it creates); IaC IN PROJECT SCOPE: includes: designing the infrastructure code; testing environment provisioning; code review for infrastructure changes; IaC ENABLES FASTER ONBOARDING: new project environments (for new developers) provisioned in minutes.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — monitoring; observability; metrics logs traces; SLA monitoring
questions.text: A project deliverable includes a new microservices application. The operations team says: 'We need monitoring and observability built into the project scope.' The PM asks what the difference is. Explain monitoring vs. observability and what should be included in project scope.

answers.text: Monitoring and observability are the same concept — both track whether systems are up or down
Only traditional monitoring (ping/uptime checks) is needed — microservices are self-monitoring
Monitoring and observability are both purely operational concerns — the project team builds the application and operations figures out monitoring after delivery

Monitoring tracks predefined metrics (CPU, memory, response time, error rates — 'known unknowns'); observability provides deep insight into system behavior through three pillars: metrics (quantitative measurements), logs (detailed event records), and traces (tracking requests across multiple services); a distributed microservices application requires observability because failures occur in complex, unpredictable interactions between services; project scope should include: dashboards for key metrics; centralized logging; distributed tracing; alerting rules; runbook documentation

explanations.a: Monitoring (tracking predefined metrics) and observability (the ability to understand any system state from external outputs) are related but distinct concepts with different capabilities for diagnosing complex failures.
explanations.b: Microservices are NOT self-monitoring — each service is a distinct process that must be explicitly instrumented with metrics, logging, and tracing.
explanations.c: Monitoring and observability must be BUILT INTO the application during development — adding instrumentation after the fact is expensive and incomplete. The project team instruments the code; operations uses the instruments.
explanations.d: MONITORING vs. OBSERVABILITY: MONITORING: WHAT: tracking predefined, known metrics (CPU utilization, memory usage, server uptime, HTTP error rate, response time); KNOWN UNKNOWNS: you know what to watch; you alert when a metric exceeds a threshold; TOOLING: Nagios, Datadog dashboards, CloudWatch alarms; LIMITATION: only answers questions you thought to ask; if a new failure mode occurs that you didn't instrument for, monitoring misses it. OBSERVABILITY: WHAT: the ability to understand the INTERNAL STATE of a system from its external outputs, even for scenarios you didn't anticipate; UNKNOWN UNKNOWNS: enables debugging novel failures; THREE PILLARS OF OBSERVABILITY: METRICS: quantitative time-series measurements (CPU, error rate, request latency, queue depth); LOGS: detailed event records (every application event, error, transaction); structured logs enable querying; TRACES (DISTRIBUTED TRACING): tracks a single request as it travels through multiple microservices; enables answering: 'This user's checkout failed — which of the 8 microservices was responsible and why?'; TOOLING: ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana); Jaeger or Zipkin (distributed tracing); Prometheus + Grafana (metrics); Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace (full observability platforms). WHY MICROSERVICES REQUIRE OBSERVABILITY: a monolith has one log file and one service — easy to find errors; a microservices app has 20 services, each generating logs — user request passes through Order Service → Inventory Service → Payment Service → Notification Service; if the request fails, which service failed?; only distributed tracing can answer this; PROJECT SCOPE INCLUSIONS: APPLICATION INSTRUMENTATION: add metrics, logs, and trace instrumentation to each microservice during development; DASHBOARDS: build dashboards showing key service health metrics (created in Grafana, Datadog); ALERTING: define alert rules (alert when error rate >1%; response time >500ms); CENTRALIZED LOG MANAGEMENT: aggregate logs from all services into a searchable system (Elasticsearch, Splunk); DISTRIBUTED TRACING: implement trace IDs that follow requests across all services; RUNBOOK: document how to use monitoring/observability tools to diagnose common issues.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — edge computing; IoT; distributed processing; latency reduction
questions.text: A project is implementing a manufacturing IoT system that collects sensor data from 500 machines and processes it in real time to detect defects. An architect proposes 'edge computing' instead of sending all data to a central cloud. The PM asks why. What is edge computing and when does it provide value?

answers.text: Edge computing means the cloud is on the edge of the building — it's the same as cloud computing

Edge computing processes data at or near the source (on the factory floor — 'the edge') rather than sending everything to a central cloud; for manufacturing IoT: sending 500 machine sensor streams to the cloud requires significant bandwidth; cloud round-trip latency (10-100ms) may be too slow for real-time defect detection (machines may require sub-millisecond response); processing locally enables immediate response (stop the machine); sending only anomalies or summaries to the cloud reduces bandwidth; edge computing adds hardware deployment complexity but provides latency and bandwidth benefits
Edge computing eliminates the need for cloud services — all data stays on the factory floor permanently
Edge computing is only for consumer devices (phones, laptops) — industrial applications always use centralized cloud

explanations.a: Edge computing is the opposite of centralized cloud — it distributes processing OUT to the location where data is generated, reducing the distance data must travel.
