explanations.b: EDGE COMPUTING for manufacturing IoT: WHAT IS EDGE COMPUTING: processing data close to where it's generated (at the 'edge' of the network) rather than sending it to a centralized cloud; EDGE DEVICES: local servers or gateways on the factory floor; mini data centers at the network edge; smart devices with local processing capability; WHY EDGE FOR MANUFACTURING IoT: LATENCY: cloud round-trip: machine sensor → factory router → ISP → internet → AWS region → processing → response → machine; total latency: 10-100ms+; edge round-trip: machine sensor → local edge server → processing → machine; latency: <1ms; for stopping a machine at 0.1mm defect resolution: 100ms is too slow; edge processing at <1ms enables immediate defect response; BANDWIDTH: 500 machines × sensor data streams = potentially gigabytes per minute of raw data; sending all raw data to cloud is expensive (cloud egress bandwidth costs + internet connection costs); with edge processing: process raw data locally; send only anomaly alerts and aggregate summaries to cloud; reduces cloud bandwidth by 90%+; RELIABILITY: factory internet connectivity may be unreliable; edge processing continues even when cloud connectivity is lost (no single point of failure for the critical machine control loop); LOCAL REGULATION: some industries require that manufacturing data stays within the facility; CLOUD ROLE WITH EDGE: long-term analytics and trend analysis; model training (ML models trained centrally; deployed to edge); configuration and monitoring of edge devices; PM IMPLICATIONS: EDGE HARDWARE: edge servers must be sourced, deployed, and maintained — physical infrastructure scope; CONNECTIVITY: edge to cloud connectivity design; EDGE SOFTWARE: IoT platform (Azure IoT Hub, AWS IoT Greengrass) for edge device management; OT/IT SECURITY: edge devices in operational technology (OT) environments have specific security requirements.
explanations.c: Edge computing and cloud are complementary — edge handles real-time local processing; cloud handles centralized analytics, model training, and long-term storage. Pure edge-only architectures lack the analytical power and capacity of cloud.
explanations.d: Edge computing is especially valuable for industrial IoT (manufacturing, utilities, oil & gas) — the low latency and local processing requirements of industrial control systems are exactly what edge computing addresses.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — IT technical requirements in projects; translating IT concepts to project requirements
questions.text: A project manager with limited IT background is tasked with gathering requirements for a cloud-native financial application. The infrastructure team uses terms like 'autoscaling groups,' 'CDN,' and 'WAF.' How should a PM develop sufficient IT literacy to gather these requirements accurately?

answers.text: The PM should pretend to understand technical terms and ask technical teams to document everything — the PM doesn't need IT literacy

The PM should develop sufficient IT literacy to: understand what each component does (not how to build it); ask clarifying questions ('what user problem does the CDN solve?'); translate technical requirements into project scope items; verify completeness with technical reviewers; the goal is business-outcome-focused technical literacy — not deep engineering expertise; engage a technical lead or architect to validate requirements completeness
PMs should only manage IT projects if they are certified engineers — non-technical PMs cannot succeed
Have the technical team write all requirements independently — PM reviews for spelling errors only

explanations.a: Pretending to understand requirements that are not understood produces: incorrect scope (missing critical infrastructure components); incorrect cost estimates (autoscaling groups, CDNs, WAFs have significant cost implications); incorrect timeline (infrastructure provisioning has lead time that won't be in the schedule).
explanations.b: PM IT LITERACY DEVELOPMENT APPROACH: WHAT THE PM NEEDS TO KNOW (not engineer-level, but concept-level): AUTOSCALING GROUP: automatically adds or removes servers based on traffic; PROJECT IMPLICATION: autoscaling group must be designed (min/max instances); tested (does it actually scale correctly?); cost modeled (how much do extra instances cost during peak?); CDN (CONTENT DELIVERY NETWORK): caches static content (images, CSS, JS) in locations worldwide; reduces latency for geographically distributed users; PROJECT IMPLICATION: CDN service must be selected, configured, integrated (testing in all regions); cost budgeted; WAF (WEB APPLICATION FIREWALL): filters malicious web traffic (SQL injection, XSS); PROJECT IMPLICATION: WAF must be configured with rules; tested (does it block attacks without breaking legitimate traffic?); maintained (rule updates); HOW TO DEVELOP THIS LITERACY: TECHNICAL GLOSSARY: create a project glossary of technical terms with plain-English explanations; ask the team: 'Can you explain this in terms of what problem it solves for the user?'; TECHNICAL REVIEWERS: engage a technical lead to review requirements for completeness; 'have we captured all infrastructure components?'; STRUCTURED ELICITATION: use architecture diagrams to visualize components and ask 'what does this box do? what happens if it fails? who manages it? what does it cost?'; ITERATION: requirements refinement through multiple rounds with technical and business stakeholders; PM VALUE: the PM ensures all requirements are captured, scoped, budgeted, and scheduled — technical expertise comes from the team; the PM provides structure, process, and communication.
explanations.c: Project managers don't need engineering certification — they need sufficient technical literacy to scope, plan, and communicate. Many highly successful IT project managers have non-engineering backgrounds and succeed through technical literacy development and strong team collaboration.
explanations.d: Having the technical team write all requirements without PM facilitation typically produces: technically complete but business-context-missing requirements; requirements that lack acceptance criteria; requirements not organized into prioritized, manageable scope items; no validation that requirements match business objectives.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — API management; iPaaS; integration platform; middleware
questions.text: A project integrates 5 systems (CRM, ERP, HR, Marketing, and Analytics). The architecture team recommends an 'integration platform (iPaaS)' instead of direct point-to-point connections. Why and what project implications does this choice create?

answers.text: Direct point-to-point connections are always better — more direct means more reliable

Point-to-point with 5 systems creates N*(N-1)/2 = 10 direct connections, each requiring custom development; iPaaS (Integration Platform as a Service) provides a centralized integration hub where all systems connect once; changes to one system only require updating the iPaaS mapping (not rebuilding multiple point-to-point connections); project implications: iPaaS is itself a project component requiring design, configuration, testing, and maintenance; reduces long-term integration complexity
Integration platforms are unnecessary — modern cloud systems connect automatically without any configuration
Only 2 systems can ever be integrated — more than 2 systems require separate projects

explanations.a: Point-to-point integration with 5 systems creates 10 custom connections; with 10 systems it's 45 connections. Each connection must be independently developed, tested, maintained, and updated when either connected system changes. This 'spaghetti integration' becomes unmanageable at scale.
explanations.b: iPaaS vs. POINT-TO-POINT INTEGRATION: POINT-TO-POINT PROBLEMS with 5 systems: NUMBER OF CONNECTIONS: N*(N-1)/2 = 5*4/2 = 10 direct connections; each connection is custom code; each system change may break multiple connections; MAINTENANCE BURDEN: if the CRM updates its API: find all connections that use the CRM API; update each one; test all affected connections; COMPLEXITY: debugging failures requires investigating which of the 10 connections is the cause; iPaaS (INTEGRATION PLATFORM as a SERVICE): WHAT IT IS: a centralized integration hub; each system connects ONCE to the platform; the platform handles: DATA TRANSFORMATION (converting CRM's data format to ERP's data format); ROUTING (sending the right data to the right system); ERROR HANDLING (retries, dead letter queues for failed messages); MONITORING (centralized view of all integration activity); EXAMPLES: MuleSoft; Dell Boomi; Azure Integration Services; AWS AppFlow; Zapier (simpler use cases); HOW IT REDUCES COMPLEXITY: instead of 10 custom connections → 5 connections (each system to the hub); when the CRM updates its API: update ONLY the CRM connector in the iPaaS platform; all other integrations automatically benefit from the updated connector; PROJECT IMPLICATIONS: iPaaS IS A COMPONENT: iPaaS selection, procurement, configuration, and testing are project scope items; iPaaS SKILLS: requires integration specialists (may need contractor or training); DESIGN EFFORT: integration mapping must be designed (what data flows from which system to which other systems?); TESTING: each integration flow must be tested end-to-end; GOVERNANCE: iPaaS becomes critical infrastructure that requires ongoing monitoring and maintenance; COST: iPaaS has subscription costs that must be included in the business case.
explanations.c: Modern cloud systems do NOT connect automatically — integration requires explicit design, API configuration, authentication, data mapping, and testing for each connection.
explanations.d: Large enterprise integration programs connect dozens of systems — SAP implementations routinely involve 20-50 integrated systems. The iPaaS approach makes this manageable.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — technical debt; its impact on projects; managing legacy systems
questions.text: A project team working on a legacy system says: 'This system has significant technical debt — it's going to take twice as long as a greenfield project.' The sponsor asks the PM to explain technical debt and its project implications. How should the PM explain it?

answers.text: Technical debt is a financial accounting term for unpaid software licenses — it has no impact on project timelines

Technical debt refers to accumulated shortcuts, outdated code, poor design decisions, and missing documentation that make a system harder to change; project implications: each change requires more time (understanding undocumented code before modifying it); higher risk of unintended side effects when changes are made; technical debt remediation may be necessary before new features can be built; in the business case, acknowledge the technical debt premium (2-3× longer timelines, higher risk); consider whether the project should also address the debt
Technical debt is always good — shortcuts produce faster delivery with no long-term cost
Technical debt is only a concern for software projects — infrastructure and process projects are not affected

explanations.a: Technical debt is a software engineering concept with direct, measurable impact on project timelines and costs. The analogy is financial debt — it accumulates interest over time (the cost of changes increases as the debt grows).
explanations.b: TECHNICAL DEBT — CONCEPT AND PROJECT IMPLICATIONS: WHAT IS TECHNICAL DEBT: the metaphor was coined by Ward Cunningham; like financial debt: takes a shortcut now (quick implementation, skip documentation, don't refactor) that must be paid back later with 'interest' (the increasing cost of working in the messy codebase); TYPES OF TECHNICAL DEBT: CODE DEBT: spaghetti code (complex, tangled; no clear structure); no unit tests (changes can't be validated easily); DOCUMENTATION DEBT: no architecture documentation; missing API documentation; no code comments; DEPENDENCY DEBT: outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities; unsupported frameworks; INFRASTRUCTURE DEBT: legacy hardware out of support; operating systems no longer patched. HOW IT AFFECTS PROJECT TIMELINES: UNDERSTANDING COST: a developer must spend 2-3 hours understanding undocumented code before making a 1-hour change (equivalent code in a clean system takes 1 hour total → 3-4 hours for technical debt system); SIDE EFFECTS: changes in one part of a tightly coupled system unexpectedly break something else; discovery and fixing side effects adds time; TESTING: lack of unit tests means manual testing is needed for every change (slower); COMPOUND EFFECT: each change made in a high-debt system without addressing the debt adds more debt (increasing future change costs). PM IMPLICATIONS: TIMELINE PREMIUM: plan for 2-3× longer timelines vs. greenfield development for heavily debt-laden systems; RISK PREMIUM: higher risk of bugs and unexpected failures — include appropriate contingency; DEBT REMEDIATION SCOPE: should the project address some technical debt as part of its scope? (adds cost and time but reduces future project costs); BUSINESS CASE TRANSPARENCY: present technical debt as a constraint and cost driver to the sponsor — set realistic expectations; DEBT VS. FEATURES: sometimes addressing technical debt is more important than new features — this is a portfolio decision for the sponsor.
explanations.c: Technical shortcuts produce faster short-term delivery but accumulate debt that makes ALL future changes slower and riskier. The 'interest' on technical debt is real and measurable.
explanations.d: Technical debt exists in infrastructure (outdated hardware, unsupported OSes), processes (undocumented procedures), and data (inconsistent data structures) — not only in software code.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — assistive technologies; screen readers; WCAG; accessibility in IT systems
questions.text: A project manager is building a government citizen services portal. The accessibility team says: 'We need to ensure WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance and test with screen readers.' The PM asks why screen reader compatibility matters and what it means for the project. How should the accessibility team explain it?

answers.text: Screen readers are only used by a tiny minority — accessibility compliance is optional for most projects

Screen readers are assistive technology used by people with visual impairments to interact with digital content through audio narration; WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance ensures the portal works with screen readers and other assistive technologies; it requires: all images have alt text; all form fields have labels; keyboard navigation works for all functions; color is not the only way to convey information; sufficient contrast ratios; for a government portal this is both a legal requirement (ADA, Section 508) and an equity obligation; project scope must include: accessibility requirements in the requirements doc; accessibility testing with actual screen readers; developer accessibility training
Screen readers are a separate accessibility product that the government provides to users — the portal itself doesn't need to support them
WCAG compliance is achieved by adding an accessibility widget at the bottom of the page — no other development changes are needed

explanations.a: Approximately 253 million people globally have some form of visual impairment (WHO). Beyond visual impairment, screen readers are used by people with learning disabilities, and keyboard navigation is essential for motor-impaired users. Accessibility affects approximately 15% of the global population.
explanations.b: SCREEN READERS AND ACCESSIBILITY: WHAT IS A SCREEN READER: software that reads the screen content aloud (text-to-speech); used by people who are blind or have severe visual impairment; POPULAR SCREEN READERS: NVDA (free, Windows); JAWS (commercial, Windows); VoiceOver (built into iOS and macOS); TalkBack (Android); HOW SCREEN READERS WORK: the screen reader reads the HTML structure of the page; it uses: aria-labels on interactive elements; alt text on images; heading hierarchy (H1 → H2 → H3) for navigation; form labels (connected to form fields via 'for' and 'id' attributes); IF THE PORTAL ISN'T CODED ACCESSIBLY: a screen reader user clicks 'Submit' and hears 'Button'; not 'Submit Application Form Button' (what it actually does); an image of a document is heard as nothing (missing alt text); a form field is heard as 'Edit' not 'Enter your National Insurance Number' (missing label); the user cannot use the portal effectively; WCAG 2.1 LEVEL AA REQUIREMENTS: perceivable: all images have alt text; color contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 for text; videos have captions; operable: all functionality works with keyboard alone (no mouse required); no content that causes seizures; understandable: form errors clearly described; predictable navigation; robust: compatible with current and future assistive technologies; LEGAL REQUIREMENTS for UK government portal: UK Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments; Government Accessibility Regulations (WCAG 2.1 AA mandatory for UK government websites); US equivalent: Section 508 (federal); ADA Title II (state and local government); PROJECT IMPLICATIONS: REQUIREMENTS: include WCAG 2.1 AA as a mandatory non-functional requirement; DEVELOPER TRAINING: accessible HTML techniques (semantic HTML, ARIA attributes); TESTING: automated testing (axe, WAVE) + manual testing with screen readers; INCLUSIVE USER RESEARCH: include participants with disabilities in user testing; LEGAL RISK OF NON-COMPLIANCE: government portals have been subject to disability discrimination claims.
explanations.c: Accessibility is built into how the portal is coded (HTML structure, ARIA attributes, contrast ratios) — it cannot be added externally as a separate product. The portal's own code must be accessible.
explanations.d: Accessibility widgets (overlay solutions) are criticized by accessibility experts as insufficient substitutes for properly coded accessible content. The underlying HTML must be accessible; widgets cannot fully compensate for inaccessible code. Real WCAG compliance requires accessible code, not overlays.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — IT infrastructure in project estimates; hardware lead times; environment provisioning
questions.text: A project manager is scheduling an 8-month software development project. The infrastructure team says: 'We need 6 weeks to provision production infrastructure — you've scheduled 2 weeks.' The PM didn't account for infrastructure lead times. What IT infrastructure concepts affect project scheduling and how should they be incorporated?

answers.text: Infrastructure provisioning takes the same amount of time regardless of the approach — all options take the same time

IT infrastructure timing concepts that affect project schedules: Hardware procurement lead time (physical servers: 4-12 weeks); Cloud environment provisioning (minutes to hours if IaC is used); Network change implementation (firewall rules, DNS, VPN: 1-5 days per change through change management); Security review and approval (1-4 weeks); Certificate procurement (1-5 days); DR environment provisioning; all environments (dev/test/staging/prod) need provisioning in sequence; the PM should map each environment to the schedule as explicit activities with dependencies
Infrastructure provisioning is always instantaneous in the cloud — no lead time planning is needed
Infrastructure is IT operations' responsibility — the project PM doesn't need to plan infrastructure timelines

explanations.a: Infrastructure provisioning times vary enormously: physical hardware takes weeks; cloud with manual configuration takes days; cloud with IaC takes hours or minutes. The approach significantly affects schedule.
explanations.b: INFRASTRUCTURE LEAD TIMES AFFECTING PROJECT SCHEDULES: HARDWARE PROCUREMENT: physical servers, storage, networking equipment; PROCUREMENT PROCESS: specification → vendor quote → purchase order → delivery → rack and cable → OS installation → handover; TYPICAL LEAD TIME: 4-12 weeks (depending on supply chain; during COVID-19, some hardware had 26+ week lead times); PM ACTION: hardware procurement must be initiated in the planning phase, not execution phase; CLOUD ENVIRONMENT PROVISIONING: MANUAL (clicking in cloud console): 1-5 days (for complex environments with all security configurations); WITH IaC (Terraform/CloudFormation): minutes to hours (once the IaC code is written); PM ACTION: investing in IaC pays off in faster environment provisioning throughout the project; CHANGE MANAGEMENT FOR NETWORK CHANGES: firewall rule changes: 2-5 business days (RFC submission to CAB to implementation); DNS configuration: 1-2 days (plus 0-48 hours propagation time); VPN configuration: 2-5 business days; PM ACTION: identify all network changes early; submit RFCs before they're on the critical path; SECURITY REVIEW AND APPROVALS: design review by security architect: 1-2 weeks; penetration test: 1-4 weeks (scheduling + execution + report); security scan results remediation: variable; PM ACTION: include security review milestones in the schedule; don't plan security review the week before go-live; TLS CERTIFICATE PROCUREMENT: standard DV certificate: minutes (automated via Let's Encrypt); OV (Organization Validated): 1-3 business days (requires organizational verification); EV (Extended Validation): 5-10 business days (strict vetting process); PM ACTION: procure certificates early; ENVIRONMENT SEQUENCE: development → test → staging → production; each environment must be provisioned before it can be used; stagger provisioning to enable earlier development start; SCHEDULE TEMPLATE: Month 1: provision development environment, initiate hardware procurement; Month 2: provision test environment, hardware delivery expected; Month 3: provision staging; Month 6: provision production (4-6 weeks before go-live); Month 8: go-live.
explanations.c: Cloud environment provisioning is faster than hardware — but not instantaneous, especially for complex environments with security configurations, network setup, and IAM configuration. Manual cloud provisioning still takes days; IaC takes hours; neither is truly instantaneous.
explanations.d: While IT operations may EXECUTE infrastructure provisioning, the PROJECT MANAGER is responsible for including it in the project schedule, identifying dependencies, and managing lead times. Ignoring infrastructure timing creates the exact problem described — 2-week planned vs. 6-week actual.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: Basic IT Concepts — comprehensive IT scenario; cloud architecture; all IT concepts applied
questions.text: A project manager is planning a new cloud-native e-commerce platform. The architecture is: 3 microservices (containerized), PostgreSQL database with HA, Redis caching, CDN, WAF, auto-scaling, and a CI/CD pipeline. The requirements specify: 99.95% uptime, RTO=1 hour, RPO=5 minutes, WCAG 2.1 AA. What project scope items and schedule considerations does this architecture require?

answers.text: Just hire developers and let them build it — architecture details don't affect project scope

The architecture requires these explicit scope items: container orchestration platform (Kubernetes setup); CI/CD pipeline design and implementation; database HA configuration and testing; Redis cache setup; CDN configuration and testing; WAF rule configuration and penetration testing; auto-scaling rules design and load testing; DR/backup configuration meeting 5-min RPO; accessibility development and testing against WCAG AA; monitoring/observability stack; security testing (SAST, DAST, pen test). Schedule considerations: cloud environment provisioning; Kubernetes requires expertise (may need contractor); load testing before go-live; DNS cutover planning
Only the database and microservices need project scope — all other components are automatic in cloud
This architecture is too complex — simplify to a single server to reduce scope

explanations.a: Architecture choices directly determine project scope. Each component must be designed, configured, tested, and documented. Without explicit scope items for each component, they will be discovered missing at go-live.
explanations.b: ARCHITECTURE TO PROJECT SCOPE MAPPING: CONTAINER ORCHESTRATION (KUBERNETES): SCOPE: K8s cluster setup; container networking configuration; pod autoscaling rules; service mesh configuration; SKILLS: Kubernetes expertise required (specialist or contractor); TIME: 2-3 weeks for initial setup; ongoing configuration throughout development. CI/CD PIPELINE: SCOPE: pipeline design; build stages; test automation integration; deployment to each environment; rollback automation; PREREQUISITE: must be built BEFORE development begins; TIME: 2-3 weeks. DATABASE HA (POSTGRESQL): SCOPE: primary-replica HA cluster configuration; replication lag monitoring; automated failover testing; backup configuration meeting 5-min RPO; point-in-time recovery testing; TESTING: actually fail the primary and verify failover within 1-hour RTO; TIME: 1-2 weeks configuration + 1 week testing. REDIS CACHE: SCOPE: cache deployment and clustering; cache invalidation strategy; monitoring for cache hit rate; TIME: 3-5 days. CDN CONFIGURATION: SCOPE: CDN service selection; cache rules per content type; invalidation strategy; geographic performance testing; TIME: 1 week. WAF: SCOPE: WAF rule configuration (OWASP Core Rule Set); tuning (prevent false positives blocking legitimate traffic); security testing validation (does WAF block SQL injection without breaking legitimate requests?); PENETRATION TESTING: validates WAF effectiveness; TIME: 1-2 weeks configuration + 1 week pen test. AUTO-SCALING: SCOPE: min/max instance definitions; scaling triggers (CPU threshold, request rate); LOAD TESTING: validate that scaling works correctly under load; critical for 99.95% uptime (scaling failures under peak load cause outages); TIME: 1 week configuration + 1 week load testing. DR/BACKUP (5-MIN RPO, 1-HOUR RTO): SCOPE: backup configuration (frequency must exceed RPO requirements); DR site or cross-region replication; DR failover test (actually test RTO — does it recover within 1 hour?); TIME: 2-3 weeks including DR test. ACCESSIBILITY (WCAG 2.1 AA): SCOPE: developer training on accessible coding; accessibility testing in each sprint; manual testing with screen readers before go-live; TIME: ongoing throughout development + 1 week dedicated testing before go-live. MONITORING/OBSERVABILITY: SCOPE: metrics dashboards; centralized logging; distributed tracing; alert rules; runbook; TIME: 2-3 weeks. SECURITY TESTING: SAST (CI/CD integrated — ongoing); DAST (before UAT); Penetration Test (before go-live); TIME: 1-2 weeks for scheduled tests. SCHEDULE NOTES: cloud environment provisioning before development; K8s expertise may require contractor (6-8 week lead for contractor procurement); DR test must complete before go-live; load test must complete before go-live; accessibility testing before UAT.
explanations.c: CDN, WAF, auto-scaling, Kubernetes, CI/CD, monitoring, and accessibility all require explicit design, configuration, and testing — none of these are 'automatic in cloud.' Assuming they are automatic is a primary source of IT project scope gaps.
explanations.d: The architecture is complex but appropriate for a high-availability e-commerce platform. Simplifying to a single server would: fail the 99.95% uptime requirement (single point of failure); fail the RTO/RPO requirements; not scale for e-commerce traffic peaks. The complexity is justified by the requirements.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — ITSM; ITIL framework; service lifecycle; project to operations
questions.text: A project manager is preparing to hand over a new system to IT operations. The operations team follows ITIL practices. What is ITIL and why does the project manager need to understand it for project delivery?

answers.text: ITIL only applies to software-as-a-service products — custom applications use different frameworks
ITIL is only relevant to IT infrastructure teams — project managers don't interact with ITIL

ITIL stands for Information Technology Infrastructure Library — a set of best practices for IT service management that defines how IT services are delivered and supported; project managers need to understand ITIL because their project deliverables will be operated under ITIL practices, which means: the project must provide operations with the runbook, SLA targets, CMDB entries, and training needed for ITIL-based service management to function effectively
ITIL is a project management methodology — it replaces PMBOK for IT projects

explanations.a: ITIL applies to all types of IT services: custom applications, commercial off-the-shelf software, SaaS integrations, and infrastructure services.
explanations.b: Project managers who deliver IT systems directly affect how ITIL-run operations teams support those systems. The handover package must include what ITIL practices require.
explanations.c: ITIL (INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY INFRASTRUCTURE LIBRARY): WHAT IT IS: a globally recognized framework of best practices for IT service management (ITSM); provides guidance on how to design, deliver, operate, and improve IT services; ITIL 4 (current version) organizes service management around a Service Value System (SVS) and four dimensions (Organizations & People, Information & Technology, Partners & Suppliers, Value Streams & Processes). KEY ITIL PRACTICES RELEVANT TO PMs: SERVICE DESIGN: ensuring the service can be operated before go-live; the project must provide what operations needs; SERVICE TRANSITION (change management): deploying the project deliverable safely (IT change management — covered in obj 4.4); SERVICE OPERATION: running the service day-to-day (incident management, problem management, service requests); CONTINUAL IMPROVEMENT: improving the service over time. WHY PMs NEED TO UNDERSTAND ITIL: OPERATIONS READINESS: operations teams following ITIL need specific handover deliverables; CMDB ENTRIES: configuration items must be registered in the CMDB before go-live; SLA DEFINITION: the project must define target SLAs that operations will then be held to; SERVICE CATALOG ENTRY: a new service must be added to the service catalog; RUNBOOK: operations need procedures for managing the service; WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING ITIL: PMs deliver the technical solution but forget the operational context — resulting in services that the operations team cannot support effectively.
explanations.d: ITIL is an IT service management framework — not a project management methodology. PMBOK and PRINCE2 are project management methodologies. ITIL and project management are complementary (projects deliver services; ITIL operates them).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — incident management; problem management; ITSM terminology
questions.text: The operations team reports two situations: (1) 'The production system is down — users cannot log in.' (2) 'We've had 5 login failures this month from the same root cause — we need to fix it permanently.' Which ITIL practice addresses each situation?

answers.text: Both situations are incidents — all IT problems are managed as incidents
Neither situation requires ITIL practices — both should be managed as project changes

Situation 1 is an INCIDENT (unplanned interruption to a service — requires fast restoration of service); Situation 2 is a PROBLEM (the underlying root cause of one or more incidents — requires root cause analysis and permanent fix to prevent recurrence); ITIL separates these because restoring service quickly (incident) and preventing recurrence (problem) require different skills and timelines
Situation 1 is a problem; Situation 2 is an incident — the terms are reversed

explanations.b: Incidents and problems are different ITIL practices with different goals, timelines, and responsibilities.
explanations.a: ITIL service operation practices (incident and problem management) are specifically for managing IT services in production — not managed as project changes.
explanations.c: INCIDENT vs. PROBLEM MANAGEMENT: INCIDENT MANAGEMENT: WHAT IS AN INCIDENT: any unplanned interruption to an IT service, or reduction in quality of an IT service; GOAL: restore normal service operation as quickly as possible; TIME PRESSURE: minimize user impact — measured in minutes/hours; APPROACH: workaround first (restore service even if not the perfect fix); root cause analysis comes later; EXAMPLE: 'Users cannot log in' = P1 incident; immediate escalation; war room; goal is restoring login within the P1 SLA (e.g., 1 hour); METRICS: Mean Time to Restore (MTTR); SLA compliance rate. PROBLEM MANAGEMENT: WHAT IS A PROBLEM: the underlying cause of one or more incidents; GOAL: prevent future incidents by identifying and permanently removing root causes; TIME PRESSURE: lower urgency than incidents — quality over speed; APPROACH: structured root cause analysis (5 Whys, Ishikawa/fishbone); permanent fix deployment; sometimes a Known Error record is created (root cause identified, fix not yet deployed); EXAMPLE: '5 login failures from the same root cause' = problem; root cause analysis reveals the authentication service has a memory leak under high load; permanent fix: memory management improvement in the next release; METRICS: number of repeat incidents; problem closure rate; time to permanent fix. KEY DISTINCTION FOR PMs: incident management = reactive (service is broken, fix it now); problem management = proactive/reactive (understand why it keeps breaking, prevent recurrence); a project might be required to implement the permanent fix identified by problem management.
explanations.d: The ITIL definition is clear: incident = current service disruption (restore service now); problem = root cause requiring permanent fix (prevent future incidents).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — service desk; support tiers; escalation path; project handover
questions.text: A project manager is preparing the transition plan for a new HR portal. The service desk will support end users after go-live. What service desk tiers exist and what does each tier need from the project for successful support?

answers.text: Service desk tiers: Tier 0 (self-service — user resolves their own issue using knowledge base, FAQs, or portal); Tier 1 (first-line support — service desk agent handles common issues using scripts and FAQs; handles password resets, access requests, 'how do I' questions); Tier 2 (technical support — specialists handle complex issues that Tier 1 cannot resolve); Tier 3 (expert/vendor support — developers, architects, or vendor engineers handle the most complex issues); each tier needs from the project: Tier 0 requires user-facing FAQs and knowledge articles; Tier 1 needs call scripts and decision trees; Tier 2 needs system documentation and troubleshooting guides; Tier 3 (project team) needs handover documentation and contact information
Service desk tiers only apply to very large organizations — smaller organizations manage all IT issues directly
Only Tier 3 support matters — developers should handle all user issues directly
Service desks have only one tier — all issues are resolved by the same support team

explanations.c: SERVICE DESK SUPPORT TIERS: TIER 0 — SELF-SERVICE: user resolves their own issue; PROJECT DELIVERABLE: knowledge base articles, FAQs, user guides, video tutorials, searchable help content; EXAMPLES: 'How do I submit a time-off request?'; 'Why can't I see my pay stub?'; RESOLUTION WITHOUT HUMAN INTERACTION reduces help desk volume significantly. TIER 1 — FIRST-LINE SUPPORT (SERVICE DESK AGENTS): handles high-volume common issues using scripts and knowledge base; PROJECT DELIVERABLE: call scripts ('If user says X, ask Y, do Z'); troubleshooting decision trees; common error message reference; training session for service desk agents before go-live; EXAMPLES: password resets; access provisioning; common navigation issues; basic how-to questions; TARGET: Tier 1 resolves 70-80% of all issues without escalation. TIER 2 — TECHNICAL SUPPORT (SPECIALISTS): handles complex issues requiring deeper system knowledge; PROJECT DELIVERABLE: system architecture documentation; database query guides; integration troubleshooting; escalation procedures from Tier 1; EXAMPLES: data sync failures between HR portal and payroll; report generation errors; complex access/permissions issues. TIER 3 — EXPERT/VENDOR SUPPORT: highest complexity issues requiring developer or vendor expertise; PROJECT TEAM ROLE: the project team is typically the initial Tier 3 during the warranty period; PROJECT DELIVERABLE: technical handover documentation; vendor support contacts; architecture decision records; source code access if needed. TRANSITION SUCCESS FACTOR: all tiers must be trained and equipped BEFORE go-live — a go-live without Tier 1 training means every user call becomes a Tier 3 escalation.
explanations.b: Service desk tiers are beneficial at any scale — even small organizations benefit from self-service and structured support processes.
explanations.a: Routing all user issues directly to developers is expensive (developer time cost), slow (developers are not trained for customer support), and unsustainable (developers should be building features, not answering 'how do I' questions).
explanations.d: Multiple tiers exist to efficiently route issues to the appropriate skill level — handling all issues at the same level is inefficient (experts spending time on password resets) or ineffective (Tier 1 agents trying to resolve complex system issues).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — SLA; service level agreement; SLA definition in projects; uptime targets
questions.text: A project manager is defining SLAs for a new financial reporting system before handover to operations. The operations team says: 'We need SLA targets before we can plan staffing.' What SLAs should be defined and how does the project influence them?

answers.text: SLA targets are always: 100% availability, 1-minute incident response — these are the industry standard for all systems
SLAs are defined by operations teams after go-live based on user complaints
SLAs are only relevant for vendor contracts — internal systems don't need SLA targets

SLA targets must be defined during the project and agreed before go-live: Availability SLA (system uptime target — e.g., 99.5% = max 43.8 hours/year downtime); Incident response SLAs (P1: respond within 15 min, resolve within 2 hours; P2: respond 30 min, resolve 4 hours; P3: respond 4 hours, resolve 2 business days); Service request SLAs (new user provisioned within 1 business day); Performance SLAs (page loads in under 3 seconds for 95% of requests); the project architecture must be designed to support the availability SLA — operations cannot meet a 99.9% SLA with a system that has no redundancy

explanations.d: 100% availability is technically impossible (planned maintenance, hardware failures) and unrealistic. Different systems have different business criticality — a batch reporting system doesn't need the same SLA as a real-time payment processor.
explanations.a: SLAs defined after go-live based on complaints are reactive and create unfair expectations — operations cannot staff appropriately without knowing SLA targets, and the architecture may already be insufficient.
explanations.b: Internal systems benefit from SLAs just as much as vendor contracts: they set expectations for users; they enable operations to plan staffing; they provide an objective measure of service quality; they create accountability for system performance.
explanations.c: SLA DEFINITION IN PROJECTS: WHY DEFINE SLAs DURING THE PROJECT: ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS: if the availability SLA is 99.9% (<8.76 hours/year downtime), the system must be designed with: no single points of failure (HA clustering, load balancing, redundant storage); automated failover; automated monitoring and alerting; a system designed without HA cannot meet a 99.9% SLA — redesigning post-go-live is expensive; OPERATIONS STAFFING: 24/7 monitoring requires different staffing than 8x5 monitoring; P1 SLA of 1-hour resolution requires on-call coverage; SLA TYPES TO DEFINE: AVAILABILITY: measured as % of scheduled uptime (99.0%, 99.5%, 99.9%, 99.95%); INCIDENT RESPONSE SLAs: PRIORITY: RESPONSE TIME / RESOLUTION TARGET; P1 (Critical — complete outage): 15 min / 2 hours; P2 (High — significant degradation): 30 min / 4 hours; P3 (Medium — minor issue): 2 hours / 1 business day; P4 (Low — informational): 4 hours / 5 business days; PERFORMANCE SLAs: specific performance targets (response time; throughput; batch processing completion time); SERVICE REQUEST SLAs: time to fulfill common requests (new user: 1 business day; password reset: 15 minutes); SLA NEGOTIATION: business requirements drive the SLA target; operations team validates it's achievable with the proposed architecture and staffing; IT leadership balances the cost of meeting the SLA vs. the business impact of not meeting it; PROJECT DELIVERABLE: completed SLA document signed by: IT operations (commits to delivering the SLA); business stakeholder (accepts the defined SLA); project manager (confirms the system architecture supports the SLA).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — CMDB; configuration management database; CI; project handover
questions.text: During project closing, the operations team requests that all project deliverables be registered in the CMDB. The project manager doesn't know what a CMDB is. How should the operations team explain it and what project information should be registered?

answers.text: A CMDB is a cloud provider's management console — it automatically tracks cloud resources

A CMDB (Configuration Management Database) is a central repository that stores information about IT infrastructure components called Configuration Items (CIs); it enables impact analysis (which services are affected if server X fails?), change planning, and incident diagnosis; project information to register: the new application as a CI (name, version, owner, SLA, dependencies); server/VM CIs hosting the application; database CI; network component CIs; relationships between CIs (application depends on database; application runs on VM; VM runs on physical host)
A CMDB only tracks physical hardware — software and services don't have CMDB entries
The CMDB stores project financial data — it tracks project budgets and actual costs

explanations.c: A cloud provider's management console (AWS Console, Azure Portal) shows cloud resources in that specific cloud provider. A CMDB is organization-wide and spans all IT assets — cloud and on-premises.
explanations.d: CMDB (CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT DATABASE): PURPOSE: centralized repository of all IT assets and their relationships — the 'single source of truth' for IT infrastructure; CONFIGURATION ITEMS (CIs): any component that needs to be managed to deliver IT services; CI ATTRIBUTES: unique identifier; name and type; version/model; owner (who is responsible?); status (active, decommissioned); SLA; location; relationships to other CIs; RELATIONSHIP TYPES: depends on (application depends on database); hosted on (application runs on VM); connected to (server connected to network switch); IMPACT ANALYSIS USE CASE: IT team receives incident: 'Database server DB-04 is down'; CMDB lookup: what CIs depend on DB-04?; result: Applications A, B, C depend on DB-04; now the incident team knows that A, B, C are all potentially impacted; they can proactively alert business users of those applications; without CMDB: incident team must ask around 'does anyone know what runs on DB-04?' — slower and error-prone. CHANGE MANAGEMENT USE CASE: before a maintenance window on DB-04: CMDB shows dependent applications; change manager ensures owners of A, B, C are notified; PROJECT CMDB REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS: the new application gets its own CI with all attributes; server/VM CIs are updated to show the new application running on them; database CI created (or the existing DB server CI updated); all dependency relationships added to the CMDB; CMDB IS NOT AUTOMATIC: unless the organization has automated discovery tools, CIs must be manually registered — the project must include CMDB registration as a closing activity.
explanations.a: CMDBs track ALL types of Configuration Items: software (applications, database instances, operating systems); hardware (servers, network devices, storage arrays); virtual resources (VMs, cloud instances, containers); services (service catalog entries); contracts and SLAs; relationships between all of these.
explanations.b: CMDB tracks infrastructure assets and their relationships — not financial data. Financial management (project costs, budgets) is tracked in financial systems and ERP.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — service catalog; service request management; user self-service
questions.text: The operations team says: 'Before go-live, the new HR portal must be added to the service catalog.' The project manager asks what a service catalog is and what information it needs. How should the operations team explain it?

answers.text: A service catalog is a project portfolio list — it tracks all active projects in the organization

A service catalog is the IT equivalent of a restaurant menu — it lists all IT services available to users; for the HR portal, the service catalog entry needs: service name and description (what it does); who can use it (eligible users/departments); how to access it (URL); available support hours; what to do when it's not working (contact service desk); how to request access; SLA targets; the catalog enables users to find and request services without needing to know the IT team
A service catalog is only for hardware procurement — it lists hardware products employees can order
The service catalog lists all IT staff and their contact information — a staff directory

explanations.b: A service catalog is for IT services, not project tracking. Project portfolios are tracked in PPM (Project Portfolio Management) tools.
explanations.d: SERVICE CATALOG: WHAT IT IS: a comprehensive list of IT services available to users and customers; each entry describes a service and how to use/request it; TYPES OF SERVICE CATALOG ENTRIES: BUSINESS SERVICES (user-facing): HR portal, email, CRM, financial reporting — services users directly interact with; IT SERVICES (technical): virtual machine provisioning, database backup, network access — services IT teams consume; WHAT A SERVICE CATALOG ENTRY CONTAINS: SERVICE NAME: 'HR Employee Self-Service Portal'; DESCRIPTION: 'Allows employees to view pay stubs, request time off, update personal information, and access training records'; ELIGIBLE USERS: All full-time employees and managers; AVAILABILITY: 24/7 (planned maintenance window: Sunday 2-4 AM); HOW TO ACCESS: [URL] — single sign-on with corporate credentials; SUPPORT: IT Service Desk at [contact]; support hours: Monday-Friday 8 AM - 6 PM; SLA: 99.5% availability; P1 incidents resolved within 2 hours; WHAT'S NOT INCLUDED (out of scope): changing employment terms; approving job requisitions; RELATED REQUESTS: access request for new employee [link]; password reset [link]; report a technical issue [link]; PROJECT RESPONSIBILITY FOR SERVICE CATALOG: writing the service catalog entry is a project closing deliverable; must be reviewed and approved by: the business owner (is the description accurate?); the IT service desk (are the support procedures correct?); published before go-live (users need to know the service exists); SERVICE REQUEST MANAGEMENT: when a user submits a request through the catalog (e.g., 'Request access for new employee'), the ITSM tool creates a service request ticket routed to the appropriate team for fulfillment.
explanations.c: Service catalogs cover ALL types of IT services — applications, infrastructure services, user support, access requests.
explanations.a: A service catalog documents IT services, not IT staff. Staff contact information may be linked from the catalog but isn't the catalog itself.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — knowledge management; knowledge base; known error database; continual improvement
questions.text: After go-live, the service desk handles 200 tickets in the first month. The service manager notices that 60% are the same 5 issues. She creates knowledge base articles for each issue. How does knowledge management improve IT service delivery and what should the project have provided?

answers.text: Knowledge management enables: faster incident resolution (agents find the known solution instead of reinventing it); ticket deflection via self-service (users solve their own issues); continual improvement through lesson capture; the project should have provided initial knowledge base articles based on known issues discovered in testing — preventing the service desk from learning the same lessons through 200 production tickets
Knowledge base articles are only useful for IT staff — end users cannot benefit from documented solutions
Knowledge management replaces the need for a service desk — a comprehensive knowledge base eliminates all support tickets
Knowledge base articles should only be created for hardware issues — software issues are too complex to document

explanations.d: KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT IN ITSM: ITIL KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT PURPOSE: capture organizational knowledge; make it available to those who need it; use it to improve service quality; KNOWLEDGE ARTICLES — TYPES: KNOWN ERROR RECORDS: root cause identified; workaround available; permanent fix planned; enables support agents to quickly apply the workaround without reinvestigating; INCIDENT RESOLUTION ARTICLES: step-by-step resolution procedures for common incidents; SELF-SERVICE ARTICLES: user-facing how-to guides; FAQs; troubleshooting steps users can follow themselves; HOW KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT IMPROVES SERVICE: FASTER RESOLUTION: Tier 1 agent searches for 'HR portal login error 401'; finds the knowledge article; applies the resolution in 5 minutes instead of 45 minutes; TICKET DEFLECTION: user searches knowledge base; finds self-service resolution; never contacts service desk → reduces ticket volume by 20-40%; ONBOARDING NEW AGENTS: new service desk agents can handle issues on day 1 by following knowledge articles; CONTINUAL IMPROVEMENT: knowledge articles capture solutions to recurring issues → input to problem management (permanent fix opportunities); 60% of 200 tickets being the same 5 issues = 120 preventable tickets/month IF knowledge articles existed from day 1. WHAT THE PROJECT SHOULD HAVE PROVIDED: based on issues discovered in: UAT (what did users struggle with?); performance testing (what performance issues emerged?); security testing (what error messages confused users?); the project team should have written initial knowledge base articles covering: known issues and workarounds; common user errors and corrections; troubleshooting steps for the most common scenarios; this transfers project knowledge to operations and prevents repeated discovery.
explanations.a: End-user knowledge base articles (user-facing FAQs and guides) are specifically designed for Tier 0 self-service — users solving their own issues without contacting the service desk.
explanations.b: Knowledge management reduces ticket volume but doesn't eliminate all tickets — novel issues, complex technical failures, and issues requiring human judgment will always generate tickets.
explanations.c: Knowledge base articles are equally (or more) valuable for software issues — software issues have specific error messages, specific causes, and documented resolutions that are very well-suited to knowledge base documentation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — PMO; Project Management Office types; supportive directive controlling
questions.text: A project manager is joining an organization that has a PMO. The PMO director says they operate a 'directive PMO.' What are the three PMO types and what level of control does each exercise over project managers?

answers.text: There is only one type of PMO — all PMOs function identically regardless of organization
A directive PMO is the weakest type — it only provides direction without enforcement
PMOs always have full authority over all project decisions — project managers have no autonomy

SUPPORTIVE PMO: provides templates, training, and best practices; project managers are free to use them or not; lowest control; acts as a consultant; CONTROLLING PMO: provides standards that must be followed; project managers comply with defined processes, tools, and templates; moderate control; DIRECTIVE PMO: directly manages projects; project managers work for the PMO; highest control; PMO directly assigns PMs to projects and has complete oversight

explanations.c: PMO structures vary significantly in their control level and organizational role. The right structure depends on organizational culture, project complexity, and governance maturity.
explanations.b: A directive PMO has the HIGHEST control — it directly manages projects and project managers.
explanations.a: PMOs vary from consultative (supportive) to fully directive — they don't all have full authority.
explanations.d: PMO TYPE COMPARISON: SUPPORTIVE PMO (LOW CONTROL): FUNCTION: consultative; provides resources for PMs to use optionally; OFFERINGS: project management templates (charter, WBS, RAID log); training programs; methodology guidance; best practice repository; CONTROL: project managers may choose whether to use PMO resources; no mandatory compliance; ORGANIZATIONAL FIT: organizations with experienced PMs who value autonomy; organizations early in PMO maturity; BENEFIT: improves project management capability without being prescriptive. CONTROLLING PMO (MEDIUM CONTROL): FUNCTION: defines standards that all project managers must follow; REQUIREMENTS: PMs must use defined tools (specific PM software); follow defined processes (change control process, risk management process); report in standardized formats; pass defined stage gates; CONTROL: compliance monitoring; PMO reviews project artifacts for process adherence; ORGANIZATIONAL FIT: organizations with variable PM quality that need consistency; regulated industries needing audit trails; BENEFIT: consistent, auditable project management across the organization. DIRECTIVE PMO (HIGH CONTROL): FUNCTION: directly manages projects; project managers are PMO employees; MANAGEMENT: PMO director allocates PMs to projects; PMO has direct oversight of all project decisions; project managers report to PMO director, not to business unit managers; CONTROL: highest; PMO owns the project management function; ORGANIZATIONAL FIT: large, complex organizations where project management is a core competency; engineering firms, consulting firms, government program offices; BENEFIT: consistent, high-quality project management; specialized PM expertise; centralized resource allocation.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — portfolio vs. program vs. project; hierarchy; scope differences
questions.text: An organization is implementing a digital transformation initiative. It includes: 5 separate IT projects (ERP, CRM, data warehouse, security modernization, cloud migration); some projects share resources and have dependencies; and all 5 must collectively achieve 'digital transformation.' How should this be organized — as projects, a program, or a portfolio?

answers.text: Treat all 5 as identical — all work is managed the same regardless of interdependencies

Manage as a PROGRAM: a program is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits and control that wouldn't be available from managing them individually; program management is appropriate because: the 5 projects have interdependencies; they share resources; their collective goal (digital transformation) is greater than the sum of individual project goals; a program manager coordinates across all 5 projects; the overall business benefit is realized at the program level

Manage as a PORTFOLIO: a portfolio is a collection of projects and programs managed to meet strategic business objectives; portfolios don't necessarily have interdependencies or shared goals — they share funding and strategic direction only
Manage as one large project: one project charter, one WBS covering all 5 initiatives simultaneously

explanations.d: Projects with interdependencies and shared resources cannot be managed identically in isolation — the dependencies create coordination requirements that individual project management doesn't address.
explanations.a: PROGRAM vs. PORTFOLIO vs. PROJECT: PROJECT: SCOPE: defined and specific deliverables; DURATION: temporary (has start and end); MANAGEMENT: project manager; EXAMPLE: 'Implement the new CRM system'; one of the 5 digital transformation projects. PROGRAM: DEFINITION: a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually; SCOPE: broader than individual projects; encompasses the collective benefit; CHARACTERISTICS: projects within the program have: INTERDEPENDENCIES (ERP data feeds the data warehouse; cloud migration is a prerequisite for security modernization); SHARED RESOURCES (the data engineering team works on both data warehouse and cloud migration); COLLECTIVE BENEFIT REALIZATION (digital transformation is only achieved when all 5 projects complete and integrate — no single project achieves it alone); PROGRAM MANAGER: coordinates across projects; manages cross-project dependencies and shared resources; manages collective program-level risks; reports progress on the overall transformation benefit; WHY PROGRAM (NOT PORTFOLIO) FOR THIS CASE: all 5 projects are actively interdependent; portfolio management would treat them as more independent (different strategies competing for funding); these 5 are all pursuing the SAME strategic goal (digital transformation) with explicit interdependencies. PORTFOLIO: DEFINITION: a collection of projects, programs, and operational work managed to achieve strategic objectives; SCOPE: entire IT investment; NO REQUIRED INTERDEPENDENCY: portfolio includes projects that may be unrelated (the digital transformation program AND an unrelated facilities management system upgrade AND an HR analytics project — all in the IT portfolio but pursuing different strategies); PORTFOLIO MANAGER: allocates resources and funding across projects/programs; selects and prioritizes investments.
explanations.b: A portfolio could be the right answer if the 5 projects were independent — but the interdependencies (ERP → data warehouse; cloud migration → security modernization) specifically require coordinated program management.
explanations.c: One large project charter for 5 complex initiatives is impractical — the scope would be unmanageable, the team size unwieldy, and the individual initiatives lose their focused accountability.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — benefits realization; business case validation; post-project value
questions.text: An organization approved a $2M ERP project with a business case promising $500K annual cost savings. The project delivered successfully. Two years later, no one has measured whether the savings were realized. The CFO asks: 'Did we get the return we expected?' What is benefits realization management and how should it have been implemented?

answers.text: Benefits are automatically realized when a project is delivered — no measurement is needed
Benefits realization is the finance team's responsibility — project managers don't track post-project value

Benefits realization management ensures the business value promised in the business case is actually achieved; it should include: defining measurable benefit indicators (cost savings per process, headcount reduction, cycle time reduction) in the business case; assigning a benefit owner (who is accountable for realizing the benefit?); measuring baseline before the project starts; measuring actual performance at 6-month and 12-month post-go-live intervals; taking corrective action if benefits are not materializing (adoption issue? scope shortfall?); reporting to the sponsor on benefits achieved
Benefits realization management means ensuring the project budget was spent correctly — financial compliance is the metric

explanations.c: Benefits are not automatically realized — they require deliberate measurement, management, and sometimes corrective action. Many projects deliver their technical scope but fail to achieve business benefits due to adoption failures, scope shortfalls, or changing business conditions.
explanations.d: Benefits realization management is a project management and organizational responsibility — the project manager defines the measurement framework; the business owner is accountable for realizing the benefits; the PMO often tracks benefits across the portfolio.
explanations.a: BENEFITS REALIZATION MANAGEMENT: THE PROBLEM DESCRIBED: $2M spent; $500K/year savings promised; no measurement 2 years later = the organization has no idea if it got its money back; if benefits weren't realized (due to low adoption, scope shortfall, or poor process change), the organization has wasted $2M without correction. WHAT IS BENEFITS REALIZATION MANAGEMENT (BRM): the practice of ensuring that the business outcomes promised in the business case are actually achieved; BENEFITS REALIZATION LIFECYCLE: (1) BENEFIT IDENTIFICATION: during business case development: what specific, measurable improvements will this project produce?; $500K savings must be decomposed: '$200K from headcount reduction in AP department (4 FTE → 2 FTE); $150K from reduced vendor invoice processing time; $100K from eliminating duplicate data entry; $50K from reduced error correction'; (2) BENEFIT BASELINE: BEFORE the project begins, measure the current state of each benefit indicator: current AP headcount, current invoice processing time, current error rate; without this baseline, 'before vs. after' comparison is impossible; (3) BENEFIT OWNER ASSIGNMENT: who is accountable for ensuring the benefit is achieved? (typically a business executive, not the PM); the PM delivers the capability; the benefit owner drives adoption and process change; (4) BENEFIT MEASUREMENT INTERVALS: 6-month post-go-live: early adoption and initial savings measured; 12-month: full-year comparison to baseline; (5) CORRECTIVE ACTION: if benefits are below target: adoption issue → additional training; scope shortfall → Phase 2 project; process change not happening → executive mandate; (6) BENEFITS REPORT: formal report to sponsor/board comparing promised vs. actual benefits; closes the accountability loop.
explanations.b: Financial compliance (was the budget spent correctly?) is project audit activity — not benefits realization. Benefits realization focuses on BUSINESS OUTCOMES, not budget compliance.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — IT governance; COBIT; TOGAF; IT governance structures
questions.text: A new CIO says: 'We're implementing COBIT for IT governance.' A project manager asks: 'What is IT governance and how does it affect how projects are managed?' How should the CIO explain it?

answers.text: IT governance is a concept only for IT teams — project managers are not involved

IT governance is the framework of structures, processes, and leadership that ensures IT investments align with business objectives and deliver value within acceptable risk levels; COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology) is a widely used IT governance framework; for project managers, IT governance means: projects require formal business case justification; project approval follows a defined portfolio process; project progress is reported to governance bodies (steering committee); project closure includes benefits realization measurement; project changes require formal change control
COBIT is a programming language for IT governance automation
IT governance only applies to IT departments in large enterprises — smaller organizations and non-IT projects are exempt

explanations.b: IT governance directly affects how projects are selected, approved, executed, and measured — project managers operate within the governance framework that IT governance defines.
explanations.a: IT GOVERNANCE AND COBIT: IT GOVERNANCE DEFINITION: the framework through which IT decisions are made and accountabilities established; ensures: IT investments align with business strategy; IT risks are managed appropriately; IT resources are used efficiently; IT performance is measured and reported. IT GOVERNANCE COMPONENTS: STRUCTURES: who makes IT decisions (steering committee, CIO, PMO, project boards)?; PROCESSES: how are IT decisions made (project approval process, portfolio review cadence, risk management process)?; RELATIONAL MECHANISMS: how do IT and business communicate (steering committees, service reviews, portfolio governance forums)?. COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology): PUBLISHER: ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association); SCOPE: enterprise governance of information and technology; COBIT 2019 KEY AREAS: governance system (how the enterprise directs and oversees IT); management system (how IT operations are planned, built, run, and monitored); COBIT GOVERNANCE OBJECTIVES (relevant to PMs): EDM02 — Ensure Benefits Delivery: projects must demonstrate ROI; EDM03 — Ensure Risk Optimization: risks must be identified and managed; APO05 — Manage Portfolio: projects are selected based on strategic alignment and value; BAI01 — Manage Programs and Projects: project management standards applied consistently. HOW COBIT AFFECTS PROJECT MANAGERS: FORMAL BUSINESS CASES: all projects above a threshold require formal ROI justification; PORTFOLIO GOVERNANCE: project selection is based on strategic value, not who asks loudest; REGULAR REPORTING: projects report to governance forums; STANDARDIZED PM PRACTICES: COBIT requires consistent project management practices across the organization; BENEFITS TRACKING: project ROI must be tracked post-delivery.
explanations.c: COBIT is an IT governance framework (a set of practices and policies) — not a programming language.
explanations.d: IT governance principles apply to all organizations that use technology — the formality scales with size, but even small organizations benefit from basic IT governance (IT investment justification; risk management).

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — project sponsor; sponsor accountability; sponsor effectiveness
questions.text: A project is struggling — the team lacks direction, the budget is insufficient, and stakeholders aren't engaged. The project manager suspects the project sponsor is not fulfilling their role. What are a project sponsor's key responsibilities and what does an ineffective sponsor create?

answers.text: An effective project sponsor: champions the project at the executive level; provides strategic direction; resolves issues the PM cannot resolve at their authority level; removes organizational barriers; ensures adequate resource allocation; makes scope/schedule/budget decisions when escalated; provides final acceptance; aligns stakeholders; an ineffective sponsor creates: resource conflicts (no one to resolve competing priorities); scope confusion (no authority to make final decisions); stakeholder disengagement (no executive champion); project drift (unclear strategic direction)
Project sponsors are responsible only for budget approval — all other decisions belong to the PM
The project sponsor only signs the project charter — their role ends after initiation
The sponsor replaces the project manager — if the sponsor is present, no PM is needed

explanations.d: PROJECT SPONSOR RESPONSIBILITIES: CHAMPION: the sponsor is the project's organizational champion at the executive level; they communicate project value to senior leadership; they build organizational support for the project; STRATEGIC DIRECTION: the sponsor ensures the project stays aligned with organizational strategy; if strategy changes, the sponsor decides whether the project continues, pivots, or cancels; GOVERNANCE AUTHORITY: final decision authority on: scope changes beyond the PM's authority; budget increases beyond contingency; schedule changes affecting committed dates; STAKEHOLDER ALIGNMENT: the sponsor uses their executive position to align other stakeholders; a PM asking a peer department head to prioritize project support has less authority than the sponsor asking; ESCALATION RESOLUTION: when the PM faces: resource conflicts that functional managers won't resolve; organizational barriers that prevent progress; decisions requiring executive judgment; the sponsor resolves these issues that exceed the PM's authority; RESOURCE ADVOCACY: ensures the project has the people, budget, and tools it needs; intervenes when resources are pulled away inappropriately; FINAL ACCEPTANCE: formally accepts the project deliverables; WHAT AN INEFFECTIVE SPONSOR CREATES: RESOURCE STARVATION: without a champion, project resources are pulled by competing priorities ('the sponsor would never know...'); SCOPE CONFUSION: no authority to make binding decisions — everything is contested; DECISION PARALYSIS: escalations have nowhere to go — the PM cannot resolve executive-level conflicts alone; STAKEHOLDER DISENGAGEMENT: without executive championing, stakeholders deprioritize project engagement; STRATEGIC DRIFT: project continues after the original business case is no longer valid (no one with authority to stop it or redirect it).
explanations.b: Sponsors are responsible for far more than budget: strategic alignment, stakeholder management, organizational barriers, and final decisions on major changes.
explanations.c: The sponsor's role is active throughout the project lifecycle — they are accountable for project success and must actively engage with governance decisions, escalations, and stakeholder alignment.
explanations.a: The sponsor and project manager serve complementary roles: the sponsor provides executive authority and organizational leadership; the PM provides day-to-day project management and delivery leadership.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — project governance; steering committee; governance framework; decision authority
questions.text: A large financial services project has a steering committee, a Change Control Board (CCB), a project manager, and work-stream leads. A stakeholder is confused about which body makes which decisions. How should the PM clarify the governance structure?

answers.text: All decisions should go to the steering committee — they have the authority to decide everything
A project governance structure is only needed for government projects — commercial projects operate without governance
Work-stream leads have the same authority as the steering committee — all decisions are equal

The governance structure defines decision authority by decision type: Steering Committee — strategic decisions (major scope changes, budget increases >15%, go/no-go decisions, project continuation or cancellation); CCB — change control decisions within defined thresholds (scope change evaluation, RFC assessment); PM — operational decisions (task assignments, minor schedule adjustments, vendor status management); Work-stream Leads — technical/execution decisions within their work-stream; clear decision authority prevents escalation overload and enables efficient project execution

explanations.a: If every decision goes to the steering committee, the PM's role is redundant and the steering committee becomes overwhelmed with operational details they shouldn't need to manage. Governance structures exist to route decisions to the appropriate level.
explanations.b: All projects benefit from clear governance — even small commercial projects need clarity on who makes what decisions. The formality scales with project complexity and organizational size.
explanations.c: Work-stream leads have authority within their domain (technical decisions for their team) — not organization-wide strategic or financial decisions.
explanations.d: PROJECT GOVERNANCE DECISION AUTHORITY MATRIX: STEERING COMMITTEE AUTHORITY: STRATEGIC DECISIONS: approve changes to project objectives or business case; authorize additional budget beyond the PM's threshold; make go/no-go decisions at phase gates; decide whether to continue, pivot, or cancel the project; resolve major conflicts between organizational units; MEETING FREQUENCY: monthly or at phase gates; COMPOSITION: executive sponsor, senior business stakeholders, CIO/CTO (as appropriate). CHANGE CONTROL BOARD (CCB) AUTHORITY: CHANGE DECISIONS: evaluate change requests within defined financial and schedule thresholds; for high-risk or high-cost changes: escalate to steering committee; for changes within thresholds: approve or reject; assess impact of proposed changes; MEETING FREQUENCY: weekly or as needed; COMPOSITION: PM (chairs), key technical leads, business representative, PMO. PROJECT MANAGER AUTHORITY: OPERATIONAL DECISIONS: daily task management and team direction; vendor status meetings and relationship management; schedule adjustments within defined buffers; risk responses within the contingency budget; escalation of issues to the CCB or steering committee when they exceed PM authority. WORK-STREAM LEADS AUTHORITY: TECHNICAL DECISIONS: design and implementation decisions within their work-stream; technical risk management; resource assignment within their team. DECISION ROUTING TABLE: change request adds 3 days to schedule → PM authority (within schedule buffer); change request adds 3 weeks to schedule → CCB review; change request adds 3 months to schedule → Steering Committee; $15K budget increase → PM authority (within contingency); $150K budget increase → Steering Committee. BENEFIT OF CLEAR GOVERNANCE: each party knows what they can decide; escalations are appropriate and targeted; the steering committee focuses on strategic issues; the PM is empowered to manage operations.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — project KPIs; success metrics; OKRs; outcome vs. output measurement
questions.text: A PMO is establishing project success metrics beyond the traditional scope/schedule/cost triangle. They want to measure whether projects deliver real business value. What metrics should be included and how does outcome measurement differ from output measurement?

answers.text: Only schedule and budget metrics are relevant — scope, quality, and business outcomes don't need measurement
Projects should only be measured at completion — in-flight metrics are unnecessary

Outcome metrics measure whether the project achieved business value (NPS improvement, revenue growth, cost reduction, user adoption rate, productivity improvement); output metrics measure what was delivered (features deployed, stories completed, milestones achieved); effective project measurement includes both: outputs confirm delivery; outcomes confirm value; the failure to measure outcomes leads to organizations that deliver on time/budget but fail to achieve business results
All project metrics are the same as financial accounting metrics — use P&L and balance sheet data

explanations.b: Schedule and budget metrics tell you whether you spent resources efficiently — they don't tell you whether the project achieved anything useful. A project delivered on time and on budget that nobody uses is a failure.
explanations.d: In-flight metrics enable early course correction — waiting until completion to measure means problems discovered are too late to fix.
explanations.c: OUTPUT vs. OUTCOME METRICS: OUTPUT METRICS (WHAT WAS BUILT): these measure project DELIVERY; examples: number of user stories completed; features deployed to production; milestones achieved on schedule; budget spent vs. authorized; defect count at go-live; team velocity (story points per sprint); LIMITATION: a project can deliver all outputs and still fail to create business value (if nobody uses the features built); OUTCOME METRICS (WHAT VALUE WAS CREATED): these measure business IMPACT; examples: USER ADOPTION RATE: % of target users actively using the system 30/60/90 days post-go-live (target: >80%); PROCESS EFFICIENCY: time to complete the target process before vs. after (e.g., invoice processing: 3 days → 1 day); COST SAVINGS: actual $ savings realized vs. business case projection; REVENUE IMPACT: revenue increase attributable to the project; CUSTOMER SATISFACTION: NPS score or CSAT improvement; ERROR RATE REDUCTION: reduction in process errors or system defects; COMPLETE PROJECT METRICS FRAMEWORK: DURING THE PROJECT (in-flight): SPI (schedule performance index); CPI (cost performance index); defect density; sprint velocity trend; AT GO-LIVE (output): features delivered vs. committed; go-live criteria met Y/N; POST-GO-LIVE (outcome): adoption rate; process efficiency; cost savings vs. business case; EXAMPLE: an ERP implementation is measured on: IN-FLIGHT: SPI=0.95 (on schedule); CPI=0.98 (on budget); AT GO-LIVE: 12 of 12 modules deployed; all acceptance criteria met; POST-GO-LIVE (6 months): order processing time: 4 days → 1.5 days (outcome met); user adoption: 94% of target users active (outcome met); error rate: 8% reduction (outcome met); cost savings: $380K vs. $500K projected (outcome partially met — investigate gap).
explanations.a: Project metrics are specific to project performance and business outcomes — they're not the same as financial accounting metrics.

questions.name: Basics of IT and Governance
questions.keyword: IT Service Management — project portfolio selection; risk vs. return; investment decision; strategic alignment
questions.text: An organization's IT portfolio has 8 project proposals competing for $5M in funding. A portfolio manager says: 'We need to balance strategic alignment, ROI, and risk in our selection.' How does portfolio-level project selection work and what criteria matter?

answers.text: Select the projects with the highest ROI — maximize return is always the right criterion
Select projects randomly — any selection method introduces bias
